questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: DNA packing is done by?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Histone

DNA packaging in eukaryotic cells is carried out by histone proteins, which help condense long DNA molecules into a compact, organized structure within the nucleus.

• DNA wraps around histone octamers (2 each of H2A, H2B, H3, H4) forming nucleosomes
• Nucleosomes further coil to form chromatin fibers and ultimately chromosomes

Functions of histones:

• DNA compaction (fits long DNA into nucleus)
• Regulation of gene expression (via histone modification like acetylation, methylation)

Why other options are incorrect:

• Glycoprotein: Not involved in DNA packaging
• Nucleic acid: DNA itself, not responsible for packing
• Helicases: Enzymes that unwind DNA during replication, not packaging

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: During surgery for patent ductus arteriosus, which anatomical structure is most susceptible to injury?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Left recurrent laryngeal nerve

The left recurrent laryngeal nerve is most susceptible to injury during surgery for patent ductus arteriosus.

The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the 6th arch artery while the right recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the 4th arch artery. This occurs because the distal portion of the 6th arch disappears on the right side along with the 5th arch artery. Thus the nerve on the right side loops under the 4th arch artery.

The patent ductus arteriosus is due to a defect in the 6th aortic arch, also known as the pulmonary arch, as it gives off a branch to the growing lung bud. On the right side, this arch forms the right pulmonary artery proximally and disappears distally. On the left side, the distal part remains patent to form the ductus arteriosus that shunts blood from the right ventricle to the dorsal aorta. This is obliterated after birth forming the ligamentum arteriosum. If the ductus arteriosus remains patent after birth, it is referred to as patent ductus arteriosus.

Pearl PF0428: Derivatives of Various Aortic Arches

The aortic arches or pharyngeal arch arteries are a series of six paired embryological vascular structures which give rise to the great arteries of the neck and head. They are ventral to the dorsal aorta and arise from the aortic sac.

The following table shows various arterial structures derived from the aortic arches:

Aortic arches

Arterial Structures

Third aortic arches

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What condition is an absolute contraindication for breastfeeding?
questions.explanation: While breastfeeding is almost always the ideal nutritional source, there are a few rare absolute contraindications. Classic Galactosemia in the infant (Option B) is an absolute contraindication because the baby lacks the enzyme to metabolize galactose, a component of the lactose found in breast milk. Continued breastfeeding in these infants leads to liver failure, cataracts, and mental retardation. HIV-positive status in the mother (Option A) is a contraindication in developed nations, but in developing countries, the WHO recommends breastfeeding with antiretroviral therapy if safe alternatives are unavailable. Hepatitis C (Option C) is not a contraindication provided nipples are not cracked or bleeding. For Tuberculosis (Option D), breastfeeding is only temporarily suspended until the mother is non-infectious; it is not an absolute, lifelong contraindication for that child. Therefore, galactosemia is the only infant-related metabolic condition listed that requires the absolute cessation of all breast milk

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Identify the marked structure in the eye.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Canal of Petit

The marked structure represents the Canal of Petit.

In front of the anterior hyaloid membrane and behind the ciliary body and zonule is the capsulohyaloid sinus (or space), or Petit's canal. This is one of the sites of retrolental hemorrhages. This is also the route along which blood sometimes enters the lens, through some rupture in the posterior lens capsule.

Other options-

Option A: Posterior capsule of lens has circular adhesions with anterior hyaloid surface called as the hyaloideocapsular ligaments of Weiger or retrolental ligament. The circular attachment is known as Egger's line. The potential space between the anterior hyaloid face and the posterior lense capsule with the circular attachment is referred to as the Berger's space.

Option B: Lens capsule is a thin, transparent, hyaline membrane surrounding the lens which is thicker over the anterior than the posterior surface

Option C: The canal of Hannover lies between orbiculo-anterocapsular and orbiculo-posterocapsular parts of zonular fibers.
questions.learning: Canal of Petit — The marked structure represents the Canal of Petit. In front of the anterior hyaloid membrane and behind the ciliary body and zonule is the capsulohyaloid sinus (or space), or Petit's canal.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A total of 60 patients were diagnosed with COVID-19, out of which 12 cases of deaths were reported. Calculate the case fatality rate.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 20%

In this scenario, among 60 diagnosed COVID-19 patients, 12 deaths were recorded, resulting in a case fatality rate of 20%.

The case fatality rate is determined using the formula: (Number of deaths from a specific disease / Total number of cases of the same disease) × 100. Applying this formula: (12 deaths / 60 cases) × 100 = 20%.

Case Fatality Rate (CFR) is a key epidemiological measure used to assess the severity of a disease by indicating the proportion of deaths among diagnosed cases. It is calculated using the formula: (Number of deaths due to a specific disease / Total number of confirmed cases) × 100.

CFR helps in understanding the lethality of an infection and is crucial in public health planning and response strategies. A higher CFR suggests a more severe disease or inadequate healthcare interventions, while a lower CFR indicates better treatment outcomes and disease management. However, CFR may vary based on factors such as healthcare access, population demographics, and disease reporting accuracy.

Pearl PF0955: Case Fatality Rate

* Case fatality rate =  (Total number of deaths due to a particular disease)/(Total number of cases due to the same disease)x 100

* It is a good indicator of severity or killing power of a disease.

* It is used mostly in acute and infectious diseases.

* No time interval is used.

* Case fatality rate is closely related to virulence.

* Limitation of CFR is that its usefulness for chronic diseases is limited because the period from onset to death is variable.

* It is expressed in percentage.

* CFR is an incidence proportion and not a true rate.

* CFR may vary for the same disease in different epidemics.

*

Case fatality of a few diseases:

* Rabies - 100% especially after symptoms manifest

* Ebola - 25 to 90%, average - 50%

* Yellow fever - 15 to 50%

* Chicken pox - 0.001%

* Diseases with a high case fatality rate: Tetanus, Rabies, Botulism, Ebola.

* Diseases with a low case fatality rate: Leprosy, Trachoma, Lymphatic filariasis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Chimeric DNA is associated with:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Organ transplantation

Chimeric DNA is associated with organ transplantation, especially bone-marrow transplantation.

In organ transplantation, chimeric DNA refers to the mixture of donor and recipient genetic material that occurs when donor cells begin functioning within the recipient's body. It is used for long-term monitoring of bone marrow transplant recipients. Detecting changes in the levels of donor-derived cells can provide early warning signs of graft failure, rejection, or relapse of underlying disease.

Note: The practical applications of recombinant DNA technology include:

• Gene mapping using techniques such as fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH).
• Producing proteins such as:

• Interferons, tPA (tissue plasminogen activator)
• Insulin, growth hormone
• Hepatitis B vaccine

• Molecular analysis of disease, to detect gene variations and mutations.
• Restriction Fragment Length polymorphism (RFLP) and single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)
• Microsatellite DNA polymorphisms
• Gene therapy and bone marrow transplantation

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which biomarker is the earliest to rise in the event of a myocardial infarction (MI)?
questions.explanation: In the evolution of biomarkers for acute coronary syndrome, Ischemia Modified Albumin (IMA) is recognized as one of the earliest markers to rise, often becoming elevated within minutes of the onset of ischemia, even before actual myocardial necrosis occurs. However, it is not very specific. Among the traditional markers of necrosis, Myoglobin is the first to rise (within 1-2 hours). CK-MB (Option A) typically begins to rise at 4-6 hours. Troponins (Option B) are the gold standard for diagnosis due to their extreme specificity but usually take 3-6 hours to become detectable in the blood. LDH (Option C) is a late marker, rising after 24 hours and staying elevated for a week. In modern clinical practice, high-sensitivity troponin assays have significantly shortened the "blind spot" for diagnosis. While IMA is physiologically the earliest, its lack of specificity means that Troponin remains the most clinically important marker for confirming a myocardial infarction in the emergency department
questions.learning: In the evolution of biomarkers for acute coronary syndrome, Ischemia Modified Albumin (IMA) is recognized as one of the earliest markers to rise, often becoming elevated within minutes of the onset of ischemia, even before actual myocardial necrosis occurs.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A postmenopausal lady with osteoporosis is advised to remain upright for at least half an hour after administration of her medication. What side effect is being prevented by doing this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Reflux esophagitis

Bisphosphonates are used in the first-line management of postmenopausal osteoporosis. Remaining upright for 30 minutes after dosing is recommended to prevent reflux esophagitis.

Bisphosphonates are not recommended to be administered with food to minimise esophageal irritation.

Oral bisphosphonates have very limited bioavailability (<1-10%). Bisphosphonates are recommended to be administered after an overnight fast with a full glass of water at least 30 minutes before breakfast. Remaining upright for 30 minutes after dosing and proton pump inhibitors at bedtime can decrease the symptoms

Other adverse effects:

* Osteonecrosis of the jaw is associated with the use of bisphosphonates

* Atypical femur fracture - occurs in the subtrochanteric femoral region or along the shaft distal to the lesser trochanter.
questions.learning: Reflux esophagitis Bisphosphonates are used in the first-line management of postmenopausal osteoporosis. Remaining upright for 30 minutes after dosing is recommended to prevent reflux esophagitis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Cytochrome oxidase is inhibited in all of the following poisonings except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Methane

Cytochrome oxidase is a hemoprotein, which is the terminal component of the respiratory chain carriers (complex IV) in mitochondria. The action of cytochrome oxidase is inhibited in carbon monoxide, cyanide, and hydrogen sulfide poisoning, resulting in prevention of cellular respiration.

Hemoproteins are metalloproteins that have a typical heme prosthetic group. They are present in myoglobin, hemoglobin, and other cytochromes. Cytochrome oxidase contains two molecules of heme, each having one Fe atom that oscillates between Fe3+ and Fe2+ during oxidation and reduction. It also contains two atoms of copper, each associated with a heme unit.

Complexes  of ETC  :

Complex I: NADH-CoQ oxidoreductase
Contains - FeS, FMN, Coenzyme Q
Inhibitors – Rotenone

Complex II: Succinate-CoQ reductase
Contains - FeS, Coenzyme Q
Inhibitor - Carboxin

Complex III: CoQH2-cytochrome c oxidoreductase
Contains - cytochrome c, b, C1, and FeS
Inhibitor - Antimycin A

Complex IV: cytochrome oxidase
Contains - Cytochrome a, a3, and Copper
Inhibitor - Cyanide, Azide, Carbon monoxide

Complex V (informally): ATP Synthase
Inhibitor - Oligomycin

Note: MELAS (mitochondrial encephalopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke) is an inherited condition due to NADH-Q oxidoreductase (Complex I) or cytochrome oxidase (Complex IV) deficiency.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: In a Delhi-based study, 100 individuals who regularly exercised were followed for one year, after which researchers assessed how many developed coronary heart disease. What type of study design does this represent?
questions.explanation: This is a cohort study because it identifies a group of people based on an exposure (exercise) and follows them over time to observe the development of an outcome (coronary heart disease). Cohort studies are observational, longitudinal designs ideal for establishing temporal relationships and calculating incidence. Case-Control studies (Option A) start with the outcome (disease) and look back at past exposures. While this is a "Prospective study" (Option B), "cohort study" is the more specific and accurate epidemiological classification. Cross-Sectional studies (Option C) measure exposure and outcome simultaneously at a single point in time, unlike the one-year follow-up described here. By tracking the participants prospectively, researchers can directly measure the risk associated with the exercise habits of the Delhi cohort
questions.learning: This is a cohort study because it identifies a group of people based on an exposure (exercise) and follows them over time to observe the development of an outcome (coronary heart disease).

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Fishtail deformity is seen in the fracture of _____________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Distal end of humerus

Fishtail deformity is seen following a fracture of the distal end of the humerus.

Fishtail deformity of the elbow is a rare complication that can occur in childhood after a distal humeral fracture. It is characterized by a contour abnormality of the distal humerus due to the absence or resorption of the lateral trochlear ossification centers.

Fishtail deformity of the distal humerus can be of 2 types:

• The first type is a sharp-angled wedge, which commonly occurs after fractures of the lateral condyle. It is caused by the persistence of a gap between the lateral condylar physis ossification center and the medial ossification of the trochlea. Because of this gap, the lateral crista of the trochlea may be underdeveloped, which may represent a small “bony bar” in the distal humeral physis
• The second type is believed to be associated with osteonecrosis of the lateral part of the medial crista of the trochlea.
questions.learning: Distal end of humerus Fishtail deformity is seen following a fracture of the distal end of the humerus. Fishtail deformity of the elbow is a rare complication that can occur in childhood after a distal humeral fracture.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient undergoes split-thickness skin grafting for a burn injury of the arm. On the sixth postoperative day, he develops stiffness of the arm during physiotherapy. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Passive extension of the joint under direct visualization of the graft
Remove the graft and regraft the area
questions.explanation: By post-operative day 6, a split-thickness skin graft is in the early phase of fibrovascular ingrowth. If the patient develops stiffness during movement, the most appropriate management is passive extension under direct visualization. This allows the therapist to gently increase the range of motion while ensuring that the graft is not experiencing shearing forces that could cause displacement or partial loss. Surgical excision of contractures (Option A) is only performed on mature, months-old scars, not on a fresh graft. Continuing physiotherapy blindly (Option C) risks damaging the fragile graft if the stiffness is due to improper adhesion. Removing the graft (Option D) is unnecessary unless there is clear evidence of total graft failure, such as infection or necrosis. Thus, cautious supervised movement is the preferred rehabilitation strategy
questions.learning: By post-operative day 6, a split-thickness skin graft is in the early phase of fibrovascular ingrowth. If the patient develops stiffness during movement, the most appropriate management is passive extension under direct visualization.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding liquid-based cytology?
options: Study of fluid in tumour microenvironment
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Urine specimen is used

Liquid-based cytology can also be done using a urine specimen. It is commonly used in cervical cancer screening in place of a pap smear.

The advantages of liquid-based cytology are:

• The process reduces obscuring inflammatory cells and mucous, blood, and debris
• The cells are deposited on the slide in a monolayer.
• Test sensitivity is improved compared with conventional pap tests.

Liquid-based cytology has found broad acceptance in non-gynecologic cytopreparation such as:

• Thyroid cyst fluid examination.
• Oral pathology: diagnostic for various types of oral lesions.
• This technique is also used to body fluids (e.g. urine, pleural effusions), brushing samples (e.g. gastrointestinal tract, lung), and fine needle aspiration.
questions.learning: Urine specimen is used Liquid-based cytology can also be done using a urine specimen. It is commonly used in cervical cancer screening in place of a pap smear.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A young girl presents with continuous urinary dribbling despite normal voiding and has never achieved full continence since birth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical history of continuous dribbling of urine in a female patient who otherwise voids normally is the pathognomonic presentation of an Ectopic Ureter (Option A). In these cases (often associated with a duplex system), the ureter bypasses the urinary sphincter and opens into the vagina or vestibule. Because the opening is distal to the sphincter, urine leaks out continuously. However, because the other ureter is normally positioned in the bladder, the child can still void normally. Ureterocele (Option B), congenital megaureter (Option C), and Vesicoureteric reflux (Option D) are all internal urinary abnormalities that may cause infections or obstruction but do not cause this specific "leakage while voiding" paradox. Therefore, because the symptoms date back to birth and follow this unique pattern, ectopic ureter is the definitive diagnosis. Diagnosis is usually confirmed by intravenous urography or MRI. Surgical reimplantation into the bladder is the curative treatment
questions.learning: The clinical history of continuous dribbling of urine in a female patient who otherwise voids normally is the pathognomonic presentation of an Ectopic Ureter (Option A).

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A 60-year-old man collapses suddenly. He is unresponsive, not breathing normally, and has no pulse. Cardiac monitoring reveals a chaotic, disorganized rhythm with no identifiable P waves, QRS complexes, or T waves. After starting high-quality CPR, what is the next best step per ACLS protocol?
options: Deliver an unsynchronized shock at 120–200 J biphasic
Deliver an unsynchronized shock of 360 J
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Deliver an unsynchronized shock at 120–200 J biphasic

Ventricular fibrillation (VF) is a shockable cardiac arrest rhythm characterized by chaotic, disorganized ventricular electrical activity with no effective cardiac output. According to the American Heart Association (AHA) ACLS guidelines, the first intervention is immediate high-quality CPR and early defibrillation.

For a biphasic defibrillator, the recommended initial shock is 200 J (or the manufacturer’s recommended energy). Defibrillation is unsynchronized because there is no organized QRS complex to synchronize with.

Why not the other options?

| Option | Why it's wrong

| ------ | --------------

| A. Amiodarone | Reserved for shock-refractory VF/pulseless VT — given after the second shock (per current AHA algorithm), not as the initial rhythm-directed intervention

| B. Synchronized cardioversion | Requires an organized QRS to sync to; VF has none, so the defibrillator may fail to discharge at all if synchronized mode is selected

| C. Unsynchronized shock at 120-200 J biphasic dose | Correct — VF is a shockable rhythm; defibrillation (unsynchronized) is the definitive treatment, given as soon as the rhythm is confirmed and the device is ready

| D. Unsynchronized shock of 360 J | Correct energy only for monophasic defibrillators; most modern devices are biphasic, using lower doses (120–200 J, per manufacturer)
questions.learning: Deliver an unsynchronized shock at 120–200 J biphasic Ventricular fibrillation (VF) is a shockable cardiac arrest rhythm characterized by chaotic, disorganized ventricular electrical activity with no effective cardiac output.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The statement, “Health is a dynamic equilibrium between man and environment and disease a maladjustment of the human organism to environment” explains which one of the following concepts of health?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ecological

The ecological concept of health defines health as a dynamic equilibrium between the individual and the environment. Disease occurs when this balance is disturbed, leading to maladjustment between the human organism and its environment. This concept emphasizes the interaction of host, agent, and environment, which forms the basis of modern epidemiology.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  Biomedical concept:

• Defines health as the absence of disease.
• Focuses on biological causes and medical treatment, largely ignoring social and environmental factors.

• C. Psychosocial concept: Emphasizes the influence of psychological, social, cultural, economic, and political factors on health.
• D. Holistic concept: Integrates physical, mental, social, environmental, and spiritual well-being, representing the broadest concept of health.
questions.learning: Ecological — The ecological concept of health defines health as a dynamic equilibrium between the individual and the environment. Disease occurs when this balance is disturbed, leading to maladjustment between the human organism and its environment.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) is used to relieve pain. What is the mechanism behind it?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gate control theory

Gate theory of pain is the mechanism behind transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS). This method uses electrodes to activate Aα and Aβ fibres near the injury to relieve pain.
At the site of sensory afferent termination, transmission in nociceptive pathways can be interrupted. This is done by the actions within the dorsal horn of the spinal cord. Pain subsiding when the site of injury is rubbed or shook is an example. Afferents of innocuous cutaneous mechanoreceptors emit collaterals that terminate in the dorsal horn. The responsiveness of dorsal horn neurons to their input from nociceptive afferent terminals is reduced by these afferents This is called the gate-control mechanism of pain modulation.

questions.learning: Gate control theory Gate theory of pain is the mechanism behind transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS). This method uses electrodes to activate Aα and Aβ fibres near the injury to relieve pain.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A middle-aged woman presented with bilateral proptosis, restriction of eye movements, and chemosis. Her thyroid profile showed she was euthyroid. What is the most probable cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thyroid ophthalmopathy

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of thyroid ophthalmopathy.

Thyroid eye disease (TED) is the most common cause of both bilateral and unilateral proptosis in an adult in the euthyroid state. The main features of TED include lid retraction, proptosis, periorbital edema, chemosis, and restrictive myopathy.

Other options-

Option A- Orbital pseudotumor presents with painful eye movements periorbital edema, erythema, proptosis, ptosis, diplopia.

Option C- Orbital lymphoma usually presents in the 7th decade, most commonly observed as a painless palpable mass in the superolateral quadrant.

Option D- Orbital cellulitis is usually a unilateral condition with pain, proptosis, and chemosis.

NOTE: Thyroid eye disease can also, though less commonly, occur in euthyroid patients.
questions.learning: Thyroid ophthalmopathy — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of thyroid ophthalmopathy. Thyroid eye disease (TED) is the most common cause of both bilateral and unilateral proptosis in an adult in the euthyroid state.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The body of an 82-year-old man has been seen for post-mortem to know the cause of death. You are examining a histopathological slide containing a section of his cardiac tissue where you notice some pigmentation. Which is the substance that is seen in the image given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lipofuscin

Lipochrome or Lipofuscin (brown lipid) is seen as a yellow-brown pigment in the histopathological image which can be seen in the liver and heart of normal aging patients.

It is also known as a wear-and-tear pigment, which is an insoluble, brownish yellow, granular intracellular material, that accumulates in various tissues like the heart, liver, and brain as a function of age. The brown pigment in large amounts can give a characteristic appearance to the tissue called brown atrophy.

Lipofuscin (brown lipid):

* Derived through lipid peroxidation of polyunsaturated lipids of subcellular membranes.

* Not injurious to the cell or its functions.

* Indicates free radical injury and lipid peroxidation.

* Seen in cells undergoing slow, regressive changes.

* Prominent in the liver and heart of aging patients, patients with severe malnutrition, and cancer cachexia.

Other options:

Hemosiderin is a hemoglobin-derived, golden yellow to brown, granular or crystalline pigment. It is one of the major storage forms of iron and can be seen in iron-overload states like hemochromatosis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 72-year-old man presents with a weak urinary stream and increased urinary frequency with small voided volumes. He experiences dizziness and hypotension while taking prazosin. Which α-blocker would be a more appropriate alternative in this case?
questions.explanation: The patient is suffering from Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) and experiencing orthostatic hypotension and dizziness, which are common side effects of non-subtype selective alpha-1 blockers like prazosin. Prazosin blocks alpha-1 receptors on both vascular smooth muscle and the prostatic urethra, leading to systemic vasodilation. Tamsulosin is a more suitable option because it is a selective alpha-1A receptor antagonist. The alpha-1A subtype is predominantly found in the prostate and bladder neck, while the alpha-1B subtype is found in the blood vessels. By selectively targeting the prostate, Tamsulosin relaxes the smooth muscle to improve urine flow with significantly less impact on systemic blood pressure compared to Prazosin, Terazosin (Option B), or Doxazosin (Option D). Alfuzosin (Option A) is also used for BPH but Tamsulosin remains the classic choice for minimizing "first-dose" syncope and dizziness in elderly patients. This uro-selectivity makes Tamsulosin the gold standard for medical management of BPH symptoms while maintaining cardiovascular stability
questions.learning: The patient is suffering from Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) and experiencing orthostatic hypotension and dizziness, which are common side effects of non-subtype selective alpha-1 blockers like prazosin.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A woman presents with numbness of her fingertips. On examination, her face is tightened. The antinuclear antibody(ANA) is found to be positive and immunofluorescence shows the nucleolar pattern. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Systemic sclerosis

Numbness of fingers associated with Raynaud's phenomenon, facial tightening, positive anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA) with nucleolar pattern in immunofluorescence is highly suggestive of systemic sclerosis.

Systemic sclerosis/ scleroderma:

Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is an autoimmune connective tissue disorder that results in fibrosis of the skin, vasculature, and internal organs. It is of two types, namely diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis and limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis.

Scleroderma is characterized by Raynaud's phenomenon, digital ischemia, sclerodactyly, calcinosis, telangiectasia, and cardiac, lung, gastrointestinal and renal disease. Skin thickening is the hallmark of SSc. Patients have a characteristic expressionless facial appearance with taut and shiny skin and microstomia.

Antinuclear antibodies (ANA) are positive in SSC. The presence of anti-topoisomerase 1 (Scl70) and anticentromere antibodies are seen in diffuse cutaneous SSC and limited cutaneous SSc respectively.

Nucleolar pattern of ANA staining in immunofluorescence is most commonly seen in systemic sclerosis. A centromeric pattern is also seen.

Image below shows nucleolar pattern in immunofluorescence seen in systemic sclerosis.

Other options:

Option B: Sjogren's syndrome is an autoimmune disease characterized by lymphocytic infiltration of salivary and lacrimal glands.

Patients present with dry eye (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) and dry mouth (xerostomia) due to fibrosis of the lacrimal and salivary gland respectively.

Anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies are positive in Sjogren's syndrome. ANA and RF (Rheumatoid factor) can also be seen. Centromeric pattern and speckled pattern of staining is seen in Sjogren's syndrome.

Image below shows speckled pattern (image 1) and centromeric pattern (image 2) of staining respectively.

Option C: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disease that most commonly presents with arthralgia with early morning stiffness.

Other important features of SLE include malar rash, discoid rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, pleuritis, pericarditis, and lupus nephritis.

ANA, Anti-dsDNA antibodies, anti-smith antibodies are positive in SLE. Homogenous or diffuse staining and peripheral staining pattern are most commonly seen in SLE.

Image below shows a homogenous or diffuse stained immunofluorescence pattern seen in SLE.

Option D: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a multisystem disease that classically presents with pain, joint swelling, and stiffness of the small joints of the hands, feet, and wrists in a symmetrical manner.

RF and anti-citrullinated peptide antibodies are positive in RA. Homogenous staining is the most common pattern seen in RA.
questions.learning: Systemic sclerosis Numbness of fingers associated with Raynaud's phenomenon, facial tightening, positive anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA) with nucleolar pattern in immunofluorescence is highly suggestive of systemic sclerosis.

Stenopaeic slit is not used for corneal tattooing.

Stenopaeic slit is an ophthalmological instrument that is used in:

• To find out the axis in astigmatism (option D) for prescribing the correction glasses.
• To find out the optimal site for optical iridectomy (option C) for treating cases of central macular or leucomatous corneal opacities.

Corneal tattooing was done mainly in the past for cosmetic purposes. It is commonly done for firm scars of corneal opacities in a eye without any useful vision.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient presented with a black, foul-smelling discharge from the nose. On examination, blackish necrotic mass filling the nasal cavity and eroding the septum and hard palate were seen. What is the most important risk factor for this disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Diabetes

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of mucormycosis and the most important risk factor among these is diabetes.

Mucormycosis is an opportunistic mycosis. It is typically seen in patients with diabetes mellitus and/or diabetic ketoacidosis, and immunocompromised patients. Mucormycosis recently emerged as an important superinfection in COVID-19 patients, especially in India. The surge in cases is most likely due to diabetes mellitus and steroid use.

Risk factors for the infection include the following:

* Uncontrolled diabetes

* Acidosis (especially diabetic ketoacidosis)

* Steroid treatment

* Lymphomas and leukemias

* Immunodeficiencies

* Severe burns

The rhino-orbital-cerebral is the most common form of mucormycosis. Patients present with rhinitis, eye or facial pain, and facial numbness followed by the onset of conjunctival suffusion and swelling along with blurry vision.

Patients can have local tissue destruction with blackish nasal discharge typically resembling the presentation of invasive mucormycosis. The blackish discoloration is due to direct fungal invasion causing arterial and venous thrombosis leading to gangrene.

Diagnosis is made by biopsy with histopathologic examination. The biopsy shows characteristic wide, ribbon-like aseptate hyphal elements that branch at right angles.

The below image shows biopsy findings seen in mucormycosis.

Treatment includes intravenous administration of amphotericin B and wide excision of necrotic tissues. Along with the reversal of underlying conditions and risk factors.
questions.learning: Diabetes — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of mucormycosis and the most important risk factor among these is diabetes. Mucormycosis is an opportunistic mycosis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following conditions is not usually associated with the formation of a greyish-white membrane over the tonsils?
questions.explanation: "Ludwig’s angina" is a rapidly spreading cellulitis of the submandibular and sublingual spaces, typically arising from an infected lower molar. It is characterized by severe swelling of the neck and floor of the mouth, which can displace the tongue and obstruct the airway; however, it does "not typically" involve the formation of a membrane on the tonsils. Diphtheria (Option B) is the classic cause of a thick, grey-white pseudomembrane that bleeds when scraped. Streptococcal tonsillitis (Option A) frequently presents with a white or yellow exudate that can appear membranous. Infectious mononucleosis (Option D) characteristically features massive tonsillar enlargement with a thick, shaggy grey-white exudate. Diagnosis of the cause of a tonsillar membrane is essential, as management varies from antibiotics (Strep) to urgent antitoxin (Diphtheria) or supportive care (Mono). Ludwig’s angina is a surgical emergency requiring airway management and intravenous antibiotics

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the most common complication of ERCP?
questions.explanation: Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is a complex procedure used to manage biliary and pancreatic diseases. The most common complication following the procedure is Post-ERCP Pancreatitis (PEP), occurring in approximately 5-10% of cases. It is characterized by new-onset upper abdominal pain and an elevation of amylase/lipase within 24 hours of the procedure. Duodenal perforation (Option A), Cholangitis (Option B), and Hemorrhage (Option C) are serious potential complications, but they are significantly less frequent than pancreatitis. Risk factors for PEP include young age, female gender, and multiple cannulation attempts. Management involves aggressive hydration and supportive care. Prophylactic measures, such as rectal indomethacin and pancreatic stent placement in high-risk patients, have been shown to reduce the incidence of this complication. Clinicians must monitor all post-ERCP patients closely for signs of pain and distress during the first 24 hours of recovery
questions.learning: Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is a complex procedure used to manage biliary and pancreatic diseases. The most common complication following the procedure is Post-ERCP Pancreatitis (PEP), occurring in approximately 5-10% of cases.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A female patient presents with nausea, vomiting, and a sensation of objects moving around her. She is diagnosed with left vestibular neuritis. Her head impulse test is positive. What is the correct finding?
options: Right saccade with right side movement
Left saccade with right side movement
Right saccade with left side movement
Left saccade with left side movement
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Right saccade with left side movement

In the case of left vestibular neuritis, the correct finding on the head impulse test is a right saccade with left-side movement.

The head impulse test is to assess the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR). The abnormal head impulse test result is due to the VOR being impaired on the side of the vestibular lesion leading to saccades. Saccades are rapid, ballistic movements of the eyes that abruptly try to return to the point of fixation/ gaze.

The head impulse test is done by asking the patient to focus on a target. Then, the patient's head is quickly rotated to the left or right. If there is a deficiency in the VOR, the head movement will be followed by a catch-up saccade in the opposite direction. Thus, in left vestibular neuritis, a rightward saccade is seen following a left-side head rotation.

Vestibular neuritis is distinguished from central causes of vertigo by its characteristic findings: a positive head impulse test, absence of skew deviation, and spontaneous unidirectional nystagmus. Central vertigo, on the other hand, presents with a normal head impulse test, vertical skew deviation, bidirectional nystagmus, and additional neurological signs like diplopia, weakness, or dysarthria. In acute vestibular syndrome, especially in older patients with vascular risk factors, evaluation for a possible stroke is warranted.

Vestibular neuritis resolves spontaneously, but glucocorticoids can improve outcomes if administered within 3 days of symptom onset. Antiviral medications are only suggested for Herpes zoster oticus (Ramsay Hunt syndrome). Vestibular suppressant medications can reduce acute symptoms. Patients should be encouraged to resume normal activity as soon as possible. Vestibular rehabilitation therapy can also be tried.
questions.learning: Right saccade with left side movement — In the case of left vestibular neuritis, the correct finding on the head impulse test is a right saccade with left-side movement.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 7-year-old child presents with leg pain. She had fever and cough 3 days prior. Currently, there is pain on palpation of the calf muscles. Reflexes and other clinical examinations are normal. Lab test reveals CK levels of 2000 IU. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Viral Myositis

The clinical picture showing pain in the calves occuring within a week of an upper respiratory tract infection (URI), with elevated creatine kinase levels suggests the diagnosis of viral myositis. The specific history of URI suggests influenza myositis.

Infectious myositis has a male predominance and is typically seen in young adults. Childhood form presents with fever, malaise, and rhinorrhea and is usually followed by severe pain, especially in the calves. The muscle pain is usually worse with movement and the symptoms last for about a week. In children, toe walking and wide-based gait may be seen because of the involvement of the gastrocnemius-soleus muscles.

Other viral causes of myositis include HIV-1 (one of the most common causes of myositis), group B coxsackievirus (epidemic myalgia), HTLV-1 (Human T-lymphotropic virus), and cytomegalovirus (CMV).

Lab features of influenza myositis include elevated CK which may be as high as 500 times normal the value. Urine myoglobin is usually positive. Detection of the virus with PCR testing of nasopharyngeal specimens can be carried out but is not of much clinical significance. The histopathological examination would reveal muscle fiber necrosis without much inflammatory change.

Treatment includes bed rest, IV fluids, and symptomatic management with analgesics and antipyretics. Amantadine and other antiviral agents may be considered in adults. Complications include myocarditis and respiratory dysfunction. Rhabdomyolysis is an uncommon complication.
questions.learning: Viral Myositis — The clinical picture showing pain in the calves occuring within a week of an upper respiratory tract infection (URI), with elevated creatine kinase levels suggests the diagnosis of viral myositis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 26-year-old man presents with erythematous plaques covered by silvery scales on the extensor surfaces of both arms, along with punctate nail pitting. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of erythematous plaques with pathognomonic silvery scales localized to the extensor surfaces (elbows/knees) is highly diagnostic of Psoriasis Vulgaris. Psoriasis is a chronic T-cell mediated autoimmune skin disease characterized by hyperproliferation of keratinocytes. A classic clinical clue provided is punctate nail pitting, which is a highly specific nail finding associated with psoriasis. Lichen planus (Option B) typically presents on flexor surfaces with "purple, pruritic, polygonal papules" and Wickham striae. Eczema (Option C) usually involves the flexural folds (anticubital fossa) and presents with poorly defined, itchy, weeping lesions. Pityriasis rosea (Option D) begins with a "herald patch" followed by a "Christmas tree" distribution of smaller scaly lesions on the trunk. Therefore, the specific combination of extensor plaques, silvery scales, and nail pitting confirms Psoriasis as the correct diagnosis
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of erythematous plaques with pathognomonic silvery scales localized to the extensor surfaces (elbows/knees) is highly diagnostic of Psoriasis Vulgaris.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 12-year-old girl came for a health checkup. She doesn't go to school. Which government program will benefit her?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram

Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK), an ambitious initiative, launched under the National Health Mission (NHM) launched envisages early screening and early intervention for children from birth to 18 years. It aims at the universal screening of the 4 ‘D’s, i.e. Defects at birth, Deficiencies, Diseases, Developmental delays, including disabilities, that would lead to early identification, timely management, and ultimately a reduction in morbidity, mortality, and lifelong disability in children.

Defects:

* Neural tube defect

* Down’s syndrome

* Cleft lip and palate

* Talipes

* Developmental dysplasia of the hip

* Congenital cataract, congenital deafness, congenital heart disease

* Retinopathy of prematurity

Deficiencies:

* Anemia, especially severe anemia

* Vitamin A deficiency

* Vitamin D deficiency

* Severe acute malnutrition

* Goiter

Diseases:

* Scabies, fungal infections, and eczema

* Otitis media

* Rheumatic heart disease

* Reactive airway disease

* Dental caries

* Convulsive disorders

Developmental delays and disabilities:

* Vision, hearing, and neuromotor impairment

* Motor, cognitive and language delay

* Autism

* Learning disorder

* Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder

Other options:

Option B: Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY) is a program under the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM), whose aim is to reduce maternal mortality by encouraging delivery in government health facilities. Under the scheme, a financial incentive is also provided for giving birth in a government health facility.

Option C: Navjaat Shishu Suraksha Karyakram includes training of doctors, nurses, and ANMs for essential newborn care, early diagnosis, and case management of common ailments of children.

Option D: Pradhan Mantri Poshan Shakti Nirman (PM POSHAN) previously known as Mid-Day Meal Scheme, is a centrally sponsored scheme that provides one hot cooked meal in Government and Government-aided Schools

Under the Scheme, there is a provision of hot cooked meal to all preschool children and also to children of classes I to VIII. The scheme is implemented across the country covering all the eligible children without any discrimination of gender and social class.
questions.learning: Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK), an ambitious initiative, launched under the National Health Mission (NHM) launched envisages early screening and early intervention for children from birth to 18 years.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 54-year-old farmer from Ohio presents to a physician with a chronic cough. A chest X-ray demonstrates a mass lesion with hilar lymphadenopathy. Biopsy of the mass and staining with lactophenol cotton blue demonstrates multiple, tiny yeast forms within macrophages as below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Histoplasmosis

The given clinical history and the presence of tiny yeast forms within macrophages are suggestive of Histoplasmosis.

Histoplasmosis is also known as Darling's disease, Cave's disease or Ohio disease. It is endemic in USA i.e. it has specific geographical distribution.

The causative agent is Histoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus. It is a facultative intracellular parasite. Yeast form occurs mainly in tissues at a temperature of 37oC and mycelial form occurs in soil at 25oC. Spores are found in bird or bat droppings in the soil which acts as reservoir of infection. Transmission occurs via inhalation of conidia. Person-to-person transmission or animal-to-man transmission is not yet known.

After inhalation, the conidia develop into yeast cells and are engulfed by alveolar macrophages. Within macrophages, the yeasts may disseminate to reticuloendothelial tissues, such as the liver, spleen, bone marrow, and lymph nodes. Biopsy reveals tiny (2-4 microns) oval-shaped yeast cells inside macrophages.

On culture and microscopy, tuberculate macroconidia and hyaline septate mould with microconidia are seen.

Itraconazole is the treatment for mild to moderate infection, while in disseminated disease, systemic treatment with amphotericin B may be required.

Pearl PF0827: Systemic fungi - Histopathological findings

Histoplasma: Tiny oval yeast cells (2- 4 μm size) with narrow-based budding within the macrophages with an underlying granulomatous response.

Blastomyces : Thick-walled round yeast cells of 8- 15 μm size with single broad-based budding (figure of 8 appearance)

Coccidoides : Mature spherules of coccidioidomycus is seen in the above image. Spherules which are large sac like structures (20--80 μm size), have thick, double refractile wall, and are filled with endospores.

Paracoccidioides : Round thick-walled yeasts, with multiple narrow-necked buds attached circumferencially giving rise to Mickey mouse or pilot wheel appearance.
questions.learning: Histoplasmosis — The given clinical history and the presence of tiny yeast forms within macrophages are suggestive of Histoplasmosis. Histoplasmosis is also known as Darling's disease, Cave's disease or Ohio disease.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 28-year-old primigravida with a low-risk pregnancy presents at 39 weeks + 6 days with labor pains. Her vitals are stable. On PV, her cervix is 3 cm dilated and 60% effaced. The fetal head is at -3 station and membranes are felt as a bag of worms beneath the head. What is the appropriate course of management?
options: Rupture of membranes and confirm cord prolapse
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Emergency Caesarean section

In this patient, the membranes are intact and the 'bag of worms' palpaeted refers to the umbilical cord within the membrane, suggestive of cord presentation. The best course of management would be to take the patient up for an emergency caesarean section.

Cord presentation refers to the presence of the umbilical cord below the presenting part over the internal os, within an intact bag of membranes, whereas in the case of a cord prolapse, the membranes are ruptured and the cord lies externally. The goal of management in the event of a cord presentation is to expedite delivery while keeping the membranes intact, and hence the best option would be to deliver the fetus via emergency LSCS. While the patient is being prepared for surgery, she may be positioned in the exagerrated Sim's position (shown below) to avoid cord compression.

In comparison, the management algorithm of cord prolapse is based on three important factors, which are: living or dead baby, maturity of the baby, degree of cervical dilatation, according to which the following steps are taken:

Other options:

Option A: Oxytocin should not be started as the patient should not be allowed to proceed to deliver via normal vaginal delivery due to the risk of cord prolapse and fetal death.

Option B: The membranes should not be ruptured as this would lead to an overt cord prolapse and complicate the situation further.

Option D: Cord presentation is an obstetric emergency requiring immediate action.
questions.learning: Emergency Caesarean section — In this patient, the membranes are intact and the 'bag of worms' palpaeted refers to the umbilical cord within the membrane, suggestive of cord presentation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A child presented with recurrent abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea following ingestion of milk-based products. Which enzyme is likely to be deficient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lactase

The given scenario indicates intolerance of milk-based products in this child, hence, the enzyme likely to be deficient is lactase.

Lactase is the enzyme that is responsible for breaking down lactose, a disaccharide found in milk and dairy products. When this enzyme is deficient, it can lead to the accumulation of lactose in the intestinal lumen where it is fermented by intestinal bacteria to lactate which produces symptoms of lactose intolerance, including recurrent abdominal pain, vomiting, and diarrhea after consuming lactose-rich food items. Lactase and maltase are present in the intestinal brush border.

Other options:

Option A- Lipases are involved in the hydrolysis of dietary triglycerides to free fatty acids and glycerol. It is deficient in exocrine pancreatic deficiency states such as chronic pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, and Crohn's. Although it might also present with abdominal pain and diarrhea, the stools are foul-smelling(due to gut bacteria) and greasy due to the presence of fat (steatorrhea) and are also associated with fat-soluble vitamin deficiency.

Option B- Maltase breaks down maltose which is a disaccharide intermediate of starch breakdown.

Option C- Amylase hydrolyses starch which is a glucose homopolymer and is present in germinating cereals, potatoes, legumes, and malt.
questions.learning: Lactase — The given scenario indicates intolerance of milk-based products in this child, hence, the enzyme likely to be deficient is lactase. Lactase is the enzyme that is responsible for breaking down lactose, a disaccharide found in milk and dairy products.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following heart sounds are best heard with the bell of the stethoscope? I. Opening snap II. Systolic click III. Third heart sound IV. Mid diastolic murmur Select the correct answer using the code below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. III and IV

The bell of the stethoscope is designed to detect low-frequency sounds, whereas the diaphragm is better for high-frequency sounds.

Sounds Best Heard with the Bell

III. Third Heart Sound (S3)

• Low-pitched early diastolic sound
• Heard best at the apex with the bell
• Associated with:

• Heart failure
• Dilated cardiomyopathy
• Normal in children and young adults

IV. Mid-Diastolic Murmur

• Low-frequency murmur
• Examples:

• Mitral Stenosis
• Tricuspid stenosis

• Heard best with the bell placed lightly over the apex (mitral stenosis)

Sounds Best Heard with the Diaphragm

I. Opening Snap

• High-frequency sound
• Due to abrupt opening of a stenotic mitral valve
• Best heard with the diaphragm

II. Systolic Click

• High-pitched sound
• Seen in Mitral Valve Prolapse
• Best heard with the diaphragm
questions.learning: III and IV — The bell of the stethoscope is designed to detect low-frequency sounds, whereas the diaphragm is better for high-frequency sounds. Sounds Best Heard with the Bell III.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is the name of the view in which the maxillary sinus is seen best?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Water's view

Occipitomental view with an open mouth is also called the water’s view.

Water's view: The patient’s head is positioned such that the nose and the chin touch the film while the X-rays are projected from backwards. The mouth is usually kept open while taking the X-ray.

Structures seen in water’s view are:

* Maxillary sinuses (seen best)

* Frontal sinuses

* Sphenoid sinus (if the film is taken with open mouth)

* Zygoma

* Zygomatic arch

* Nasal bone

* Frontal process of maxilla

* Superior orbital fissure

* Infratemporal fossa

Pearl PF1766: Radiographic views of temporal bone

Pearl PF1596: Radiographic views of paranasal sinuses and mastoid

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32-year-old pregnant woman at 28 weeks of gestation presents with hypertension and has a history of well-controlled asthma. She is currently not on any medications, and her blood pressure is 150/95 mmHg. Which treatment option is most appropriate for managing her hypertension?
questions.explanation: This 32-year-old pregnant woman at 28 weeks’ gestation has mild–moderate hypertension (150/95 mmHg) with a history of asthma. When selecting antihypertensive therapy in pregnancy, it is essential to choose a drug that is safe for the fetus and does not exacerbate maternal comorbidities. Although labetalol is commonly used as a first-line agent for hypertension in pregnancy, it has β-blocking activity. Even though it is relatively β₁-selective, labetalol can still precipitate bronchoconstriction, making it less suitable in patients with asthma, including those with well-controlled disease. This concern applies to both IV labetalol (Option A) and oral labetalol (Option D). Additionally, IV labetalol is mainly reserved for hypertensive emergencies, which this patient does not have. ACE inhibitors (Option C) are contraindicated in pregnancy because they can cause fetal renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, and neonatal renal failure. Nifedipine, a calcium channel blocker, is safe and effective in pregnancy, does not affect bronchial smooth muscle, and is therefore the best choice for managing hypertension in a pregnant patient with asthma

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 24-year-old woman presents with fatigue and intermittent low-grade fever. She reports dizziness and weakness of her left upper limb during physical activity. On examination, the pulse in the left radial artery is diminished compared with the right, and there is a marked difference in blood pressure between the two arms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Takayasu arteritis

Takayasu arteritis is a chronic granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis that primarily affects the aorta and its major branches, especially in young women (<40 years). Inflammation causes arterial wall thickening, stenosis, and occlusion, leading to diminished or absent peripheral pulses, blood pressure discrepancy between the arms, upper limb claudication, diminished left radial pulse and vascular bruits. Because of these characteristic findings, it is known as the “pulseless disease.”

These findings result from stenosis of the subclavian artery or aortic arch branches.

Why not the other options?

• A. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener granulomatosis): A small-vessel ANCA-associated vasculitis presenting with upper airway disease, pulmonary nodules, and glomerulonephritis, not absent pulses.
• C. Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN): A medium-vessel vasculitis affecting kidneys, gastrointestinal tract, skin, and peripheral nerves; classically associated with hepatitis B, but does not cause pulse deficits or inter-arm BP differences.
• D. Giant cell (temporal) arteritis: A large-vessel vasculitis affecting patients >50 years, presenting with headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, and vision loss, often associated with polymyalgia rheumatica.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 14-day-old baby is being evaluated in the pediatric department for ambiguous genitalia. On examination, the baby is dehydrated. Investigations reveal hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia. Karyotyping evaluation demonstrates 46, XX chromosomal pattern. Measurement of which of the following will help in the confirmation of the diagnosis in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 17-hydroxyprogesterone

The above clinical scenario is suggestive of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (classical 21-hydroxylase deficiency). Measurement of 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels will help in the confirmation of the diagnosis in this case.

Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH)/adrenogenital syndrome is a family of autosomal-recessive disorders associated with the diminished synthesis of cortisol and aldosterone. The most common cause of ambiguous genitalia in a newborn is a classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency.

Children usually present with salt-wasting crises as seconded by dehydration with hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia. Virilization is usually apparent at birth in females and within 2 to 3 years of life in males.

The diagnosis is confirmed by markedly elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels. The most commonly performed neonatal screening programs screen only for 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels in dried blood obtained by heel stick and absorbed on filter paper cards. Also, these same cards are screened in parallel for other congenital conditions, such as hypothyroidism and phenylketonuria.

Glucocorticoids are the mainstay of treatment. Patients with salt-wasting and virilizing forms are treated with hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone. Surgical treatment is usually done between 2-6 months of age for significantly virilized females.

Males with 21-hydroxylase deficiency who have had inadequate corticosteroid therapy may develop testicular adrenal rest tumors. These usually regress following increased steroid dosage.

The image below summarizes the pathway involved in steroid hormonal production and the pearl summarizes the various non-classical forms of congenital adrenal hyperplasia.

Note:  In congenital adrenal hyperplasia, as a result of the deficient enzyme(21-hydroxylase), there is an impaired conversion of 17-hydroxyprogesterone to 11-deoxycortisol. This results in the overproduction of adrenal androgen precursors and adrenal androgens. The diagnostic hormone 17-hydroxyprogesterone is markedly elevated in CAH. If the 17-hydroxyprogesterone level is markedly elevated (>10,000 ng/dL), the diagnosis of classic CAH is likely, whereas levels >2000 ng/dL but <10,000 ng/dL typically reflect non-classic disease.

Other options:

Option A: Although 21-hydroxylase is the deficient enzyme in this condition. Its level is not routinely measured to confirm the diagnosis.

Options C and D: 17-hydroxylase and 11β hydroxylase deficiency generally present with salt retention crises and hypertension.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman presents with intermenstrual bleeding after the insertion of an intrauterine device (IUD). She reports no other symptoms. What is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.explanation: Intermenstrual bleeding and spotting are the most common side effects associated with the insertion of an intrauterine device (IUD), particularly within the first three to six months of use. If the patient is clinically stable and reports no severe pain, fever, or heavy bleeding, the most appropriate initial step is to reassure her and observe. Most cases of IUD-related spotting resolve spontaneously as the uterine lining adapts to the device. Removing the IUD (Option A) is premature unless the bleeding is intolerable or persistent after several months. A pelvic ultrasound (Option C) is only indicated if there is suspicion of device displacement or other pelvic pathology. Prescribing hormonal therapy (Option D) is generally not the initial step for mild spotting immediately post-insertion. Patient education regarding the expected side-effect profile of the IUD is essential for improving long-term adherence and satisfaction with this effective contraceptive method
questions.learning: Intermenstrual bleeding and spotting are the most common side effects associated with the insertion of an intrauterine device (IUD), particularly within the first three to six months of use.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is not a part of damage control surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vascular anastomosis

Vascular anastomosis is undertaken as a part of definitive surgery, not damage control surgery (DCS).

DCS is minimal intervention done in order to stabilize the patient and followed by definite surgery later. It aims to coordinate staged operative interventions with periods of aggressive resuscitation to salvage trauma patients sustaining major injuries.

The initial focus is hemorrhage control, resuscitation, followed by control and limitation of contamination. It includes an abbreviated laparotomy, temporary packing, and closure of the abdomen in an eﬀort to blunt the physiologic response to prolonged shock and massive hemorrhage.

After the initial steps of DCS, definitive surgery involving vascular anastomosis may be done. This is individualized to the patient and preferred to be completed in the first 24–72 hours.

Note: Vascular anastomosis is the option least likely to be part of the initial stages of DCS. Hence, it is the best option out of the four for this testing point.
questions.learning: Vascular anastomosis Vascular anastomosis is undertaken as a part of definitive surgery, not damage control surgery (DCS). DCS is minimal intervention done in order to stabilize the patient and followed by definite surgery later.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A woman presents with sudden onset of high- grade fever, hypotension, and a diffuse rash, with a history of prolonged tampon use. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of high fever (>38.8°C), hypotension, and a diffuse erythrodermic rash in the context of prolonged tampon use is diagnostic of Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS). This condition is most often caused by toxin-producing Staphylococcus aureus (specifically TSST-1), which acts as a superantigen to trigger massive T-cell activation and cytokine release. General septic shock (Option A) can cause fever and hypotension but lacks the specific diffuse rash and tampon association. Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (Option C) presents with pelvic pain and cervical motion tenderness rather than systemic shock and rash. Streptococcal pharyngitis (Option D) is a localized infection that doesn't match this severe systemic pattern. Treatment involves intensive supportive care with IV fluids and antistaphylococcal antibiotics
questions.learning: The clinical triad of high fever (>38.8°C), hypotension, and a diffuse erythrodermic rash in the context of prolonged tampon use is diagnostic of Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following is not seen in nutritional rickets?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Urine calcium: creatinine ratio > 15

Urine calcium: creatinine ratio > 15 is not seen in a case of nutritional rickets. Instead low urine calcium and high urinary phosphate excretion are seen due to stimulation of PTH(parathormone) in vitamin D deficiency(nutritional rickets).(Option C)

Initially, low calcium levels in the blood stimulate increased PTH secretion from the parathyroid glands that results in bone resorption and increased reabsorption of calcium and increased excretion of phosphorus in the kidneys.

Hence blood calcium levels can be low to normal with low phosphorus levels and high ALP due to increased bone resorption activity.

Note - High urinary calcium excretion is associated with hereditary hypophosphatemic rickets with hypercalciuria.

Nutritional rickets is a skeletal disorder primarily caused by a deficiency in vitamin D, calcium, or phosphorus, or a combination of these nutrients. Rickets typically affect children during periods of rapid growth and bone development.

25-hydroxy vitamin D level should be measured to diagnose vitamin D deficiency rickets. The initial lab tests in this child should also include serum calcium, phosphorous, alkaline phosphatase (ALP), and parathyroid hormone (PTH). Lab findings reveal decreased calcium and phosphate levels, increased PTH, and ALP.

Treatment with oral vitamin D is preferred. Patients who show no response should be evaluated for other disorders, such as hypophosphatemic rickets, vitamin D-dependent rickets, renal tubular acidosis-associated rickets, and chronic kidney disease-associated rickets.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 20-year-old male presented with yellowish discoloration of his skin and sclera. He is otherwise normal. He gives a history of viral infection 10 days ago which resolved 2 days back. He also gives a history of similar episodes in the past following any illness. Lab values are given below. What is the most likely diagnosis? Serum bilirubin: 2.4 mg/dL Unconjugated bilirubin: 2.1mg/dL Conjugated bilirubin: 0.3mg/dL Serum AST and ALT: Normal
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Gilbert syndrome

The above clinical vignette points toward the diagnosis of Gilbert syndrome.

This patient's mild jaundice seen only during a period of stress along with an increase in unconjugated bilirubin and normal AST, and ALT levels strongly point towards a diagnosis of Gilbert syndrome.

Gilbert syndrome is a benign, familial disorder inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern characterized by mild intermittent jaundice usually seen during stress, illnesses, or any other precipitating factors. There is no hemolysis or underlying liver disease. The condition is recognized to arise from a mutation in the promoter region of the UGT1A1 gene, which results in mildly decreased UDP-Glucoronyltransferase production. UDP-Glucoronyltransferase is required for the conjugation of bilirubin.

Precipitating factors in Gilbert syndrome:

* Dehydration

* Fasting

* Menstrual periods

* Illness

* Vigorous exercise.

Other options:

Option A: Dubin-Johnson syndrome is a benign autosomal recessive disease that is characterized by chronic conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and conspicuous brown-black melanin-like pigment deposition in the liver. The disease is caused due to mutation in multidrug resistance protein 2 (MRP-2) in hepatocytes, which is required for the transport of non-bile salt organic anions at the canalicular membranes. Liver biopsy shows characteristic deposition of black-colored pigment.

Option B: Crigler-Najjar syndrome is of two types with type 1 having absent/trace UDP-Glucoronyltransferase production and type 2 having <10% of the normal enzyme activity. Hence, type 1 is far more severe and leads to kernicterus and neurological damage in babies. Type 2 may also lead to kernicterus occasionally. Unconjugated bilirubin is elevated. Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia in a 20-year-old male is less likely to be due to Criggler Najar type 1 syndrome. It is because patients usually die in infancy or early childhood despite the best treatment.

Option D: Rotor syndrome is similar to Dubin-Johnson syndrome but with a milder presentation. Increased conjugated bilirubin levels. Liver biopsy does not show black colored liver

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: All of the following are contraceptive methods used post-coitus except: (NEET PG 2020)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Danazol

Emergency contraception (postcoital contraception) is used to prevent pregnancy after unprotected intercourse.

Methods used for emergency contraception include:

• High-dose combined estrogen-progestin pills (Yuzpe method)
• Levonorgestrel pills
• Mifepristone (RU-486)
• Copper IUCD (CuT 200/CuT 380A)

Copper IUCD is one of the most effective methods when inserted within 5 days of unprotected intercourse. Danazol is not used for emergency contraception. It is a synthetic androgen primarily used for:

• Endometriosis
• Fibrocystic breast disease
• Hereditary angioedema

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A young patient is admitted with a history of fever for 5 days. BP is 90/60 mmHg, PR-120 bpm, RR-24 breaths/min, GCS score-10; laboratory tests show leucocytosis with neutrophilia and serum creatinine level of 2.6 mg/dL. An intern doctor wants to calculate the qSOFA score to predict prognosis and hospitalization duration. Which of the following comprises the qSOFA score?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. SBP, RR, GCS score

qSOFA score comprises of SBP, RR, and GCS.

qSOFA score (quickSOFA) is a bedside prompt that may identify patients with suspected infection who are at greater risk for a poor outcome outside the intensive care unit (ICU).

It uses three criteria, assigning one point each for

• low blood pressure (SBP≤100 mmHg),
• high respiratory rate (≥22 breaths/min),
• altered mentation (GCS score, <15).

The score ranges from 0 to 3 points. The presence of 2 or more qSOFA points is a simple prompt to identify infected patients outside the ICU who are likely to develop sepsis. This is a simplified derivative of SOFA score. The primary method to evaluate the risk of organ dysfunction (sepsis) in patients with suspected infection is by determining the Sequential (sepsis-related) Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score, which includes assessment of:

• Circulation - Systolic BP and need for vasopressors; platelet count
• Respiration - PaO2/FiO2 and need for mechanical ventilation
• Mentation - Glasgow Coma Scale score
• Hepatic function - Bilirubin level
• Renal function - Creatinine level

Organ dysfunction is defined by a SOFA score of ≥2.

The SOFA score is limited by its requirement of multiple laboratory tests which makes it complex and time-consuming. In order to simplify the scoring process, the "Sepsis - 3" task force recommended the quick sepsis-related organ dysfunction assessment "qSOFA" score.

SOFA vs. qSOFA:

• SOFA is a more comprehensive and accurate scoring system, which is particularly superior to qSOFA in the ICU setting.
• qSOFA is a simplified derivative of SOFA for bedside assessment of individuals at risk for sepsis, particularly useful outside the ICU setting (i.e. ward/emergency department). However, note that it was originally designed as a predictive tool that calculates the risk of death from sepsis rather than a diagnostic tool.

Thereby, the best description of sepsis based on "Sepsis-3" task force recommendations would be as follows:

• Suspected or documented infection with SOFA score of ≥2  or
• Suspected or documented infection with qSOFA score of ≥2

Another score that has been used is the National Early Warning Score (NEWS). It ranges from 0 to 20 and is based on respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, use of supplemental O2, temperature, systolic blood pressure, pulse rate, and level of consciousness. ≥5 out of 20 is considered a positive score.

Other scoring systems for sepsis:

The Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS) score is no longer recommended as is it not specific to infection.

The Logistic Organ Dysfunction System (LODS) score is not recommended as it is complex and has too many variables.
questions.learning: SBP, RR, GCS score qSOFA score comprises of SBP, RR, and GCS. qSOFA score (quickSOFA) is a bedside prompt that may identify patients with suspected infection who are at greater risk for a poor outcome outside the intensive care unit (ICU).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following CVS changes are not seen in pregnancy?
questions.explanation: A diastolic murmur is never considered a normal physiological finding in pregnancy and always warrants further investigation for underlying heart disease. In contrast, several other cardiovascular adaptations are common: a soft systolic murmur (Option A) is frequently heard due to increased blood flow and decreased viscosity. A third heart sound (S3) (Option C) often occurs because of rapid ventricular filling. Exaggerated splitting of the first heart sound (S1) (Option D) is also typically observed. Additionally, the apex beat shifts laterally, and systemic vascular resistance decreases due to the smooth muscle-relaxing effects of progesterone. While systolic, S3, and mammary murmurs are physiologic results of the hyperdynamic state, a diastolic murmur is always pathologic
questions.learning: A diastolic murmur is never considered a normal physiological finding in pregnancy and always warrants further investigation for underlying heart disease.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following can be prevented by transfusing irradiated RBCs?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Graft versus host disease

Transfusion of irradiated RBCs prevent the incidence of graft versus host disease (GVHD) associated with the transfusion.

GVHD occurs when immunologically competent cells or their precursors are transplanted into immunologically compromised recipients and the transferred cells recognize the alloantigens in the host and attack host tissues. It is seen most commonly during hematopoietic stem cell transplantation but may occur following transplantation of solid organs too.

GVHD maybe of two types: acute and chronic.

Acute GVHD occurs within days to weeks after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. It mainly involves the immune system and the epithelia of the skin (in the form of generalized rash), liver( in the form of jaundice), and intestines (in the form of bloody diarrhea). But the affected tissues are not heavily infiltrated by lymphocytes.

Chronic GVHD may follow acute GVHD or may occur insidiously. These patients have extensive skin damage, with destruction of skin appendages and fibrosis of the dermis, resembling systemic sclerosis. Cholestatic jaundice and esophageal strictures are also common. There will be involution of the thymus and depletion of lymphocytes in the lymph nodes. There will also be recurrent bouts of life-threatening infections. Some may even develop autoimmunity, owing to the grafted CD4+ helper T cells reacting with host B cells and stimulating them, which may result in autoantibodies production.

Depletion of donor T cells by irradiation, before transfusion can eliminate the occurrence of GVHD. But irradiation also has its side effects such as recurrence of tumor in leukemic patients, increased incidence of graft failures and EBV-related B-cell lymphoma.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Regarding thyroid storm, which statement is false?
options: Symptoms can include diarrhea, vomiting, jaundice, and confusion
High-dose propranolol can reduce T4 to T3 conversion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mortality is 10% despite treatment

Thyroid storm is a life-threatening exacerbation of thyrotoxicosis characterized by severe hypermetabolic state and multisystem involvement.

• High fever, tachycardia, agitation, confusion
• Gastrointestinal symptoms: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice
• Can be precipitated by stressors such as infection, trauma, or surgery (including non-thyroid surgery).
• Management principles:

• β-blockers (high-dose propranolol) to control adrenergic symptoms and reduce peripheral conversion of T4 → T3
• Antithyroid drugs (PTU or methimazole)
• Iodine and glucocorticoids

Mortality remains high (\~20–30% even with treatment), therefore the statement “mortality is 10% despite treatment” is false.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 50-year-old female presents with painless hematuria. Imaging shows a bladder mass. Biopsy reveals transitional cell carcinoma. Which risk factor is most commonly associated with this cancer?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tobacco smoking

Tobacco smoking is the most important and common risk factor for urothelial (transitional cell) carcinoma of the bladder.

• Cigarette smoke contains aromatic amines and carcinogens that are metabolized in the liver and excreted in urine → prolonged exposure of urothelium → malignant transformation.

• Smoking accounts for \~50–60% of bladder cancers.

Other risk factors:

• Occupational exposure to aniline dyes, aromatic amines (benzidine, β-naphthylamine)

• Cyclophosphamide therapy

• Chronic irritation (stones, catheters)

• Pelvic radiation

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Deficiency of which of the following causes increased glutamine in blood?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ornithine transcarbamoylase

Deficiency ornithine transcarbamoylase causes increased glutamine in blood

Ornithine transcarbamoylase catalyzes the condensation of carbamoyl phosphate with ornithine to form citrulline in the urea cycle. Its deficiency leads to the accumulation of carbamoyl phosphate. The carbamoyl phosphate is then shunted to pyrimidine biosynthesis, resulting in high ammonia and orotic acid levels in the blood. This condition is thus called hyperammonemia type 2.

As a compensatory mechanism, ammonia is then combined with glutamate to form glutamine (by the enzyme glutamine synthetase). The levels of glutamine are elevated in the blood, cerebrospinal fluid, and urine, probably as a result of this dysregulated glutamine synthesis.

Other options:

Option A: Deficiency of argininosuccinate lyase leads to argininosuccinic aciduria

Option C: Deficiency of alpha-galactosidase-A leads to Fabry’s disease and an accumulation of globotriaosylceramide.

Option D: Deficiency of arginase leads to hyperargininemia
