questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 65-year-old man dies due to myocardial infarction. Which of the following stains can be used to see the infarct in the heart while conducting an autopsy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Triphenyl tetrazolium chloride

Triphenyl tetrazolium chloride stain can be used to see the infarct in the heart.

Myocardial infarcts less than 12 hours old are usually not apparent on gross examination. However, if the infarct preceded death by 2 to 3 hours, it is possible to highlight the area of necrosis by immersion of tissue slices in a solution of triphenyl tetrazolium chloride.

This gross histochemical stain imparts a brick-red color to intact, noninfarcted myocardium where lactate dehydrogenase activity is preserved. Because dehydrogenases leak out through the damaged membranes of dead cells, an infarct appears as an unstained pale zone.

Other options:

Option A: The stain used for fat is the oil red O stain. It can identify neutral lipids and fatty acids in smears and tissues.

Option C: Sudan Black B (SBB) is a lipophilic dye that binds irreversibly to an undefined granule component in granulocytes, eosinophils, and some monocytes. It stains intracellular lipids and phospholipids.

Option D: Collagen fibres are stained blue and muscle fibres are stained red using Masson trichrome stain.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 17-year-old female presents with primary amenorrhea but experiences abdominal pain every month. She has normal secondary sexual characteristics. On examination, an abdominal lump is noted, and a bluish bulge is observed when parting the labia. Considering the suspected diagnosis, what would be the appropriate management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cruciate incision on the hymen

A history of primary amenorrhea, cyclical abdominal pain, presence of a palpable abdominal lump, and visualization of a tense bluish bulging membrane on the separation of the labia suggests the diagnosis of imperforate hymen and the appropriate management would be cruciate incision on the hymen.

Cryptomenorrhoea, also known as hematocolpos, is a condition where menstruation occurs but is not visible due to an obstruction of the outflow tract. The most common cause is an intact (imperforate) hymen or the presence of a vaginal septum. A vaginal septum is differentiated from the imperforate hymen by a pinkish concave covering in contrast to the bluish convex bulge in the latter. An ultrasound scan of the pelvis confirms the diagnosis.

Treatment: A simple cruciate incision of the hymen allows the free drainage of the collected menstrual blood, and leads to normal reproductive function, in cases of imperforate hymen.

Note:

In the case of a vaginal septum (i.e. atresia), more extensive dissection and vaginoplasty are required.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: In a middle-aged diabetic patient with chronic kidney disease stage 5, which of the following drugs can be given safely without altering the dose?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Linagliptin

Linagliptin can be given safely without altering the dose for this patient.

Linagliptin is a dipeptidyl-peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitor and is eliminated by the hepatobiliary route. Hence no dosage adjustment is needed in renal failure.

It is used in type 2 diabetes as monotherapy or as combination therapy with other drugs when metformin is not tolerated or contraindicated.

Other DPP-4 inhibitors like sitagliptin, vildagliptin, saxagliptin, alogliptin show renal elimination.
questions.learning: Linagliptin Linagliptin can be given safely without altering the dose for this patient. Linagliptin is a dipeptidyl-peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitor and is eliminated by the hepatobiliary route.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The most common neuroendocrine tumor of the pancreas is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Insulinoma

The most common neuroendocrine tumor of the pancreas is insulinoma (4 per million).

Insulinoma is an insulin-producing tumor of the pancreas, with more than 90% of them being benign. It occurs in >40 years in patients without MEN 1 syndrome and <40 years in patients with MEN 1. It presents with symptoms of hypoglycemia such as weakness, headaches, sweating, faintness, seizures, and altered behavior. These occur after fasting or exertion and improve after glucose intake.

The investigation of choice for insulinoma is the determination of 72-hour fasting glucose and serum insulin levels. C-peptide and proinsulin levels are also elevated.

Medical management includes:

• Frequent carbohydrate-rich meals
• Somatostatin analogs like octreotide are effective in controlling symptoms due to excess insulin secretion. They should be used with caution as they can suppress counterregulatory hormones, such as growth hormone (GH), glucagon, and catecholamines, and precipitously worsen hypoglycemia.
• Diazoxide can be used in the initial management of insulinoma as it inhibits insulin release. Its side effects include sodium retention and nausea.
• Everolimus has been found to be highly effective in improving glycemic control in patients with insulinoma owing to its antitumor effect and induction of insulin resistance.

Enucleation and pancreatectomy are the definitive surgical management of insulinoma.

Other options:

Option A: Gastrinoma has an incidence of 0.5 to 4 in a million.

Options B & D: Somatostatinoma and VIPoma are much rarer than gastrinoma.
questions.learning: Insulinoma — The most common neuroendocrine tumor of the pancreas is insulinoma (4 per million). Insulinoma is an insulin-producing tumor of the pancreas, with more than 90% of them being benign.

questions.text: Identify the investigation and the lesion depicted in the image given below.
options: Retrograde cystourethrogram with membranous urethra stricture
Retrograde cystourethrogram with penile urethral stricture
Micturating cystourethrography with prostratic urethra stricture

Correct answer: B. Retrograde cystourethrogram with penile urethral stricture

The given image shows retrograde cystourethrogram with findings consistent with penile urethral stricture.

The male urethra can be visualized by retrograde urethrography (RGU) or voiding cystourethrogram (VCU), also known as micturating cystourethrogram (MCU).

In RGU, the urethra is visualized with the instillation of contrast into the anterior urethra (penile urethra and bulbar urethra). It is helpful for diagnosing anterior urethral abnormalities.

The following image shows an RGU with bulbar urethral stricture:

In VCU, after injecting contrast into the bladder using a Foleys catheter, the posterior urethra (membranous urethra and prostatic urethra) is visualized during micturition. It is helpful for diagnosing posterior urethral abnormalities and bladder abnormalities. It is the investigation of choice for vesicoureteric reflux (VUR) and posterior urethral valve.

The following image shows a voiding cystourethrogram in a patient with grade V VUR:

options: Aspirin loading dose should be commenced immediately

questions.text: Patients suffering from which of the following condition(s) can get symptomatic relief by consuming a gluten-free diet? 1. Coeliac disease 2. Peptic ulcer disease 3. Dermatitis herpetiformis Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1 and 3 only

• 1. Coeliac disease: Correct

• Coeliac disease is an immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by gluten.
• A strict gluten-free diet is the mainstay of treatment and leads to improvement of symptoms and intestinal mucosal healing.

• 2. Peptic ulcer disease: Incorrect

• A gluten-free diet has no established role in the treatment of peptic ulcer disease.
• Treatment focuses on H. pylori eradication, acid suppression, and avoidance of NSAIDs when appropriate.

• 3. Dermatitis herpetiformis: Correct

• Dermatitis herpetiformis is the cutaneous manifestation of gluten-sensitive enteropathy.
• A strict gluten-free diet improves the rash and reduces the need for medications such as dapsone.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency department with severe maxillofacial trauma from a road traffic accident, resulting in airway compromise. What is the most appropriate immediate airway management?
questions.explanation: In the setting of severe maxillofacial trauma where the airway is acutely compromised, standard methods such as orotracheal intubation (Option B) may be impossible due to massive bleeding, edema, or anatomical disruption. In such an emergency "can't intubate, can't oxygenate" scenario, Cricothyroidotomy is the most appropriate immediate surgical airway intervention. It is faster and easier to perform than a formal tracheostomy (Option A) and provides a secure airway below the site of the trauma. Bag-mask ventilation (Option D) is often ineffective when there is structural damage to the face or upper airway obstruction. Cricothyroidotomy involves an incision through the cricothyroid membrane, allowing for rapid cannulation. While it is a temporary life-saving measure, it must eventually be converted to a formal tracheostomy if long-term airway support is needed. Clinicians must be trained in this procedure as part of advanced trauma life support (ATLS) to prevent hypoxic brain injury or death in patients with complex head and neck injuries
questions.learning: In the setting of severe maxillofacial trauma where the airway is acutely compromised, standard methods such as orotracheal intubation (Option B) may be impossible due to massive bleeding, edema, or anatomical disruption.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A baby is born with sensory neural deafness, patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), and salt pepper appearance on retinoscopy. Identify the infection in the mother.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rubella

The given clinical scenario of sensorineural deafness, patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), and a salt-and-pepper appearance on retinoscopy is indicative of congenital rubella syndrome, suggesting that the mother had a rubella infection.

Triad of Gregg is seen in babies with congenital rubella syndrome. The features include:

* Ocular defects: congenital cataract, salt and pepper chorioretinopathy, microphthalmos, glaucoma, and anterior uveitis

* Sensorineural hearing loss

* Heart defects: patent ductus arteriosus, pulmonary stenosis, and ventricular septal defects.

Blueberry muffin rash and microphthalmos are also seen in this condition.

The image below shows a neonate with papulo-nodular erythematous-bluish lesions of a blueberry muffin baby:

Rubella or German measles is a serious infection in pregnancy that causes abortions or severe fetal defects if infection occurs in the first trimester. The transplacental spread of the rubella virus is known to cause congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) in the baby.  When this infection develops in the first, second or third months, there is a 60%, 25%, or 10% chance of significant abnormalities, respectively. Transmission of the virus also occurs through nasopharyngeal secretions (droplet transmission).

The mother usually has a fever and generalized body rash. The rash is maculopapular, first emerging on the face and later spreading to the trunk and limbs. The incidence and severity reduce as the pregnancy advances and are rare after 20 weeks of gestation.

There is no specific treatment for rubella virus infection in mothers. Post-exposure passive immunization can be beneficial if given within 5 days of exposure to droplets. The incidence of this disease has reduced due to the availability of MMR vaccines. MMR vaccines can be administered only to non-pregnant females as it is a live, attenuated virus. Women are advised to delay pregnancy for at least one month after being vaccinated.

Other Options:

Option A: Pregnant females infected with varicella-zoster virus present with fever, dry cough, dyspnoea, tachypnoea and pleuritic chest pain. The highest risk of transmission to fetus is between 13 to 20 weeks of gestation.

Option B: Congenital toxoplasmosis is due to toxoplasma gondii. The child usually presents with a classic triad of chorioretinitis, calcifications within the brain and hydrocephalus. Blueberry muffin baby appearance is also seen in this. Calcifications occur randomly throughout the brain in congenital toxoplasmosis, while periventricular calcification is characteristic of congenital CMV infection.

Option D: Pregnant females affected with cytomegalovirus present with infectious mononucleosis-like symptoms, that is fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy and polyarthritis. Transmission to the fetus increases as pregnancy advances and is maximum in the third trimester. Congenital infection includes growth restriction, microcephaly, intracranial (periventricular) calcifications, chorioretinitis, mental and motor deficits, hepatosplenomegaly, hemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenic purpura. Most infected neonates are asymptomatic at birth and later present with these symptoms.

Pearl PF1853: Rubella and congenital rubella syndrome

Congenital rubella syndrome:

* The triad of Gregg in congenital rubella syndrome includes:

* Sensorineural hearing loss - Nerve deafness is the single most common finding among infants with congenital rubella syndrome

* Congenital cataract

* Congenital heart disease - The most common cardiac defect is patent ductus arteriosus

* Maximum damage to the fetus occurs in the first trimester

* Infection in the second trimester causes only deafness

* If infection occurs after 16 weeks there are no major abnormalities

* Diagnosis - Presence of IgM rubella antibodies in the infant shortly after birth or persistence of IgG antibodies for >6 months.

The given image shows bilateral cataract in an infant with congenital rubella syndrome

The given image shows blueberry muffin rash in an infant with congenital rubella syndrome

Rubella:

* Also called the German measles

* Causative organism belongs to the family Matonaviridae

* Period of infectivity is -5 to +6 days after the onset of the rash

* Droplet trasmission

* The incubation period is 2-3 weeks

* The rash appears on day 1

* Forchheimer spots are seen, which are tiny, rose-colored lesions in the oropharynx

* Associated with post-infectious thrombocytopenia

* The most serious complication is encephalitis

* Vaccination is done with the live attenuated RA 27/3 strain of the rubella
questions.learning: Rubella — The given clinical scenario of sensorineural deafness, patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), and a salt-and-pepper appearance on retinoscopy is indicative of congenital rubella syndrome, suggesting that the mother had a rubella infection.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An alcoholic male patient diagnosed with hollow viscus perforation is taken up for laparotomy. Intraoperatively, a 2 cm-sized perforation is seen in the gastric region as shown below. How can this patient be managed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Omental pedicle repair

The given scenario of an alcoholic male patient of gastric perforation showing intra-op large 2 cm size perforation can be managed by an Omental pedicle repair.

Gastroduodenal perforations are a common surgical emergency in developing countries. Causes: Peptic ulcer disease (PUD), Smoking, alcohol, chronic analgesic use. Patients present with hypotension and signs and symptoms of peritonitis- tenderness, guarding and rigidity. Management: Multiple surgical options exist depending on the perforation's location and size. Larger perforations and ulcers with fibrotic edges can be managed by an omental pedicle flap repair. A tongue of omentum is brought up to cover the ulcer defect and secured with a series of interrupted sutures. (Modified Graham's patch)

Option A: Small subcentric perforations with healthy margins can undergo primary repair and buttressed with an omental patch. (Graham's repair)

Option C: Removal of gastric antrum (antrectomy) with gastroduodenostomy is Billroth I reconstruction. It was done historically and avoided now due to higher morbidity with high rates of post-gastrectomy syndromes. In PUD, the duodenum may be scarred as well.

Option D: In Billroth II, two-thirds of the stomach is removed, the duodenal stump is closed and the stomach is anastomosed to the jejunum. It is now reserved for gastric malignancy and perforations associated with malignancy. It has higher rates of post-gastrectomy syndromes.
questions.learning: Omental pedicle repair — The given scenario of an alcoholic male patient of gastric perforation showing intra-op large 2 cm size perforation can be managed by an Omental pedicle repair.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is false regarding confounding factor?
options: It can be reduced by matching
It is associated individually with both cause and effect
It is distributed equally in both study and control groups
It is associated with the exposure of the study
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It is distributed equally in both study and control groups

A confounding factor is a factor that is associated with both exposure and diseases and is distributed unequally in study and control groups. It can be reduced by matching.

For example, if the study is that a sedentary lifestyle can lead to coronary artery diseases, then age can act as a confounding factor as it is individually linked to both sedentary lifestyle and coronary artery diseases.
questions.learning: It is distributed equally in both study and control groups A confounding factor is a factor that is associated with both exposure and diseases and is distributed unequally in study and control groups.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: An 8-year-old boy presents with continuous, profuse diarrhea of rice-water consistency for the past 20 hours, accompanied by drowsiness, altered responsiveness, sunken eyes, and decreased skin turgor. Which pathogen is most likely responsible for this clinical presentation?
questions.explanation: The description of "rice-water stools" is the hallmark of Cholera, caused by Vibrio cholerae. The boy’s symptoms—drowsiness, sunken eyes, and poor skin turgor—indicate severe dehydration resulting from massive secretory diarrhea. Vibrio cholerae toxin causes the permanent activation of adenylate cyclase in the intestinal cells, leading to the massive efflux of water and electrolytes into the gut lumen. Entamoeba coli (Option B) is a non-pathogenic commensal. Escherichia coli (Option C), specifically ETEC, can cause watery diarrhea but it is rarely as severe as the rice-water stools of cholera. Shigella sonnei (Option D) typically causes inflammatory diarrhea with blood and mucus (dysentery) rather than profuse watery stools. Immediate management of cholera focuses on aggressive fluid resuscitation using Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) or intravenous fluids to prevent hypovolemic shock. Therefore, the specific stool consistency and rapid dehydration confirm Vibrio cholerae as the pathogen
questions.learning: The description of "rice-water stools" is the hallmark of Cholera, caused by Vibrio cholerae. The boy’s symptoms—drowsiness, sunken eyes, and poor skin turgor—indicate severe dehydration resulting from massive secretory diarrhea.

questions.text: The presence of which structure is responsible for infants to be able to breathe simultaneously while suckling milk?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. High larynx

Infants can breathe and suckle simultaneously because of a highly placed larynx in the neck. Anatomical basis:

• In infants, the larynx lies at C2–C3 level (higher than adults)
• Epiglottis lies close to the soft palate
• Creates a near-separate airway and food passage
• Allows milk to pass laterally while airway remains patent

Changes with age:

• With growth, larynx descends to C4–C6 level
• Separation between airway and food passage increases
• Adults cannot breathe and swallow simultaneously

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is a correct triple drug regimen for the treatment of Helicobacter pylori infection?
questions.explanation: The eradication of H. pylori is crucial for treating and preventing the recurrence of peptic ulcer disease. The standard "Triple Therapy" regimen consists of a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) like Omeprazole combined with two antibiotics, most traditionally Clarithromycin and Metronidazole (or alternatively, Amoxicillin). This regimen is typically administered for 14 days. Option B is incorrect as Ciprofloxacin is not part of the standard first-line triple eradication therapy. Options A and C are variants but do not represent the classic clarithromycin-based triple therapy which is the internationally recognized benchmark. In regions with high macrolide resistance, Quadruple Therapy—which includes a PPI, Bismuth, Tetracycline, and Metronidazole—may be used instead. However, among the provided options, the combination of a PPI with clarithromycin and metronidazole is the definitive triple-drug standard

questions.text: Which one of the following statements regarding Cantlie’s line is correct?
options: Runs between gall bladder fossa and right hepatic vein
Runs between gall bladder fossa and right branch of portal vein
Runs between gall bladder fossa and middle hepatic vein
Runs between gall bladder fossa and left branch of portal vein
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Runs between gall bladder fossa and middle hepatic vein

Cantlie’s line is an imaginary line extending from the gallbladder fossa anteriorly to the inferior vena cava posteriorly, following the course of the middle hepatic vein. It divides the liver into the functional right and left hemilivers based on vascular inflow and biliary drainage.

Why not the other options?

• A. Right hepatic vein: Right hepatic vein divides the right lobe into anterior and posterior sectors.
• B. Right branch of portal vein: Not the landmark for Cantlie’s line.
• D. Left branch of portal vein: Not the landmark for Cantlie’s line.

questions.text: Which of the following is not a component of School Health under Ayushman Bharat Program?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Monthly IFA supplementations

Under the School Health Programme of Ayushman Bharat, services include periodic health check-ups, biannual deworming with albendazole, and menstrual hygiene support, including sanitary napkin distribution.

Iron–folic acid supplementation under this program follows the Weekly Iron and Folic Acid Supplementation (WIFS) strategy, not monthly dosing.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 65-year-old man has the following lesion over the face. He complains of bleeding while itching. The most likely diagnosis is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. BCC

The given history with the image showing an ulcer over the face with pearly, rolled-out borders points to a diagnosis of basal cell carcinoma.

Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is an epithelial tumor arising from basal cells. It is the most common type of skin cancer most commonly seen over the face, above the line joining corner of the mouth, and lobule of the ear. Risk factors for BCC include ultraviolet radiation (strongest risk factor), age 40-80 years with excessive sun exposure, light-skinned people, and exposure to arsenic compounds, coal tar, aromatic hydrocarbons, and infrared light. It is more common in males than females. It is also associated with syndromes such as xeroderma pigmentosum and Gorlin's syndrome.

Features of BCC include:

• Pearly nodule with rolled border
• Tortuous telangiectatic vessels
• Surface which can get ulcerated with raised and beaded edge, often with a central depression or umbilication
• Bleeding on minor trauma

BCC has various subtypes such as nodular (most common type), pigmented, nodulocystic, morphoeic, infiltrative, and fibroepithelioma of Pinkus.

It is locally aggressive and can erode the bone or facial sinuses. It rarely metastasizes via lymph nodes.

The occasional presence of melanin in the nodular variant of BCC (pigmented BCC) may lead to confusion with melanoma.

Depending upon the type of the lesion, a shave, punch or excisional biopsy may be employed for diagnosis. X-ray or CT may be needed if there is a local invasion. Histology shows peripheral palisading of cells.

Treatment:

• Surgical: Wide excision (4-6 mm clearance) with a skin graft or flap or primary suturing
• Mohs' surgery for BCC close to the eyes, nose, or ear to preserve more tissue.
• Non-surgical: Radiotherapy, vismodegib and sonedegib.

Other options:

Option A: Dermatofibrosarcoma, also known as dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP) is a rare, slow-growing, well-differentiated primary fibrosarcoma of the skin, associated with increased production of platelet-derived growth factor-beta. It presents as a protuberant nodule within a firm, indurated plaque that can ulcerate. They are locally aggressive tumors with high recurrence rates. Treatment is wide excision and Mohs microscopic surgery. Imatinib is used for unresectable, metastatic, and recurrent tumors. The given image below shows a DFSP near the umbilicus.

Option B: Marjolin's ulcer is a painless, slow-growing, locally malignant, well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma that occurs in a chronic scar (burns scar, scar of venous ulcer). It presents as an indurated, non-tender ulcer with raised and everted edges with scarring in the surrounding area with marked fibrosis. The ulcer can spread to the lymph nodes when it reaches the normal skin. A wedge biopsy and MRI of the region involved confirm the diagnosis. Management is by wide excision, for larger ulcers, amputation is done. The given image below shows a marjolin's ulcer of the leg.

Option D: Naevus is a common benign neoplasm caused due to mutations in the components of the RAS signaling pathway. It has various types, such as congenital naevus, blue naevus, Spitz naevus, halo naevus, and dysplastic naevus. The given image below shows a patient with multiple dysplastic nevi.
questions.learning: BCC — The given history with the image showing an ulcer over the face with pearly, rolled-out borders points to a diagnosis of basal cell carcinoma. Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is an epithelial tumor arising from basal cells.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following cranial nerve nuclei is not a part of the special visceral afferent (SVA) column?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Trochlear nerve

The trochlear nerve nucleus is a part of the general somatic efferent (GSE) column, not the special visceral afferent column.

The trochlear nerve is a motor nerve that innervates superior oblique muscle in the orbit.

The neurons of the general somatic efferent (GSE) column innervate the extrinsic ocular muscles and muscles of the tongue (III, IV, VI, and XII cranial nerves).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: All the following cause widening of confidence interval except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increase in sample size

All the given options cause a widening of confidence interval except for an increase in sample size. An increase in sample size leads to a narrower confidence interval.

Research is usually done with samples drawn from a population, rather than by using the entire population. In order to get a fair idea of the population parameters, sample statistics and estimates of error in the sample are used to get a range of values. This range is the confidence interval (CI). It is estimated based on a desirable confidence level.

The confidence interval is calculated as the difference between upper and lower confidence limits.

The width of the CI is an indication of the utility of our population parameter estimation. Factors affecting the width of the confidence interval include:

• Desired confidence level- width of CI is directly proportionate to the confidence level
• Variability in the sample- width of CI is directly proportionate to the variability in the data
• Sample size- width of the CI is inversely related to the sample size

Therefore, increases in variability and confidence levels and decreases in sample size lead to wider confidence intervals.
questions.learning: Increase in sample size All the given options cause a widening of confidence interval except for an increase in sample size. An increase in sample size leads to a narrower confidence interval.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following congenital heart disease has equal saturation in all the chambers of the heart?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Total anomalous pulmonary venous circulation

In total anomalous pulmonary venous circulation (TAPVC), there is equal saturation in all chambers of the heart.

In TAPVC, the oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins reaches the right atrium (having deoxygenated blood) instead of the left atrium. It occurs due to the draining of the pulmonary veins to the superior vena cava or to the inferior vena cava or to both. This is a total mixing lesion. The blood from this right atrium (RA) passes to the right ventricle and pulmonary artery. This blood also reaches the left atrium through the atrial septal defect or the patent foramen ovale, and subsequently, to the left ventricle The left atrium is not receiving any blood because all of the pulmonary veins are draining to the right atrium. Therefore, this shunt will be the only source of blood to it. Since blood from right atrium reaches all the other chambers, the oxygen saturation of the blood in all four chambers is the same.

In (TAPVC), there are three main types: supra-cardiac, cardiac, and infra-cardiac. In supra-cardiac TAPVC, the pulmonary veins merge to form a single vein that drains into either the superior vena cava or the left innominate vein. In cardiac TAPVC, the pulmonary veins directly drain into the right atrium or coronary sinus. The most dangerous type is infra-cardiac TAPVC, which is always obstructive. In this type, the pulmonary veins drain into either the portal vein or the inferior vena cava.

Diagnosis of TAPVC is the demonstration of any vein with doppler flow away from the heart because the normal venous flow is usually toward the heart.

Surgical correction of TAPVR is done in infancy. Pulmonary venous confluence is anastomosed directly to the left atrium, the ASD is closed, and any connection to the systemic venous circuit is interrupted.

Other options

Option A - Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) comprises right ventricular outflow tract obstruction, ventricular septal defect (VSD), overriding of the aorta over the ventricular septum, and right ventricular hypertrophy. Right ventricular outflow tract obstruction increases the pressure in the right ventricle. This causes right to left shunt through the ventricular septal defect. The deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle mixes with the oxygenated blood in the left ventricle. Therefore, in this condition, the left atrium has a higher oxygen saturation compared to the left ventricle due to mixing. The right atria and ventricles have the least oxygen saturation.

Option C - Tricuspid atresia is the congenital absence of the tricuspid valve. Therefore, the blood in the right atrium is shunted to the left atrium through the patent foramen ovale or the atrial septal defect. In the left atrium, the blood from the right atrium mixes with the oxygenated blood and the oxygen saturation decreases. However, the oxygen saturation in the left atrium and left ventricle is still greater compared to that of the hypoplastic right ventricle.

Option D -  Transposition of great arteries (TGA) is characterized by the aorta arising from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left ventricle. Because of this, the pulmonary and systemic circulations remain separate. The right side of the heart has deoxygenated blood and the left side of the heart has oxygenated blood. The pulmonary artery saturation is always higher than the aortic saturation.
questions.learning: Total anomalous pulmonary venous circulation — In total anomalous pulmonary venous circulation (TAPVC), there is equal saturation in all chambers of the heart.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which intermediate of the TCA cycle participates in fatty acid synthesis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Citrate

Citrate is the TCA cycle intermediate that links carbohydrate metabolism with fatty acid synthesis.

Role of citrate in fatty acid synthesis

• In the mitochondria, acetyl-CoA enters the TCA cycle and combines with oxaloacetate to form citrate.
• When cellular energy is abundant, citrate is transported from the mitochondria to the cytosol.
• In the cytosol, ATP-citrate lyase cleaves citrate into:

• Acetyl-CoA
• Oxaloacetate

The acetyl-CoA produced in the cytosol is the precursor for fatty acid synthesis.

Citrate also Activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase, the rate-limiting enzyme of fatty acid synthesis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Male infertility is diagnosed with karyotype 47 XXY. Which of the following statement is false:
questions.explanation: The karyotype 47, XXY is diagnostic for Klinefelter syndrome, the most common genetic cause of male infertility. The hallmark of the condition is primary hypogonadism. Because the seminiferous tubules undergo hyalinization and fibrosis (Option B is true) and the Sertoli cells are dysfunctional, there is a lack of inhibin production. This results in the loss of negative feedback to the pituitary, leading to a significant increase in FSH levels; therefore, stating FSH is decreased (Option A) is the FALSE statement. Other characteristic features include decreased testis size (Option C is true), azoospermia, and increased LH levels due to Leydig cell dysfunction. Physically, these patients often present with tall stature, gynecomastia, and reduced secondary sexual hair. Both A and B (Option D) is incorrect because B is a true pathological finding. Klinefelter syndrome remains a high-yield clinical entity in medical examinations, emphasizing the biochemical-pathological correlation of hypergonadotropic hypogonadism resulting from the extra X chromosome
questions.learning: The karyotype 47, XXY is diagnostic for Klinefelter syndrome, the most common genetic cause of male infertility. The hallmark of the condition is primary hypogonadism.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which substance inhibits the iron transporter on the basal side of the enterocyte?
questions.explanation: Iron homeostasis is primarily regulated by hepcidin, a peptide hormone produced by the liver. Hepcidin controls iron levels by binding to and triggering the internalisation and degradation of ferroportin (Option D). Ferroportin is the only known iron exporter, located on the basolateral (basal) membrane of enterocytes and on macrophages. By inhibiting ferroportin, hepcidin prevents iron from entering the bloodstream, effectively lowering serum iron levels. Ferritin (Option B) is the primary intracellular storage protein for iron. Transferrin (Option C) is the primary transport protein that carries iron through the blood. During inflammation, hepcidin levels rise as an acute-phase reactant, leading to the sequestration of iron and the development of "anemia of chronic disease". Conversely, in hereditary hemochromatosis, hepcidin levels are inappropriately low, leading to excessive iron absorption and systemic iron overload. This molecular switch is the master regulator of body iron stores
questions.learning: Iron homeostasis is primarily regulated by hepcidin, a peptide hormone produced by the liver. Hepcidin controls iron levels by binding to and triggering the internalisation and degradation of ferroportin (Option D).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-year-old girl was brought by her mother with complaints of enlarged clitoris. Karyotype revealed 46XX. What is the likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 21 hydroxylase deficiency

The given clinical scenario of a girl (46XX) with an enlarged clitoris is highly suggestive of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency.

Congenital adrenal hyperplasia/adrenogenital syndrome is a family of autosomal-recessive disorders caused by the deficiency of enzymes involved in the synthesis of steroid hormones in the adrenal cortex. The majority of cases of CAH are caused by 21-hydroxylase deficiency. This deficiency leads to a lack of synthesis of cortisol and aldosterone, resulting in the salt-wasting form of the disease, which is the most severe form.

Severe 21-hydroxylase deficiency presents with symptoms including weight loss, dehydration, weakness, hypotension, and electrolyte imbalances. Accumulated steroid precursors like 17-hydroxyprogesterone, are shunted into the pathway of androgen synthesis leading to elevated levels of androstenedione and testosterone. This can result in abnormal genital development in affected female fetuses during early gestation.

Females may have masculinized external genitalia. This can include enlargement of the clitoris, partial or complete labial fusion, and a shared opening of the vagina and urethra (urogenital sinus).

Untreated individuals develop signs of androgen excess after birth.  These signs include accelerated skeletal maturation, premature epiphyseal closure leading to stunted adult stature, excessive muscular development, the appearance of pubic and axillary hair, acne, and deepening of the voice. In males, enlargement of the penis, scrotum, and prostate. In females, the clitoris may become further enlarged.

Diagnosis of confirmed by elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone levels. Glucocorticoid replacement with hydrocortisone is done. In a salt-wasting crisis, fludrocortisone supplementation is given. Vaginoplasty and clitoral recession are done for females with ambiguous genitalia.
questions.learning: 21 hydroxylase deficiency The given clinical scenario of a girl (46XX) with an enlarged clitoris is highly suggestive of congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 48-year-old woman undergoes a minor pelvic surgery involving dissection along the lateral pelvic wall. During the procedure, a nerve that passes through a canal is inadvertently injured. Postoperatively, she has difficulty in adduction of thigh while walking, along with loss of sensation over the medial aspect of the thigh. Which nerve was most likely injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Obturator nerve

The obturator nerve (L2–L4) arises from the lumbar plexus and exits the pelvis through the obturator canal to supply the adductor muscles of the thigh and provide sensory innervation to the medial aspect of the thigh. It is at risk of injury during pelvic lymph node dissection, gynecologic surgery, and surgery along the lateral pelvic wall.

Why not the other options?

• A. Femoral nerve: Supplies the quadriceps (knee extension) and sensation over the anterior thigh and medial leg; injury causes difficulty climbing stairs and reduced patellar reflex, not isolated loss of thigh adduction.
• B. Sciatic nerve: Supplies the posterior thigh and most muscles below the knee; injury causes foot drop and weakness of knee flexion, not medial thigh sensory loss.
• D. Superior gluteal nerve: Supplies gluteus medius and minimus; injury causes a Trendelenburg gait due to hip abductor weakness.
questions.learning: Obturator nerve — The obturator nerve (L2–L4) arises from the lumbar plexus and exits the pelvis through the obturator canal to supply the adductor muscles of the thigh and provide sensory innervation to the medial aspect of the thigh.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is the best line of treatment in a 3-year-old child presenting with a recent onset of 15-degree accommodative esotropia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Refractive correction

The best line of treatment in accommodative esotropia is a refractive correction.

Esotropia for distance is corrected by the treatment of hypermetropia: convex glasses

Esotropia for near is corrected by +3DS lens.

Algorithm for the management of accommodative esotropia is as follows:

* R: Refractive correction: Glasses/Miotics

* O: Orthoptics/Occlusion: for amblyopia

* O: Operative correction: for non-accommodative component

* P: Prism correction: for remaining error
questions.learning: Refractive correction — The best line of treatment in accommodative esotropia is a refractive correction. Esotropia for distance is corrected by the treatment of hypermetropia: convex glasses Esotropia for near is corrected by +3DS lens.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient with occupational exposure to benzene presents with repeated infections, easy fatigability, weight loss, and evening rise of temperature. This occupational exposure will predispose him to which of the following cancers?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Leukemia

Occupational exposure to benzene predisposes to leukemia. The given clinical history of repeated infections, easy fatigability, weight loss, and evening rise of temperature with benzene exposure points towards a diagnosis of leukemia.

Benzene is oxidized to an epoxide through hepatic CYP2E1. The epoxide and other metabolites disrupt progenitor cell differentiation in the bone marrow and lead to marrow aplasia and acute myeloid leukemia.

Acute myeloid leukemia is a tumor of hematopoietic progenitors caused by acquired oncogenic mutations that impede differentiation. This leads to the accumulation of immature myeloid blasts in the marrow. The replacement of the marrow with blasts produces marrow failure and complications related to anemia, thrombocytopenia, and neutropenia.

Other options:

Option B: Exposure to arsenic and its compounds, asbestos, beryllium and its compounds, chromium compounds, nickel compounds, radon, and its decay products can cause lung cancer.

Option C: Exposure to aryl amines, particularly 2-naphthylamine and related compounds, cyclophosphamide, cigarette smoking, irradiation can cause bladder cancer.

Option D: Exposure to UV rays, arsenic, and its compounds can cause skin cancer.
questions.learning: Leukemia Occupational exposure to benzene predisposes to leukemia. The given clinical history of repeated infections, easy fatigability, weight loss, and evening rise of temperature with benzene exposure points towards a diagnosis of leukemia.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Under RBSK screening which one of the following diseases is not covered?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Congenital glaucoma

All of the above conditions are included in child health screening & early intervention services under RBSK (Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram) except congenital glaucoma.

The RBSK aims at the universal screening of the 4 ‘D’s i.e Defects at birth, Deficiencies, Diseases, Developmental delays including disabilities that would lead to early identification, timely management, and ultimately a reduction in morbidity, mortality, and lifelong disability in children.

Health conditions selected for the child (0-18 years) health screening and early intervention services are:

Defects:

• Neural tube defect
• Down’s syndrome
• Cleft lip and palate
• Talipes
• Developmental dysplasia of the hip
• Congenital cataract, congenital deafness, congenital heart disease
• Retinopathy of prematurity

Deficiencies:

• Anemia especially severe anemia
• Vitamin A deficiency
• Vitamin D deficiency
• Severe acute malnutrition
• Goitre

Diseases:

• Scabies, fungal infections, and eczema
• Otitis media
• Rheumatic heart disease
• Reactive airway disease
• Dental caries
• Convulsive disorders

Developmental delays and disabilities:

• Vision, hearing, and neuro-motor impairment
• Motor, cognitive and language delay
• Autism
• Learning disorder
• Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
questions.learning: Congenital glaucoma All of the above conditions are included in child health screening & early intervention services under RBSK (Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram) except congenital glaucoma.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32-year-old G2P1 is diagnosed to have DVT at 30 weeks. The drug of choice is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. LMWH (Low Molecular Weight Heparin)

LMWH is the treatment of choice for DVT in pregnancy because it does not cross the placenta and has a predictable safety profile. Warfarin and DOACs (e.g., apixaban) cross the placenta and are unsafe. Fondaparinux is reserved for HIT.
questions.learning: LMWH (Low Molecular Weight Heparin) LMWH is the treatment of choice for DVT in pregnancy because it does not cross the placenta and has a predictable safety profile.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Epiblast first migration lead to formation of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endoderm

The correct answer is Endoderm.

During gastrulation, the first wave of epiblast cell migration displaces the hypoblast to form the definitive endoderm.

The second wave forms intraembryonic mesoderm, while cells remaining in epiblast become ectoderm.

The notochord is derived later from axial mesoderm, not the initial migration.
questions.learning: Endoderm — The correct answer is Endoderm. During gastrulation, the first wave of epiblast cell migration displaces the hypoblast to form the definitive endoderm.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which among the following is not preferred as an analgesic in rheumatoid arthritis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ketorolac

Ketorolac is not preferred in rheumatoid arthritis. It is a potent analgesic but a moderately effective anti-inflammatory drug.

Ketorolac is not administered in chronic painful conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and its use is limited to 5 days or less for acute conditions.
questions.learning: Ketorolac Ketorolac is not preferred in rheumatoid arthritis. It is a potent analgesic but a moderately effective anti-inflammatory drug.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Anti-citrullinated peptide antibody is useful in diagnosis of:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Rheumatoid arthritis

Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (Anti-CCP or ACPA) antibodies are highly specific serological markers for Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA). They may be detected years before the onset of symptoms and are associated with more aggressive, erosive disease and a poorer prognosis.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Sjögren’s syndrome: Characteristically associated with Anti-Ro (SSA) and Anti-La (SSB) antibodies.
• C. Scleroderma: Associated with Anti-centromere antibodies (limited cutaneous disease) and Anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I) antibodies (diffuse disease).
• D. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE): Characteristically associated with ANA, Anti-dsDNA, and Anti-Smith (Sm) antibodies.
questions.learning: Rheumatoid arthritis Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (Anti-CCP or ACPA) antibodies are highly specific serological markers for Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA).

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: The most specific and typical sign of juvenile dermatomyositis in a 17-year-old patient is
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Gottron’s papules.

Gottron papules are typical and specific sign of juvenile dermatomyositis.

Gottron papules and a heliotropic rash of the eyelids are the classical criteria that are required for the diagnosis of juvenile dermatomyositis along with three of the following:

Weakness

Symmetric

Proximal

Muscle enzyme elevation (≥1)

Creatine kinase

Aspartate aminotransferase

Lactate dehydrogenase

Aldolase

Electromyographic changes

Short, small polyphasic motor unit potentials

Fibrillations

Positive sharp waves

Insertional irritability

Bizarre, high-frequency repetitive discharges

Muscle biopsy

Necrosis

Inflammation

Gottron’s papules are violaceous (of violet color), lichenoid (red-purple), inflammatory, flat-topped papules on proximal interphalangeal joints, distal interphalangeal joints, and metacarpophalangeal joints.

This should not be confused with Gottron's sign.

Gottron's sign is erythematous or violaceous, macules or patches in the same symmetric distribution pattern but sparing the interphalangeal spaces and sometimes involving elbows and knees.

The heliotrope rash is a violet discoloration of the eyelids that may be associated with periorbital edema. Rarely, an erythematous, scaly rash develops on the palms of the children called ‘mechanic hands’. Nail bed capillary changes are visible as individual thickened and telengiectatic capillary loops, which can be well seen with the help of capillaroscopy. Facial erythema mimicking malar rash of systemic lupus erythematosus, but with the involvement of nasolabial folds are also common.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In case of professional misconduct, the patient's records on demand should be provided within:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 72 hours

In case of professional misconduct, the patient's records on demand should be provided within 72 hours.

If a doctor does not maintain the medical records of the patients for a period of three years as per the regulation, and refuses to provide the same within 72 hours, when the patient or his/her authorized representative makes a request for it, then it is professional misconduct.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 22-year-old pregnant woman at 13 weeks of gestation informs you about accidental exposure to radiation from a chest X-ray at 7 weeks of gestation. What should be the next step advised to her?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Continue pregnancy

In the given clinical case, the patient should be advised to continue the pregnancy.

The radiation dose to the fetus during the declared term of pregnancy should be less than 1 mSv. In chest X-ray PA view, the absorbed dose of radiation by the fetus is less than 0.1 mSv. Hence, pregnancy can be continued.

An X-ray has a very limited role in obstetric imaging. There are very few indications where an X-ray will be useful:

• Fetal: congenital malformation of the fetus and neonates, skeletal malformations, birth injuries like fractures or dislocations.
• Maternal:  Patients having cardiopulmonary disease may require an X-ray chest during pregnancy and that should be done beyond 12 weeks.

Radiation can cause fetal morbidity (FGR, genetic mutations, neurologic abnormalities, mental retardation, childhood leukemia) and mortality. The risks are high with radiation after the first 2 weeks postconception and within the first trimester (period of organogenesis).

Radiation during pregnancy can damage the early phase of the embryo but the risk can be minimized by using the ‘10-day rule’. This rule states that no woman should be exposed to an X-ray for a nonurgent indication outside 10 days from her last period during the reproductive period unless the pregnancy is excluded.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: False statement regarding nephroblastoma?
options: Treatment is chemotherapy followed by surgery
Most common intra abdominal malignancy in children
questions.explanation: Nephroblastoma (Wilms tumor) is the most common intra-abdominal malignancy in children and usually presents as a localized renal mass. It primarily spreads via the hematogenous route, most commonly to the lungs, and less commonly to the liver and bones. Hence, option (C) is correct. However, early lung metastasis is NOT typical. In most cases, Wilms tumor is confined to the kidney at diagnosis, and metastasis occurs later in advanced stages (Stage IV). Therefore, stating that early lung metastases are common is false, making option (B) the correct answer. Option (A) is considered correct in many exam settings following the SIOP protocol, where neoadjuvant chemotherapy is given before surgery to shrink the tumor and reduce surgical complications. Option (D) is also correct as Wilms tumor is the most common intra-abdominal malignancy in children
questions.learning: Nephroblastoma (Wilms tumor) is the most common intra-abdominal malignancy in children and usually presents as a localized renal mass. It primarily spreads via the hematogenous route, most commonly to the lungs, and less commonly to the liver and bones.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Patient has pain in the facial nerve distribution while chewing and speaking. Which of the following drug should be given for the treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Carbamazepine

The clinical symptoms are suggestive of trigeminal neuralgia. Carbamazepine, a Sodium-channel blocker, is the primary agent for the treatment of trigeminal neuralgia.

It slows the recovery rate of voltage-activated sodium channels from their inactivated state.

Carbamazepine is most effective in complex partial seizures. It is also used in GTCS and simple partial seizures, trigeminal and related neuralgias, manic depressive psychosis.

Carbamazepine potentiates the action of antidiuretic hormone (ADH). It can result in water retention with decreased osmolarity and hyponatremia, especially in elderly patients with cardiac disease. Carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine can cause leukopenia, aplastic anemia, or hepato-toxicity, and hyponatremia in the elderly.

Idiosyncratic blood dyscrasias with carbamazepine, include fatal cases of aplastic anemia and agranulocytosis. The most common idiosyncratic reaction is an erythematous skin rash. It can rarely cause Steven Johnson Syndrome.
questions.learning: Carbamazepine — The clinical symptoms are suggestive of trigeminal neuralgia. Carbamazepine, a Sodium-channel blocker, is the primary agent for the treatment of trigeminal neuralgia.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In evaluating a patient with nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR), which of the following findings would be atypical for a classification of 'very severe’?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Neovascularization of disc

Very severe nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR) is defined by the “4-2-1 rule”:

• 4 quadrants of severe retinal hemorrhages/microaneurysms
• 2 quadrants of venous beading
• 1 quadrant of IRMA (intraretinal microvascular abnormalities)

These findings indicate severe ischemia but WITHOUT neovascularization.

| NPDR Severity Level | Findings on Dilated Eye Exam

| ------------------- | ----------------------------

| Mild NPDR | Microaneurysms only

| Moderate NPDR | Microaneurysms with additional findings (dot & blot hemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton wool spots), but less than severe NPDR

| Severe NPDR | Any one of the following (4-2-1 rule) and no signs of proliferative DR:• ≥20 intraretinal hemorrhages in all 4 quadrants• Venous beading in ≥2 quadrants• IRMA in ≥1 quadrant

| Very Severe NPDR | Any two of the 4-2-1 rule features

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a 7-year- old boy with intellectual disability who presents with widespread warty crusts on the trunk, hands, and feet, along with severe fissuring and scaling of the soles?
questions.explanation: Norwegian Scabies, also known as Crusted Scabies, is an extreme infestation seen in patients with weakened immune systems or significant intellectual/neurological disabilities who cannot scratch. In these cases, the mites multiply into the millions, resulting in the formation of thick, warty crusts on the hands, feet, and trunk, rather than the typical few burrows. Severe scaling and fissuring on the soles are characteristic. Scabies incognito (Option A) occurs when steroid use masks typical inflammation. Animal scabies (Option B) is a self-limiting condition from pets. Nodular scabies (Option C) presents as persistent itchy bumps in children. Because the clinical description emphasizes "extensive warty crusts" and an underlying disability, crusted/Norwegian scabies is the definitive diagnosis. It is highly contagious and requires aggressive treatment with oral Ivermectin and topical permethrin
questions.learning: Norwegian Scabies, also known as Crusted Scabies, is an extreme infestation seen in patients with weakened immune systems or significant intellectual/neurological disabilities who cannot scratch.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 26-year-old man touches a hot metal surface and immediately withdraws his hand, experiencing a burning pain sensation. The receptor responsible for detecting this stimulus is most likely mediated by which of the following ion channels?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. TRPV1

TRPV1 (Transient Receptor Potential Vanilloid 1) is a nociceptive ion channel present on sensory nerve endings that detects noxious heat and burning pain.

• Activated by temperatures > 43°C, capsaicin (from chili peppers), and acidic conditions.
• Opening of the channel allows Na⁺ and Ca²⁺ influx, leading to depolarization of pain fibers (C fibers) and perception of burning pain.

Other channels:

A. TRPM8: Detects cold temperatures and menthol.

C. TRPA1: Detects chemical irritants and environmental toxins.

D. Piezo channels: Mechanoreceptors involved in touch and pressure sensation.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A child develops fever, severe pain, and swelling of the left eye a few days after sustaining a dog bite near the eye. Clinical examination reveals mild proptosis with restricted ocular movements. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The key clinical findings that point specifically to Orbital Cellulitis in this scenario are restricted ocular movements (ophthalmoplegia) and proptosis (bulging of the eye). These signs indicate that the infection has spread posterior to the orbital septum, affecting the extraocular muscles and orbital contents. Why the other options are incorrect: (D) Preseptal cellulitis: While this also causes eyelid swelling and fever, it is a superficial infection. Crucially, in preseptal cellulitis, ocular movements are normal, there is no proptosis, and vision is unaffected. (B) Endophthalmitis: This is an inflammation of the inner coats of the eye, usually following surgery or penetrating trauma. While it causes pain and vision loss, it does not typically cause proptosis or restricted eye movements unless it progresses to panophthalmitis. (C) Panophthalmitis: This is a more severe, destructive inflammation of all coats of the eye, including the Tenon's capsule. While it does feature proptosis and restricted movement, the patient would be much more toxic, usually with a complete loss of vision and a globe that is essentially a "bag of pus." Given the history of a dog bite (external trauma), orbital cellulitis is the more direct and likely progression
questions.learning: The key clinical findings that point specifically to Orbital Cellulitis in this scenario are restricted ocular movements (ophthalmoplegia) and proptosis (bulging of the eye).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 26-year-old pregnant woman, on examination was found to have infra-umbilical flattening. The fetal heart sounds were heard over the lateral side. What could be the fetal presentation/position?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Occipitoposterior

The presence of infra-umbilical flattening and fetal heart sounds on the lateral side indicates that the fetus is in the occipito-posterior position.

Occipito-posterior (OP) position of the fetus is when the occiput is situated posteriorly over the sacroiliac joint, or directly over the sacrum. The fetus is in vertex presentation.

Examination findings of OP position:

• On inspection, the abdomen appears flattened below the umbilicus (infra-umbilical flattening).
• Pelvic grips:

• The head is not engaged.
• The sinciput (cephalic prominence) is not prominently felt.

• Auscultation: Fetal heart sounds are heard maximally over the flanks. However, in the direct OP position, they are heard in the midline.

There are three variants of OP position:

• Left OP position (fourth position of the vertex) - When the occiput points towards the left sacroiliac joint.
• Right OP position (third position of the vertex) - When the occiput points towards the right sacroiliac joint. It is more common than the left OP position.
• Direct OP position - When the occiput points directly towards the sacrum.

All three positions may be primary (present before the onset of labor) or secondary (develops after the onset of labor).

Other options:

Option A: Brow presentation is a rare type of cephalic presentation where the position of the head is in between full flexion and full extension. The part of the head between the orbital ridge and the anterior fontanel presents at the pelvic inlet.

Option B: Knee presentation is a type of breech presentation. Here, the thighs are extended but the knees are flexed, presenting at the pelvic inlet. The head will be palpable as a hard globular mass at the fundus.

Option D: Right dorso-anterior position is when the fetal back is directed anteriorly. This occurs in a transverse lie. On examination, the abdomen appears wide, and a hard plane of resistance is felt. The fundus extends just above the umbilicus. The head is felt in one iliac fossa and the breech is felt in the other.
questions.learning: Occipitoposterior — The presence of infra-umbilical flattening and fetal heart sounds on the lateral side indicates that the fetus is in the occipito-posterior position.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Gutter fracture of skull bone is associated with impact due to ___.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. a bullet

A gutter fracture of the skull is a furrow in the outer table of the skull, ordinarily the result of a glancing blow by a missile from a rifled firearm.

Gutter fractures refer to furrows in the outer table of the skull, as a result of a blow by a missile from a rifled firearm. These may be accompanied by comminuted depressed fractures of the inner table of the skull.

Pearl PF0368: Types of skull vault fracture

Diastatic fracture - Separation of sutures due to blow with blunt weapon or from cerebral edema. It is also called sutural fracture.

Fissured fracture/Linear fracture:

* Linear skull fractures are breaks in the bone that traverse the full thickness of the skull from the outer to inner table.

* They are usually fairly straight with no bone displacement.

* The common cause of injury is blunt force trauma where the impact energy transferred over a wide area of the skull.

Pond fracture - Occurs in children due to elasticity of bones. It is also known as indented fracture.

Depressed fracture - Caused by a heavy weapon with a small striking surface. Its shape indicates the type of weapon which is produced. So it is also called 'signature fracture'.

Comminuted fracture - It is also called spider web fracture and has a stellate appearance where there is no displacement of fracture.
questions.learning: a bullet A gutter fracture of the skull is a furrow in the outer table of the skull, ordinarily the result of a glancing blow by a missile from a rifled firearm.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient, a known case of chronic alcoholism is brought to the emergency room with confusion and tremors. On examination, there is ataxia and ophthalmoplegia. Deficiency of which of the following is responsible for the condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vitamin B1

This patient's clinical features are suggestive of Wernicke's encephalopathy. It is seen due to the deficiency of thiamine/vitamin B1.

Wernicke's encephalopathy/alcoholic encephalopathy is an acute neurological disorder. Glucose infusions may precipitate Wernicke’s disease in a previously unaffected patient or cause a rapid worsening of an early form of the disease (as in this patient). For this reason, thiamine should be administered to all alcoholic patients requiring parenteral glucose.

The triad is (mnemonic - GOA):

* Global Confusion

* Ophthalmoplegia (first symptom to improve with thiamine +dextrose infusion)

* Ataxia

Alcohol abuse leads to thiamine deficiency by the following mechanisms:

* Poor nutritional habits

* Folate deficiency which reduces thiamine absorption from the gastrointestinal tract

* Direct damage of the intestinal mucosa

The initial treatment in a patient with Wernicke's disease should be emergent thiamine infusion, either IM or IV. This should be given daily until a normal diet is resumed and before treatment with IV glucose. Administration of glucose before thiamine can worsen Wernicke's encephalopathy.
questions.learning: Vitamin B1 — This patient's clinical features are suggestive of Wernicke's encephalopathy. It is seen due to the deficiency of thiamine/vitamin B1.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 3-month-old infant presents with severe hepatomegaly, bilateral cataracts, lethargy, and hypotonia. Based on these clinical features, which enzyme deficiency is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: The clinical constellation of hepatomegaly, jaundice, lethargy, and bilateral cataracts in early infancy is highly suggestive of Classic Galactosemia. This autosomal recessive disorder is caused by a deficiency in the enzyme Galactose-1-phosphate uridyl transferase (GALT). The accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate in tissues is toxic, leading to liver failure and renal damage, while the conversion of galactose to galactitol in the lens causes cataracts. Galactokinase deficiency (Option A) also causes cataracts but typically does not present with severe systemic disease or hepatomegaly. Hepatic Glucose-6-Phosphatase deficiency (Option C) is von Gierke's disease, which causes severe hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly but not cataracts. Hepatic Synthase deficiency (Option B) would lead to glycogen depletion and hypoglycemia but lacks the specific ocular and hepatic toxicity of galactosemia. Early diagnosis and a lactose-free diet are critical to preventing irreversible brain damage and improving the prognosis for infants with GALT deficiency
questions.learning: The clinical constellation of hepatomegaly, jaundice, lethargy, and bilateral cataracts in early infancy is highly suggestive of Classic Galactosemia.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is not true about T1-weighted MRI images? (NEET Pg 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fluid appears bright

On T1-weighted MRI sequences, fluid appears dark (hypointense), not bright. This fundamental principle of MRI physics is demonstrated throughout clinical imaging, where cerebrospinal fluid in the ventricles and spinal canal appears dark on T1-weighted images, providing natural contrast against the brighter surrounding tissues.

Other Options:

Option A. Short TR - T1-weighted sequences utilize a short TR (repetition time). The repetition time between radiofrequency pulses is deliberately kept short to emphasize T1 relaxation properties of tissues.

Option B. Short TE - T1-weighted sequences utilize a short TE (echo time). The brief interval between the pulse and the resultant echo minimizes T2 effects and maximizes T1 contrast.
questions.learning: Fluid appears bright On T1-weighted MRI sequences, fluid appears dark (hypointense), not bright. This fundamental principle of MRI physics is demonstrated throughout clinical imaging, where cerebrospinal fluid in the ventricles and spinal canal appears…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A person has recently traveled from Nigeria to the United States. Which vaccination is mandatory for international travel from Nigeria to the USA?
questions.explanation: Nigeria is classified as a Yellow Fever endemic zone. Under the WHO's International Health Regulations, travelers moving from endemic areas to other countries, including the USA, are required to present a valid international certificate of vaccination for Yellow Fever to prevent the global spread of the virus. The Yellow Fever (17D) vaccine is a live-attenuated viral vaccine given as a single subcutaneous dose, which provides life-long immunity. The certificate is valid starting 10 days after vaccination. The JE vaccine (Option B) is recommended for travel to rural Asia-Pacific regions, not for Nigeria–USA travel. Measles (Option C) and Rabies (Option D) vaccines are part of general public health or high-risk group immunization but are not mandatory regulatory requirements for international transit on this specific route
questions.learning: Nigeria is classified as a Yellow Fever endemic zone. Under the WHO's International Health Regulations, travelers moving from endemic areas to other countries, including the USA, are required to present a valid international certificate of vaccination for…

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 74-year-old man presents with low back pain radiating to the leg. Spinal examination reveals a palpable “step” in the lumbosacral region, as seen on the provided X-ray. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient’s clinical finding of a palpable "step-off" in the lumbosacral region is pathognomonic for Spondylolisthesis (Option B) . Spondylolisthesis is defined as the forward translation or slipping of one vertebra over another. The provided X-ray confirms this, showing the L5 vertebral body clearly displaced anteriorly relative to the S1 segment. Spondylolysis (Option A) refers to a defect or stress fracture in the pars interarticularis but without the actual "slip" or step-off. Spondylosis (Option D) is a general term for age-related degenerative changes (osteoarthritis) of the spine. Disc prolapse (Option C) causes radiating pain but would not result in a structural bony step on palpation or lateral X-ray. Therefore, because of the definitive radiological visual of vertebral displacement and the corresponding physical exam finding, spondylolisthesis is the correct diagnosis. It is commonly associated with degenerative changes in older adults or prior lysis in younger patients
questions.learning: The patient’s clinical finding of a palpable "step-off" in the lumbosacral region is pathognomonic for Spondylolisthesis (Option B) . Spondylolisthesis is defined as the forward translation or slipping of one vertebra over another.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which hormones are produced from the zones labelled in the image given?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. A-aldosterone, B-cortisol, C-androgens, D-epinephrine

Option D is the correct option. This is a section through an adrenal gland showing both the medulla and the zones of the cortex. Following are the zones of the cortex and medulla, and the hormones they secrete.

A – Zona Glomerulosa  – secretes mineralocorticoids (aldosterone)

B – Zona Fasciculata  – secretes glucocorticoids (cortisol, corticosterone)

C – Zona Reticularis –  secretes androgens (dehydroepiandrosterone)

D – Adrenal Medulla – Produces Catecholamines: Norepinephrine, Epinephrine, and Dopamine

On histological examination, the different layers are identified as:

• Outer zona glomerulosa - small, compact cells
• Central zona fasciculata - larger lipid-rich cells arranged in radial columns
• Inner zona reticularis - pigmented, compact cells
• Adrenal medulla - thin layer of large chromaffin cells
questions.learning: A-aldosterone, B-cortisol, C-androgens, D-epinephrine Option D is the correct option. This is a section through an adrenal gland showing both the medulla and the zones of the cortex.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Respiratory System · Pleural Effusion Pulmonary Embolism Pah
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman is diagnosed with pulmonary arterial hypertension. Which of the following is the most appropriate drug for reducing pulmonary arterial pressure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Bosentan

Bosentan is an endothelin receptor antagonist (ETA and ETB blocker) used in the treatment of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). Endothelin-1 is a potent vasoconstrictor and smooth muscle mitogen. By blocking endothelin receptors, bosentan reduces pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary arterial pressure, improves exercise capacity, and delays disease progression.

Why not the other options?

• A. Furosemide: Used to relieve fluid overload and right heart failure symptoms, but does not directly reduce pulmonary arterial pressure.
• B. Amlodipine: A calcium channel blocker that is beneficial only in the small subset of PAH patients with a positive vasoreactivity test; it is not the standard treatment for most patients.
• D. Enalapril: An ACE inhibitor used for systemic hypertension and heart failure, but it has no established role in treating PAH.
questions.learning: Bosentan Bosentan is an endothelin receptor antagonist (ETA and ETB blocker) used in the treatment of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). Endothelin-1 is a potent vasoconstrictor and smooth muscle mitogen.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient on fluoxetine was started on a pain control drug for neuropathic pain. He developed an episode of syncope after 2 weeks. ECG reveals QT interval of 477 ms. Which of the following is the causative drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Methadone

Methadone is the causative drug for this patient's presentation of syncope and prolonged QT interval after coadministration other QT prolonging drugs such as fluoxetine.
Unlike other opioids, QT prolongation is primarily a side effect of methadone, which is additive with other agents known to cause QT prolongation such as fluoxetine. Serious cardiac arrhythmias including torsades de pointes have been noted with methadone use. Normal QTc is about 440 ms. Values of more than 440 ms in males and 460 ms in females are considered to be prolonged. QT prolongation can present as syncope or cardiac arrest.
Methadone is a synthetic opioid that is chemically different but has similar pharmacological action to that of morphine (Option B). It is a long-acting mu-opioid receptor agonist. Although an effective analgesic, the primary use of methadone hydrochloride is detoxification and maintenance therapy treatment for opioid use disorder. Methadone is also used for the management of chronic pain.
Side effects of methadone are similar to that of morphine such as lethargy, constipation, respiratory depression, and hypotension. Like other opioids, methadone will produce tolerance and dependence. Development of physical dependence during the long-term administration of methadone can be demonstrated following abrupt drug withdrawal or administration of an opioid antagonist.
Other options :
Option B : Morphine is not associated with QT prolongation.

Option C : Meperidine, also known as pethidine, though chemically unrelated to morphine interacts with µ opioid receptors and its actions are blocked by naloxone. Apart from usual opioid side effects, pethidine produces some atropinic effects like dry mouth, blurred vision, tachycardia. Pethidine injected in patients receiving a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) may produce serotonin syndrome. It is occasionally used to control shivering during recovery from anaesthesia.

Option D : Propoxyphene is a methadone analogue that was used to treat mild-tomoderate pain. Due to reports of cardiotoxicity, it was withdrawn in UK, Europe, and USA and it was banned in India in 2013.
questions.learning: Methadone Methadone is the causative drug for this patient's presentation of syncope and prolonged QT interval after coadministration other QT prolonging drugs such as fluoxetine.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: A 4-week-old, full-term boy is brought to the emergency department due to vomiting. His parents describe the emesis as undigested formula without blood or bile. The vomiting occurs after feeds and has increased in frequency and force over the past 3 days. Examination shows a sunken anterior fontanelle and dry mucous membranes. Arterial blood gas analysis is most likely to reveal which of the following sets of values?
options: pH 7.29, PaCO2 30, HCO3 14, Anion gap elevated
pH 7.30, PaCO2 50, HCO3 28, Anion gap normal
pH 7.48, PaCO2 46, HCO3 34, Anion gap normal
pH 7.53, PaCO2 22, HCO3 22, Anion gap normal
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. pH 7.48, PaCO2 46, HCO3 34, Anion gap normal

Projectile, non-bilious vomiting in a 4-week-old infant suggests hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.

Loss of gastric HCl leads to metabolic alkalosis with:

• ↑ pH
• ↑ HCO₃⁻
• Compensatory ↑ PaCO₂ (respiratory hypoventilation)
• Normal anion gap
• Often associated with hypokalemia and hypochloremia

Thus, persistent vomiting of gastric contents causes hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation.
