questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A P1L1 woman, with a history of uneventful previous delivery, presents with secondary infertility and amenorrhea for 2 years. The laparoscopy performed is shown below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tuberculosis

The clinical scenario of secondary infertility with previous uneventful delivery and the laparoscopy image showing multiple granulomatous foci which are tuberculous lesions point towards the diagnosis of genital tuberculosis.

Genital tuberculosis is almost always secondary to a primary focus elsewhere. The most frequent location is the lungs (50%), although it can also come from lymph nodes (40%), kidneys, joints, the gastrointestinal system, or as part of a broad miliary infection. It mostly spreads via the haematogenous route or lymphatics sometimes.

In Genital tuberculosis, the leading presenting complaints include infertility, abdominal pain, vaginal discharge, and suspicion of neoplasm. 10-15% of women are found to be asymptomatic as well.

The fallopian tubes are the most common site to be affected. The disease subsequently spreads to other genital organs and the peritoneum.

Investigations:

1. Complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), enzyme-linked immunoabsorbent assay (ELISA) tests - lgG and IgM, and Mantoux tests are done to evaluate the case of genital tuberculosis. The nucleic acid amplification technique (NAAT) can detect tuberculosis within a few hours compared to culture.

2. Hysterosalpingography (HSG) - If genital tuberculosis is suspected, HSG should not be performed because of the risk of spread of infection.

If performed in an asymptomatic woman, the following patterns may be seen:

• The tobacco-pouch appearance of hydrosalpinx and pyosalpinx with blocked fimbrial end.
• Rigid non-peristaltic pipe-like tube (lead-pipe appearance).
• Beading and variation in filling defect.
• The jagged fluffiness of the tubal outline.
• Golf club appearance with slight or moderate dilatation of the ampullary portion of the fallopian tube.

3. The investigation of choice in genital tuberculosis is an endometrial biopsy. Endometrium tissue is obtained by D&C/hystroscopy-directed biopsy. The endometrial scrapings are used for histopathology, PCR testing, and AFB smear and culture.

Diagnostic laparoscopy is widely used to establish the diagnosis of genital tuberculosis/ abdominal pelvic tuberculosis. Tuberculous lesions can be seen on the parietal peritoneum, intestinal serosa, omentum, surface of the uterus, and fallopian tubes.
questions.learning: Tuberculosis — The clinical scenario of secondary infertility with previous uneventful delivery and the laparoscopy image showing multiple granulomatous foci which are tuberculous lesions point towards the diagnosis of genital tuberculosis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which specific monoclonal antibody is used in the treatment of cancer?
questions.explanation: Rituximab is a chimeric monoclonal antibody that specifically targets the CD20 antigen found on the surface of B-lymphocytes. It is a cornerstone in the treatment of various B-cell malignancies, including Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma and Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia. By binding to CD20, it triggers cell lysis through antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity and complement-dependent pathways. Omalizumab (Option A) is used for severe allergic asthma and chronic urticaria by targeting IgE. Denosumab (Option B) targets RANKL and is used for osteoporosis and giant cell tumors of the bone, but it is not primarily classified as a direct anti-cancer cytotoxic agent in this context. Methotrexate (Option D) is a conventional folic acid antagonist chemotherapy drug, not a monoclonal antibody. Rituximab’s ability to selectively deplete B-cells makes it effective not only in oncology but also in autoimmune disorders like rheumatoid arthritis. Therefore, among the monoclonal antibodies listed, Rituximab is the primary agent utilized for malignant cancer therapy

questions.text:
Arrange the following structures in the hearing pathway from the receptors to the cortex -

The spiral ganglion situated in Rosenthal's canal contains bipolar cells. The dendrites of these bipolar cells join to form the cochlear branch of the vestibulocochlear nerve which ends in the cochlear nuclei.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An intern is assisting with laparoscopic surgery, and the resident is orienting the intern to the instruments and the operating ports. Your surgeon asks you what the angle between the camera port and the working port is.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Azimuth's angle

The angle between the camera port and the working port is known as Azimuth's angle. The angle must be a minimum of 30° to avoid any clashing between these instruments.

Other options

Option B: Manipulation angle is the angle between two working ports. The minimum angle should be 60°.

Option C: Crossing angle refers to the intersection of instruments inside the abdominal cavity.

Option D: The elevation angle is the angle between the working port and the horizontal line. The minimum angle must be 60° to avoid colliding the instrument with the abdominal wall.
questions.learning: Azimuth's angle — The angle between the camera port and the working port is known as Azimuth's angle. The angle must be a minimum of 30° to avoid any clashing between these instruments.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Loss of flexion at the interphalangeal joint of thumb after supracondylar fracture is due to the involvement of?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Anterior interosseous nerve

Loss of flexion at the interphalangeal (IP) joint of the thumb, is due to the involvement of the anterior interosseous nerve (AIN).

Flexion of thumb occurs at 2 joints:

1. IP joint: Flexor pollicis longus (FPL) supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve (a branch of the median nerve, C7 and C8).
2. MCP joint: Flexor pollicis brevis (FPB) supplied by the recurrent motor branch of the median nerve.

Other options:

• Deep branch of ulnar nerve > ulnar claw hand
questions.learning: Anterior interosseous nerve Loss of flexion at the interphalangeal (IP) joint of the thumb, is due to the involvement of the anterior interosseous nerve (AIN).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In a triage setting, which of the following categories requires the highest priority intervention?
questions.explanation: In disaster medicine and emergency departments, triage is used to prioritize patients based on the severity of their condition. The Red category (Priority I) is reserved for patients with life-threatening injuries who have a high chance of survival if given immediate intervention. Examples include tension pneumothorax or major airway obstruction. The Yellow category (Priority II) includes patients with serious but not immediately life-threatening injuries who can wait for a few hours (e.g., stable large fractures). The Green category (Option C, Priority III) includes the "walking wounded" with minor injuries. The Black category (Option D, Priority 0) is for those who are already deceased or have injuries so catastrophic that survival is unlikely even with care. Therefore, "Red" always receives the absolute highest priority. Efficient triage is essential to maximize the number of lives saved when medical resources are limited during a mass casualty incident

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 6-week-old boy was brought by his parents with complaints of noisy breathing, present since a few days after birth. Inspiratory stridor is heard. It subsides with prone positioning and increases with crying. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Laryngomalacia

The above clinical scenario of a 6-week-old child with inspiratory stridor which is relieved in the prone position is suggestive of laryngomalacia.

Laryngomalacia is the most common congenital abnormality of the larynx and the most common cause of stridor in children. It is characterized by excessive flaccidity of the supraglottic larynx which is sucked in during inspiration producing stridor and sometimes cyanosis. The presentation is just after birth and subsides by 2 years. Stridor improves(decreases) in the prone position, and worsens during feeding. The cry is normal. Laryngomalacia leads to the collapse of supraglottic structures during inspiration which results in airway obstruction.

The given image shows omega-shaped glottis on direct laryngoscopy.

Treatment of Laryngomalacia:
Mostly, it self-corrects by 2 years of age.
A tracheostomy may be required for some cases of severe respiratory obstruction.
Supraglottoplasty is required in cases of severe laryngomalacia.

Stridor is noisy respiration produced by turbulent airflow through narrowed air passages. Stridor may be heard during inspiration, expiration or both.

Inspiratory stridor is seen in supraglottic lesions. It is often produced in obstructive lesions of the supraglottis or pharynx, e.g. laryngomalacia or retropharyngeal abscess.
Expiratory stridor is produced in lesions of the thoracic trachea, primary and secondary bronchi, e.g. bronchial foreign body, and tracheal stenosis. (option B)
Biphasic stridor is seen in lesions of the glottis, subglottis, and cervical trachea, e.g. laryngeal papillomas, vocal cord paralysis, and subglottic stenosis. (options C & D)
questions.learning: Laryngomalacia — The above clinical scenario of a 6-week-old child with inspiratory stridor which is relieved in the prone position is suggestive of laryngomalacia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the sign shown in the image below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Popeye sign

The sign shown in the above image is the popeye sign, which occurs due to the rupture of the tendon of the long head of the biceps brachii.

On flexing the elbow, the characteristic deformity appears due to the bulging of the muscle belly caused by the contraction of the unrestrained muscles.

Option B: Hill-Sachs sign refers to a defect in the postero-lateral surface of the humeral head due to repeated impact against anterior glenoid rim. It is a common complication of Anterior shoulder dislocation.

Option C: Griesinger sign refers to oedema of the postauricular soft tissues overlying the mastoid process as a result of thrombosis of the mastoid emissary vein. It is a complication of acute mastoiditis.

Option D: Rising sun sign , also known as Schwartze sign, is the otoscopic sign of active otospongiosis characterised by reddish discolouration of the cochlear promontory.
questions.learning: Popeye sign — The sign shown in the above image is the popeye sign, which occurs due to the rupture of the tendon of the long head of the biceps brachii.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 52-year-old male with Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD) was started on tolvaptan therapy. A few weeks later, he presents with symptoms of dry mouth and increased thirst. What is the likely mechanism behind these symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increased free water clearance

Tolvaptan is a vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist used in ADPKD to slow cyst growth. Blocking V2 receptors in the collecting duct decreases aquaporin-2 insertion → reduces water reabsorption → increases free water clearance. This causes aquaresis (excretion of free water), leading to polyuria, thirst, and dry mouth.

Why not other options:

B. V2 receptor agonism: Tolvaptan is a V2 antagonist, not agonist.

C. Increased renal cAMP levels: Tolvaptan decreases cAMP, slowing cyst growth in ADPKD.

D. Increase in urine osmolality: Causes dilute urine → decreased urine osmolality.
questions.learning: Increased free water clearance Tolvaptan is a vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist used in ADPKD to slow cyst growth. Blocking V2 receptors in the collecting duct decreases aquaporin-2 insertion → reduces water reabsorption → increases free water clearance.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding single exposure point source epidemic ?
options: Has more than one incubation period
Occurs due to prolonged exposure to an agent
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Explosive in nature

The true statement regarding single exposure point source epidemic is that it is explosive in nature.

Single exposure point source epidemics occur due to a brief and simultaneous exposure to an agent. It has the following characteristics:

* It has a single peak with no secondary waves.

* The epidemic tends to be explosive, there is a clustering of cases within a narrow interval of time.

* The epidemic curve has a sharp, rapid rise and fall as all cases are clustered within one incubation period.

The exposure can be an infectious agent or contaminant in the environment (air, water, food, soil) by industrial chemicals or pollutants. Examples are food poisoning and the Bhopal gas tragedy in India due to methyl isocyanate.

The following graph represents single exposure point source epidemic.

Pearl PF0959: Epidemics and its Types

Epidemics and its Types

An epidemic is an occurrence in a community or region of cases of an illness that is clearly in excess of normal expectancy.

Types

Common source epidemics

* Single exposure or 'point source' epidemics

* Multiple or continuous exposure epidemics

Propagated epidemics

* Person to person

* Arthropod vector

* Animal reservoir

Slow or modern epidemics

* Non-communicable diseases
questions.learning: Explosive in nature — The true statement regarding single exposure point source epidemic is that it is explosive in nature. Single exposure point source epidemics occur due to a brief and simultaneous exposure to an agent.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All of the following increase the rate of diffusion across a membrane, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Increased membrane thickness

The rate of diffusion across a membrane follows Fick’s law of diffusion, which states that diffusion is directly proportional to the surface area, concentration gradient, and permeability, and inversely proportional to the membrane thickness.

Factors that increase diffusion:

• Higher temperature → increases molecular kinetic energy.
• Greater lipid solubility → substances cross lipid membranes more easily.
• Larger surface area → more area available for diffusion.

Increased membrane thickness decreases diffusion because molecules must travel a longer distance.
questions.learning: Increased membrane thickness — The rate of diffusion across a membrane follows Fick’s law of diffusion, which states that diffusion is directly proportional to the surface area, concentration gradient, and permeability, and inversely proportional to the…

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What is the value of normal tissue oncotic pressure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 12 mmHg

The value of normal tissue oncotic pressure is 12 mmHg. It refers to the interstitial osmotic pressure.

The interstitial oncotic pressure, while very small, is the pressure exerted by a small amount of protein present in the interstitium that tends to pull fluids out of the capillaries. It is different for each organ based on the level of protein components. It is mostly negligible, but sometimes can be as high as 6 mmHg in the brain. The values are also positive in the liver and kidneys.

The colloid osmotic pressure or oncotic pressure is the osmotic pressure exerted due to the presence of colloidal proteins like albumin and globulin within the plasma. The colloidal proteins are impermeable to the semi-permeable cell membrane and cannot cross the membrane. Thus, it exerts osmotic pressure, which pulls fluid into the capillaries.

The lowest number in the given options is 12 mmHg and, hence, is the best possible answer to this question.
questions.learning: 12 mmHg The value of normal tissue oncotic pressure is 12 mmHg. It refers to the interstitial osmotic pressure.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following defects causes familial hypercholesterolemia?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. LDL receptor

Familial hypercholesterolemia (FH) is most commonly caused by a defect in the LDL receptor, which is responsible for removing low-density lipoprotein (LDL) particles from the bloodstream. When the LDL receptor is defective or absent, LDL cannot be efficiently taken up by the liver, leading to markedly elevated plasma LDL cholesterol levels.

This results in premature atherosclerosis, tendon xanthomas, and an increased risk of early coronary artery disease.

Other options are associated with different lipid disorders:

• Apo E defect → Type III hyperlipoproteinemia
• Apo CII defect → Impaired lipoprotein lipase activation (Type I hyperlipoproteinemia)
• Apo B48 → Involved in chylomicron formation, not FH.
questions.learning: LDL receptor Familial hypercholesterolemia (FH) is most commonly caused by a defect in the LDL receptor, which is responsible for removing low-density lipoprotein (LDL) particles from the bloodstream.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which article of the Indian Constitution confers Right to Life to the citizens of India?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Article 21

The Right to Life is given in Article 21 of the Indian Constitution.

Option A: Article 11 defines the right of the parliament to regulate the right of citizenship by law.

Option C: Article 23 defines the prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labor.

Option D: Article 25 defines the freedom of conscience and free profession, practice, and propagation of religion.
questions.learning: Article 21 — The Right to Life is given in Article 21 of the Indian Constitution. Option A: Article 11 defines the right of the parliament to regulate the right of citizenship by law.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents with severe abdominal pain following alcohol consumption. Based on the provided X-ray, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The X-ray displays a crescent-shaped pocket of air under the right dome of the diaphragm, which is the pathognomonic finding for Pneumoperitoneum (air in the abdominal cavity). In a patient with severe abdominal pain, this finding indicates a perforated hollow viscus, such as a perforated peptic ulcer or a ruptured bowel segment. SBO (Small Bowel Obstruction, Option B) would show multiple dilated bowel loops with air-fluid levels. Esophageal perforation (Option C) and pneumomediastinum (Option D) typically present with air around the heart or in the neck tissues, rather than specifically under the diaphragm. Severe pain following alcohol intake could point toward a perforated gastric or duodenal ulcer. Pneumoperitoneum is a surgical emergency requiring immediate resuscitation and urgent laparotomy to find and repair the site of perforation. Erect abdominal and chest X-rays are the standard first-line investigations for identifying this critical sign
questions.learning: The X-ray displays a crescent-shaped pocket of air under the right dome of the diaphragm, which is the pathognomonic finding for Pneumoperitoneum (air in the abdominal cavity).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A chest X-ray of a sand mine worker is shown. Based on the radiographic findings and occupational history, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The chest X-ray features "eggshell calcification," which is a thin rim of calcification along the periphery of enlarged hilar lymph nodes. This finding, combined with the patient's occupational history as a sand mine worker, is diagnostic of silicosis. Silicosis results from the chronic inhalation of silica dust, leading to progressive pulmonary fibrosis and upper lobe nodules. Sarcoidosis (Option A) also presents with hilar lymphadenopathy but lacks the classic eggshell calcification pattern. Tuberculosis (Option B) typically presents with cavitation or consolidation rather than peripheral node calcification. Asbestosis (Option D) primarily involves the lower lobes and presents with pleural plaques rather than hilar eggshell signs. Thus, the occupational context and the hallmark radiologic sign confirm silicosis
questions.learning: The chest X-ray features "eggshell calcification," which is a thin rim of calcification along the periphery of enlarged hilar lymph nodes. This finding, combined with the patient's occupational history as a sand mine worker, is diagnostic of silicosis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
Which of the following methods can detect the alterations in DNA sequence?

1. Restriction fragment length analysis
2. Flow cytometry
3. Pyrosequencing
4. FISH
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1 and 3

The alterations in DNA sequence can be detected by restriction fragment length analysis and pyrosequencing.

Restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) is also called cleaved amplified polymorphic sequence (CAPS) assay. RFLP is a technique in which organisms may be differentiated by variations in their DNA sequence by restriction endonucleases. This technique involves cutting a particular region of DNA with known variability, with restriction enzymes, then separating the DNA fragments by agarose gel electrophoresis and determining the number of fragments and relative sizes.

Pyrosequencing is a synthesis type of approach of DNA sequencing. This technique employs four enzymatic reactions in a single tube to monitor DNA synthesis. Nucleotides are incorporated into the reaction and pyrophosphate (PPi) is released. PPi triggers a series of reactions resulting in the production of light, which is proportional to the amount of DNA and number of incorporated nucleotides. The generated light is detected and recorded by a detector system in the form of a peak signal, which reflects the activity of all four enzymes in the reaction.

The practical applications of recombinant DNA technology include:

• Gene mapping using techniques such as fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH).
• Producing proteins such as:

• Interferons, tPA (tissue plasminogen activator)
• Insulin, growth hormone
• Hepatitis B vaccine

• Molecular analysis of disease, to detect gene variations and mutations.
• Restriction Fragment Length polymorphism (RFLP) and single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)
• Microsatellite DNA polymorphisms
• Gene therapy and bone marrow transplantation

Flow cytometry is a laser-based method that analyzes the cells and cell components based on the presence of certain cell surface molecules which are named as per cluster of differentiation (CD) nomenclature. It is very effective for the study of the immune system and its response to infectious diseases and cancer. It cannot detect the alterations in DNA sequence.

Fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) is a technique where cells are stained with fluorescent stains. It uses DNA probes that recognize sequences specific to particular chromosomal regions. It cannot detect the alterations in DNA sequence. FISH can be performed on prenatal samples, peripheral blood cells, touch preparations from cancer biopsies, and even fixed archival tissue sections. Uses include :

• Numerical abnormalities of chromosomes e.g., aneuploidy.
• Subtle microdeletions and rearrangements.
• Complex translocations that are not demonstrable by routine karyotyping.
• Gene amplification of HER2 in breast cancer or NMYC amplification in neuroblastomas.
questions.learning: 1 and 3 The alterations in DNA sequence can be detected by restriction fragment length analysis and pyrosequencing. Restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) is also called cleaved amplified polymorphic sequence (CAPS) assay.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A health worker had a needle stick injury. While handling a chronic Hepatitis B case. She has taken 2 complete schedules (6 doses) of HBV vaccination. She was tested and was diagnosed as a non-responder to vaccination 3 months back, What is the most appropriate management in this case:
options: Give 2 doses of HBIG one now and another 4 weeks later
Give HBV vaccination starting now, after 4-6 weeks, check HBV titres and decide on giving HBIG
HBIG single dose with HBV vaccination (first dose beginning now)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Give 2 doses of HBIG one now and another 4 weeks later

A documented vaccine non-responder exposed to an HBsAg-positive source requires passive immunization only. Two doses of HBIG are given: one immediately and another at 1 month, as further vaccination is ineffective in proven non-responders. HBIG provides immediate anti-HBs protection after high-risk exposure. Revaccination strategies are used only in unknown or incomplete responders, not confirmed non-responders.

| Criteria | Meaning

| -------- | -------

| Anti-HBs <10 mIU/mL | No protective immunity

| After 2 full vaccine series | True non-responder

Non-responder : anti-HBs < 10 after 2 full series

What to do: HBIG × 2 doses: 4 weeks apart; No further vaccine
questions.learning: Give 2 doses of HBIG one now and another 4 weeks later A documented vaccine non-responder exposed to an HBsAg-positive source requires passive immunization only.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A boy is severely beaten by 4 to 5 people and arrives at the hospital with serious injuries. A dying declaration is recorded. Which of the following statements about dying declarations in India is false?
options: It must always be recorded by a magistrate
An oath is not administered before recording a dying declaration.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It must always be recorded by a magistrate

The statement that is not applicable to the dying declaration is it must be always recorded by a magistrate.

While it is ideal for a Magistrate to record a dying declaration, there is no legal provision that states that it must always be recorded by a magistrate. The statement can be recorded by a magistrate, the doctor, the village headman, a police officer, or any member of the public.

A dying deposition, on the other hand, must always be recorded by a Magistrate.

A dying declaration (Sec. 32 IEA) is a form of a written or oral statement made by a person whose imminent death is a result of an unlawful act. The statement made relates to the facts of the cause of death and the circumstances surrounding it.

Procedure:

* As soon the severely injured person is brought to the hospital, the medical officer should inform the magistrate to have a dying declaration recorded. The fitness of the declarant to make the statement should be examined first.

* The doctor can record it himself or herself if he thinks that the person will not survive till the arrival of the magistrate. In such a case, the police or the doctor concerned must note down the reason as to why waiting for the magistrate for recording this statement was not feasible.

* Treatment should not be delayed while recording dying declaration.

* An oath is not administered in these circumstances because of the belief that the dying person tells the truth. (Option D)

* Before documenting a dying declaration, the doctor has to ascertain that the person is conscious and of sound mind with normal mental faculties (compos mentis).(Option A)

* If the person dies or becomes unconscious while recording the dying declaration, the doctor must record the information obtained upto that point.

* Usually recorded in the form of a simple narrative in the patient's own language.

* No suggestions, prompting, help, or leading questions from other people are allowed. (Option C)

* No outsider is allowed to be present

* After completing writting, it has to be read back to the patient who has to approve it by signing/thumb impression. The signature of two witnesses is also mandatory.

A dying deposition is a form of oral evidence that is recorded in the presence of the accused or their lawyer, with the provision of cross-examination. There is no legal provision for a dying deposition in the Indian Evidence Act (it is not followed in India).
questions.learning: It must always be recorded by a magistrate — The statement that is not applicable to the dying declaration is it must be always recorded by a magistrate.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents to the casualty with a sudden loss of vision and painful ocular movements. On examination of the affected eye, a relative afferent pupillary defect with a normal optic disc is seen. Visual field testing was done which revealed central scotoma in the same eye. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Optic neuritis

The given clinical scenario of a sudden painful loss of vision in the absence of fundoscopic changes, RAPD and central scotoma is suggestive of optic neuritis, specifically retrobulbar neuritis.

There are 3 types of optic neuritis: papillitis, neuroretinitis, and retrobulbar neuritis. The common causes of retrobulbar neuritis include demyelinating disorders such as multiple sclerosis (MS) and neuromyelitis optica (NMO or Devic's disease).

Clinically, optic neuritis is characterized by sudden, progressive visual loss.  Ocular movements are painful in retrobulbar neuritis and painless in papillitis and neuroretinitis. Glowing sensations known as phosphenes may be induced with sound or movement. Color vision may also be impaired.

On examination, Marcus Gunn pupil or relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) is usually noted due to asymmetric involvement. The most common visual field defect is a central or centrocecal scotoma.

Type
Retrobulbar neuritis
Papillitis
Neuroretinitis

Pathology
Inflammation of the optic nerve behind the disc
Inflammation of the optic nerve head
Inflammation of the optic nerve head and the macula

Fundus appearance
Optic disc appears normal

Hyperemia and oedema of the optic disc with or without peri-papillary flame-shaped hemorrhages

Macular star (due to exudates that form around macula)

Prevalence
Most common in adults

Most common in children

Least common type

Associated conditions
Strong association with demyelinating disorders like MS, NMO

Weak association with demyelinating disorders

Cat-scratch disease, Lyme disease, Syphilis etc.

The image below shows papillitis.

The image below shows macular star appearance in neuroretinitis.

Causes of RAPD:

* Severe retinal disease (e.g., central retinal artery occlusion, extensive retinal detachment)

* Maculopathy (macular degeneration )

* Optic nerve lesions (e.g., optic neuritis, retrobulbar neuritis in multiple sclerosis , anterior ischemic optic neuropathy , glaucoma)

* Optic tract lesions (e.g., infarction)

Causes of central/centrocaecal scotoma

* Optic neuritis

* Compressive lesion eg. Pituitary adenoma

* Optic neuropathy due to

* Poor nutrition

* Tobacco

* Alcohol

* Drug- induced optic neuropathy

*

* Toxin- induced optic neuropathy

* Hereditary optic atrophy

* Sarcoidosis

* Leukemia
questions.learning: Optic neuritis — The given clinical scenario of a sudden painful loss of vision in the absence of fundoscopic changes, RAPD and central scotoma is suggestive of optic neuritis, specifically retrobulbar neuritis.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The recommended amount of space per student in a classroom should be
questions.explanation: In school health and environmental sanitation standards, providing adequate space is essential to prevent overcrowding and the spread of respiratory infections. The government-recommended minimum floor space for a student in a classroom is more than 10 square feet. This standard ensures sufficient room for a desk and chair while allowing for adequate air circulation and easy movement within the room. Options A, C, and D do not reflect the standard Indian public health guidelines for school infrastructure. Overcrowding in classrooms is a major risk factor for the transmission of airborne diseases such as tuberculosis, influenza, and meningococcal meningitis. In addition to floor space, classrooms should have a minimum ceiling height and adequate ventilation (at least 10% of the floor area should be windows). Maintaining these environmental standards is a critical component of the school health service to ensure a safe and healthy learning environment for children's physical and cognitive development
questions.learning: In school health and environmental sanitation standards, providing adequate space is essential to prevent overcrowding and the spread of respiratory infections.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Which of the following are properties of ventricular cardiac muscle?

1. All or none phenomenon
2. Length tension relationship
3. Long refractory period
4. Tetanus
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1,2,3

All or none phenomenon, length tension relationship and long refractory period applies to cardiac muscles. Cardiac muscle cannot be tetanized due to long refractory period.

In cardiac myocytes, depolarization proceeds rapidly and an overshoot of the zero potential is present. This is followed by a plateau before the membrane potential reaches the RMP (-90mV). This plateau phase lasts for 200 msec or more. Repolarization is therefore not complete until contraction is 50% completed.

Phases of cardiac action potential

• 0→ Depolarisation and overshoot-Due to opening of voltage-gated Na+ channels
• 1→ Initial rapid repolarization-Due to closure of Na+ channels and opening up of K+ channels
• 2→ Plateau phase - Due to slow but prolonged opening of Ca2+ channels
• 3→ Late rapid repolarization
• 4→ Baseline (RMP)

Phases 3 and 4 are due closure of Ca2+ channels and a slow, delayed increase of K+ efflux through K+ channels.

During phases 0 to 2 and about half of phase 3 of cardiac action potential, cardiac muscle cannot be excited again, that is, it is in its absolute refractory period. It remains relatively refractory until phase 4. Thus, cardiac muscle cannot be tetanized.
questions.learning: 1,2,3 All or none phenomenon, length tension relationship and long refractory period applies to cardiac muscles. Cardiac muscle cannot be tetanized due to long refractory period.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 30-year-old lactating woman presents with localized redness, warmth, and tenderness of one breast. Fluctuation is positive, and ipsilateral axillary lymph nodes are mildly enlarged. Repeated aspirations with antibiotics have failed, and ultrasound confirms a fluid collection. What is the appropriate management for her breast abscess and the recommended course of action for treating her pain and fever?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a lactating mother with localized breast inflammation, fluctuation (indicating pus), and axillary lymphadenopathy is diagnostic of a breast abscess . The history of failed aspirations and persistent fever despite antibiotics confirms that the infection has progressed to an encapsulated collection that requires surgical intervention. The gold-standard treatment for a confirmed breast abscess is surgical incision and drainage (Option A). This allows for the complete evacuation of the abscess cavity and rapid resolution of the source of infection. Antibiotics alone (Option B) are insufficient for a fluctuant collection. Breast conservation surgery (Option C) and punch biopsy (Option D) are used for managing breast malignancies, which is not suggested by this acute infectious picture. Therefore, because of the presence of a non-draining fluid collection confirmed by ultrasound, incision and drainage is the definitive next step in management
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a lactating mother with localized breast inflammation, fluctuation (indicating pus), and axillary lymphadenopathy is diagnostic of a breast abscess .

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Macula densa is formed by which part of the nephron?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. DCT

Macula densa is formed by specialized tubular epithelial cells of the distal convoluted tubule.

The juxtaglomerular apparatus consists of the following parts:

• Macula densa: At the end of the thick ascending limb of Henle, and at the beginning of the distal tubule, the tubular epithelial cells are specialized to form the macula densa. They detect sodium concentration of the fluid in the tubule (chemoreceptor). In response to elevated sodium, the macula densa cells trigger the contraction of the afferent arteriole, reducing the flow of blood to the glomerulus and the glomerular filtration rate. This happens as follows: When there is increased sodium, there is increased sodium-potassium ATPase activity which leads to increased ATP hydrolysis causing more adenosine formation. The adenosine receptors on the macula densa cells stimulate it to release more calcium, so that there is vasoconstriction of the afferent arteriole, thereby decreasing the GFR.
• Lacis cells: Extraglomerular mesangial cells situated between afferent and efferent arteriole.
• Granular cells/JG cells: Modified smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole, they secrete renin. Fall in pressure in afferent arteriole stimulates renin release (mechanoreceptor), which, in turn, increases blood pressure.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A young male patient was brought to the emergency department in an unconscious state after having suddenly collapsed at a railway station. As there was no pulse felt, cardiopulmonary resuscitation was started and the monitor showed ventricular fibrillation. Immediate defibrillation was performed. What is the next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Resume chest compressions

Chest compressions should be resumed immediately following shock delivery.

A pulse check and reanalysis of the cardiac rhythm is performed only after 2 minutes of chest compression and rescue breaths.

This is done because the defibrillator shock temporarily stuns the heart. Maintaining coronary perfusion during this period is aided by performing chest compressions.

Pearl PF1316: Adult Basic Life Support (BLS) Algorithm (Updated as per 2020 guidelines)
questions.learning: Resume chest compressions Chest compressions should be resumed immediately following shock delivery. A pulse check and reanalysis of the cardiac rhythm is performed only after 2 minutes of chest compression and rescue breaths.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 58-year-old man with a history of multiple sexual partners presents with anorexia and jaundice. Liver biopsy reveals hepatocytes with a characteristic ground-glass appearance. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The biopsy finding of ground-glass hepatocytes in a patient with clinical jaundice and risk factors like multiple sexual partners is pathognomonic for chronic Hepatitis B infection. This ground-glass appearance is caused by the massive accumulation of Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) within the smooth endoplasmic reticulum of the infected cells. Hepatitis A (Option A) is typically transmitted via the feco-oral route and shows hepatocyte ballooning rather than ground-glass cells. Hepatitis C (Option C) histology usually features lymphoid aggregates in the portal tracts and steatosis. In Hepatitis D (Option D), any observed ground-glass cells are actually a result of the co-existing HBV component. Therefore, ground-glass opacity is the definitive histological signature of chronic HBV infection
questions.learning: The biopsy finding of ground-glass hepatocytes in a patient with clinical jaundice and risk factors like multiple sexual partners is pathognomonic for chronic Hepatitis B infection.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 14-year-old girl presents with cyclical abdominal pain, a midline hypogastric mass, and primary amenorrhea. On per vaginal examination, a bluish swelling is observed. What is the most likely cause of her condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of primary amenorrhea (no menarche), cyclical abdominal pain, and a bluish bulging membrane at the introitus is pathognomonic for an imperforate hymen . The blue color is due to the accumulated menstrual blood (hematocolpos) reflecting through the translucent hymenal membrane. This accumulation also explains the midline hypogastric lump (hematometra). A transverse vaginal septum (Option B) can cause similar symptoms but would not show the distinct bulging bluish membrane at the vulvar surface. Bartholin cysts (Option A) are located at the posterior introitus and are not associated with amenorrhea. Endometrioma (Option D) is an ovarian "chocolate cyst" seen in older women. Treatment for imperforate hymen is a simple cruciate incision to allow the trapped blood to drain. Therefore, the physical visual of the bulging blue introitus definitively confirms the diagnosis. Recognizing this early prevents complications like endometriosis or retrograde menstruation
questions.learning: The clinical triad of primary amenorrhea (no menarche), cyclical abdominal pain, and a bluish bulging membrane at the introitus is pathognomonic for an imperforate hymen .

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A hypertensive patient is taking three antihypertensive medications, including diuretics, but his blood pressure is uncontrolled. In addition, he has hypokalaemia. Which of the following drugs should be prescribed to treat this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Eplerenone

The given clinical case with resistant hypertension and labs showing hypokalaemia suggests a diagnosis of primary hyperaldosteronism, which is treated with aldosterone receptor antagonists like spironolactone and eplerenone.

For the diagnosis of resistant hypertension, the patient should have uncontrolled hypertension despite taking three antihypertensive drugs, including at least one diuretic. Most patients with CKD/diabetes develop resistant hypertension.

While a calcium channel blocker, beta blocker, or alpha blocker can be part of the antihypertensive regimen, the inclusion of a diuretic is necessary for the diagnosis of resistant hypertension. The diuretic helps in addressing fluid retention, which is often a significant contributor to hypertension. Resistant hypertension is more common in patients aged >60 years than in younger patients. It may be related to nonadherence to therapy, obesity, and excessive alcohol intake. In the absence of a specific identifiable cause, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists like spironolactone have been found to be the most effective add-on drugs for the treatment of resistant hypertension.

Management of resistant hypertension according to NICE guidelines:

* Aldosterone antagonist (spironolactone) is to be used only when serum potassium is <4.5 mmol/L.

* A higher dose of thiazide is to be used only when serum potassium is >4.5 mmol/L.

* β-blocker or α1-blocker is to be considered only if an aldosterone antagonist or higher-dose thiazide is ineffective or not tolerated or contraindicated.

Primary hyperaldosteronism, also known as Conn’s syndrome, is characterized by excessive production of aldosterone by the adrenal glands, leading to sodium retention, potassium excretion, and subsequent hypertension. Drug-resistant hypertension is a hallmark of this condition. The initial test for this condition is the concurrent measurement of plasma renin and aldosterone, followed by the calculation of the aldosterone-renin ratio (ARR). The aldosterone-renin ratio is the most appropriate screening test for primary hyperaldosteronism; this can be followed by a saline infusion test, which is used to confirm the diagnosis of Conn’s syndrome.

Spironolactone has some significant adverse effects, especially in men (erectile dysfunction, gynecomastia, and benign prostatic hyperplasia).

Primary hyperaldosteronism has to be differentiated from secondary hyperaldosteronism, which can be done using this table.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: During the management of shoulder dystocia during childbirth, which maneuver is typically attempted first as the initial step?
questions.explanation: The McRoberts maneuver is the critical first-line physical intervention for managing shoulder dystocia. It involves hyperflexing the mother's thighs against her abdomen. This action flattens the sacral promontory and rotates the symphysis pubis superiorly, increasing the space available for the anterior shoulder to pass under the pelvic bone. Rotational maneuvers like the Rubin (Option C) and Woods corkscrew (Option B) are performed only if simpler measures like McRoberts and suprapubic pressure fail. Delivery of the posterior arm (Option D) is an internal maneuver attempted later in the algorithm. Because of its high success rate and relative simplicity, the McRoberts maneuver is the mandated starting point in emergency shoulder dystocia protocols
questions.learning: The McRoberts maneuver is the critical first-line physical intervention for managing shoulder dystocia. It involves hyperflexing the mother's thighs against her abdomen.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with sudden, painful vision loss and a fixed, vertically oval pupil. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of sudden severe eye pain, blurred vision, and a mid-dilated, fixed, vertically oval pupil is pathognomonic for Acute Congestive Glaucoma (Angle-closure glaucoma). The eye will often appear red (ciliary congestion) and feel "stony hard" on palpation due to critically high intraocular pressure. Macular degeneration (Option A) results in a slow, painless loss of central vision. Optic neuritis (Option B) causes painful vision loss, but the pupil will exhibit an Afferent Pupillary Defect (Marcus-Gunn pupil) rather than being fixed and oval. Acute anterior uveitis (Option D) also causes a painful red eye, but the pupil is characteristically small and irregular (miotic) due to sphincter spasm and synechiae. Acute glaucoma is a medical emergency that requires immediate pressure-lowering agents followed by laser peripheral iridotomy
questions.learning: The combination of sudden severe eye pain, blurred vision, and a mid-dilated, fixed, vertically oval pupil is pathognomonic for Acute Congestive Glaucoma (Angle-closure glaucoma).

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text:
A 30-year-old patient presents with progressive difficulty in swallowing both solids and liquids for 8 months. A barium swallow was done and is shown in the image below. What other investigations should be done to confirm the diagnosis in this patient?

UGIE- Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy

PET- Positron emission tomography
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. UGIE + manometry

The given clinical scenario and the barium swallow showing bird beak sign are suggestive of achalasia cardia. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy (UGIE) and manometry should be done to confirm the diagnosis.

Achalasia is a motility disorder and is less common. It typically presents as dysphagia for solids and liquids. Other features such as regurgitation and chest pain are also present.

On fluoroscopy, a grossly dilated esophagus with tapering end towards the gastroesophageal junction is seen. This is called the bird beak sign.

Barium is retained in the esophagus for more than 5 minutes and is a significant finding.

Diagnosis is confirmed with endoscopy and manometry.
questions.learning: UGIE + manometry — The given clinical scenario and the barium swallow showing bird beak sign are suggestive of achalasia cardia. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy (UGIE) and manometry should be done to confirm the diagnosis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: 2,3-BPG causes the unloading of oxygen to tissues by _________.
options: Binding to beta subunit of Hb
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Binding to beta subunit of Hb

2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate (BPG) causes the unloading of oxygen to tissues by binding to the beta subunit of Hb.

2,3 BPG is formed from glycolysis. It is found in high amounts in red blood cells and in trace amounts in most other cells. 2,3 BPG facilitates increased oxygen delivery by reducing the affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen.

Hemoglobin exists in 2 forms in the blood. The deoxyhemoglobin form is called the taut or T form. This hemoglobin has a low affinity for oxygen. The oxyhemoglobin form is called the relaxed or R form. This hemoglobin has a high affinity for oxygen.

2,3 BPG binds more selectively to deoxyhemoglobin and stabilizes the taut conformation of hemoglobin (Option C).

Other options:

Options A and D: The process of unloading oxygen by 2,3 BPG is independent of ATP production.
questions.learning: Binding to beta subunit of Hb 2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate (BPG) causes the unloading of oxygen to tissues by binding to the beta subunit of Hb. It is found in high amounts in red blood cells and in trace amounts in most other cells.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: All of the following are features of Ganser Syndrome, except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Verbigeration

Ganser syndrome is best remembered by its hallmark triad:

1. Approximate answers (vorbereiden)
2. Clouding of consciousness
3. Hallucinations

It may also present with conversion symptoms, but verbigeration is not part of the typical clinical picture and is more aligned with psychotic disorders like schizophrenia.
questions.learning: Verbigeration Ganser syndrome is best remembered by its hallmark triad: 1. Approximate answers (vorbereiden) 2.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: During a dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR), which of the following bones are typically removed?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lacrimal

During a dacryocystorhinostomy, a portion of the lacrimal bone is typically removed to create a passage for tear drainage.

The lacrimal bone is indeed a key bone involved in dacryocystorhinostomy. In this procedure, a portion of the lacrimal bone is often removed to create a passage for tear drainage.

Other options:

Frontal (a): The frontal bone is not typically removed during a dacryocystorhinostomy. DCR primarily involves the lacrimal bone and sometimes parts of the nasal bone.

Ethmoidal (b): The ethmoidal bone is not typically removed during a standard DCR. The primary bone involved is the lacrimal bone.

Maxillary (c): The maxillary bone is not typically removed during a dacryocystorhinostomy. The main focus is on the lacrimal bone.
questions.learning: Lacrimal During a dacryocystorhinostomy, a portion of the lacrimal bone is typically removed to create a passage for tear drainage. The lacrimal bone is indeed a key bone involved in dacryocystorhinostomy.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: An elderly woman with a known history of Myasthenia Gravis presents with symptoms including fatigue, facial congestion, dilated neck veins, and breathlessness, which are indicative of superior vena cava (SVC) obstruction. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Thymoma

The diagnosis of myasthenia gravis along with the CT scan image showing an anterior mediastinal mass, is suggestive of thymoma.

Thymoma is the most common mediastinal tumor and is derived from the thymus gland. Thymomas vary in behaviour from benign to aggressively invasive. Superior vena cava obstruction is a possible complication of mediastinal mass.

Masoaka classification system is used to stage thymomas.

Myasthenia gravis is often related to thymomas. Symptoms of myasthenia gravis can improve after excision of the thymus gland even in the absence of a thymoma.

Complete thymectomy is the treatment for thymoma. It can be performed by two approaches:

• A median sternotomy approach
• A transcervical approach with or without an additional VATS procedure (Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery) for smaller thymomas

Other options:

Option A: Lipomas are benign and slow-growing, less likely to cause significant compression of the SVC and produce the acute symptoms described.

Option B: Ectopic thyroid tissue can be found in the mediastinum, but it is typically asymptomatic and does not usually cause SVC obstruction.

Option D: Germ cell tumours can occur in the mediastinum and cause SVC obstruction, but they are less commonly associated with Myasthenia Gravis compared to thymomas.

questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 52-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has been receiving hydroxychloroquine therapy for the past 8 years. She presents for routine follow-up and asks about the long-term safety of her medication, particularly concerning ocular toxicity. Fundus examination is currently normal, and she undergoes regular ophthalmologic screening. To minimize the risk of developing bull’s-eye maculopathy, what is the maximum recommended safe daily dose of hydroxychloroquine?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 5 mg/kg/day

Hydroxychloroquine retinal toxicity (bull’s-eye maculopathy) is a serious long-term adverse effect related to cumulative dose and daily dosing.

To minimize risk:

• Maximum safe dose: ≤5 mg/kg/day (based on actual body weight)
• Risk increases with therapy >5 years, high cumulative dose, renal disease, or concomitant tamoxifen use
• Regular ophthalmologic screening (fundus exam, OCT, visual fields) is essential

Maintaining hydroxychloroquine dose at ≤5 mg/kg/day significantly reduces the risk of irreversible retinal toxicity while preserving its disease-modifying benefits in SLE and rheumatoid arthritis.
questions.learning: 5 mg/kg/day Hydroxychloroquine retinal toxicity (bull’s-eye maculopathy) is a serious long-term adverse effect related to cumulative dose and daily dosing.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 7-year-old child post-tonsillectomy comes to you with complaints of snoring, palpitations, mouth breathing and a slight decrease in hearing. On examination, you notice a high-arched palate. His school performance has deteriorated as well. His mother is worried. What is the next line of management for this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Adenoidectomy with grommet insertion

The patient is suffering from serous otitis media secondary to adenoid hypertrophy causing eustachian tube obstruction. The best line of management is adenoidectomy with grommet insertion.

Serous otitis media is also known as secretory otitis media or mucoid otitis media or glue ear. It is characterized by the accumulation of nonpurulent effusion in the middle ear cleft.

Glue ear is thought to happen due to either malfunctioning (adenoid hyperplasia, chronic sinusitis or tonsillitis or rhinitis, palatal defects, tumors of nasopharynx) or increased secretory activity of the eustachian tube (allergy, unresolved otitis media, viral infections).

It is often seen in children 5-8 years of age. They present with hearing loss not exceeding 40 dB, which is insidious in onset. Speech may be delayed and defective due to hearing loss. Mild earaches with a history of upper respiratory tract infection are usually seen.

On otoscopy,

* Dull and opaque tympanic membrane with loss of light reflex

* Thin leash of vessels along the handle of the malleus

* If the tympanic membrane is transparent fluid levels and air bubbles can be seen

The tuning fork test reveals a conductive type of hearing loss. X-ray mastoid reveals clouding of air cells.

Treatment is mainly aimed at the removal of fluid and preventing recurrence.

* Medical management includes decongestants, antihistamines, antibiotics, and middle ear aeration techniques.

* Surgical management includes myringotomy and aspiration of fluid, grommet insertion, tympanotomy, or cortical mastoidectomy.
questions.learning: Adenoidectomy with grommet insertion — The patient is suffering from serous otitis media secondary to adenoid hypertrophy causing eustachian tube obstruction.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: An anesthetist used the airway device shown in the image given below on a patient. Which among the following statements is true regarding the adjunct?
options: It can cause damage to the teeth
It can be used in conscious patients
It can be safely used in facial trauma cases
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It can be used in conscious patients

The image shows a nasopharyngeal airway and its insertion. The true statement is that it can be used in conscious patients.

A nasopharyngeal airway is used to provide artificial airway passage to the hypopharynx. To place a nasopharyngeal airway, the device should be lubricated and inserted into the nose with the bevel facing the nasal septum, at a 90-degree angle to the longitudinal axis of the body. It bypasses the gag reflex as they do not go through the mouth. Thus, it can be used in conscious patients or those who have been lightly anesthetized.

Care should be taken to avoid excessive force as damage to the nasal mucosa can result in epistaxis. The nasal approach should be avoided in conditions that put patients at higher risk for epistaxis. These conditions include but are not limited to coagulopathy, pregnancy, hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, and uncontrolled hypertension. Absolute contraindications include basilar skull fractures, facial trauma, midface disruption, and injury to the roof of the mouth.

An oropharyngeal airway is used to maintain the airway in anesthetized patients. This adjunct prevents the tongue and epiglottis from falling back against the posterior pharynx and blocking the airway. They can cause coughing, retching, or laryngospasm in conscious patients.

To place an oropharyngeal airway, the device is inserted with the curved portion facing downwards. It is then rotated 180 degrees to be put in place. The below image shows the oropharyngeal airway:

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which among the following is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Malignant melanoma

Malignant melanoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults

Intraocular tumours are tumors affecting the ocular tissue. They are often malignant. They are initially dormant but can cause secondary glaucoma based on the location. It can cause extraocular extension and finally metastasis if left untreated. Types of intraocular tumours:

* Malignant melanoma: Involves the choroid, ciliary body, or iris. Its start as lens-shaped masses and enlarges. Retinal melanoma can cause retinal detachment. Radiological investigations like CT, MRI, and radioactive tracers, fluorescein angiography are used for diagnosis. Treatment includes surgery, radiation therapy, and enucleation in severe cases

* Retinoblastoma: Is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in children. It presents as a yellow pupillary reflex and cataract. Diagnosis is via demonstration of calcifications in radiographs and CT. Treatment involves brachytherapy and surgery.

* Reticulum cell sarcoma: It is a primary neoplasm of histiocyte similar to a microglioma in the CNS

* Secondaries: These mostly arise from the breast and alimentary canal.
questions.learning: Malignant melanoma Malignant melanoma is the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults Intraocular tumours are tumors affecting the ocular tissue.

questions.text: Which of the following conditions would not be managed through mass drug administration?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin A deficiency

Mass drug administration (MDA) is used for worm infestation, scabies, and filariasis, where community-wide treatment interrupts transmission. Vitamin A deficiency is addressed through targeted supplementation, not MDA. Hence, vitamin A deficiency is not managed via MDA.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presented with symptoms of peripheral neuropathy and macrocytic anemia. She was given folate 5mg and the blood picture improved. However, the neurologic manifestations were aggravated. What is the most likely cause?
options: Treatment with folate unmasking pyridoxine deficiency
Deficiency of folate reductase in CNS
Folate therapy using the B12 stores
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Folate therapy using the B12 stores

The most likely cause is folate therapy which used up the B12 stores, aggravating the symptoms.

Administration of folic acid for patients with macrocytic anemia can partially reverse the hematologic abnormalities associated with vitamin B12 deficiency. However, the neurologic manifestations of vitamin B12 deficiency are not treated by folic acid.

Administration of folic acid to an individual with vitamin B12 deficiency can potentially mask untreated vitamin B12 deficiency or even worsen the neurologic complications. Hence, testing for and/or treatment of vitamin B12 deficiency is required in all patients being treated with folic acid.

Variceal hemorrhage is an emergency that can be treated medically by inducing splanchnic vasoconstriction or endoscopically by sclerotherapy, balloon tamponade, or variceal ligation.

Other options:

Option A: Gastric ulcers are often found near the lesser curvature of the stomach, especially in the antral area. Although duodenal ulcers are more common overall, gastric ulcers are frequently located near the lesser curvature, within a few centimetres of the pylorus. A significant cause of these ulcers is infection with Helicobacter pylori.

Option C: Esophageal candidiasis is a fungal infection of the esophagus caused by the overgrowth of yeast, commonly Candida albicans. This condition is often seen in individuals with weakened immune systems, such as those with HIV/AIDS, diabetes, or those undergoing immunosuppressive treatments.

The following is an endoscopic image of esophageal candidiasis:

Option D: Barrett's esophagus is a type of metaplasia at the gastro-esophagal junction due to chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Autoclaving and 70% ethanol

The most effective sterilization technique for the tip of disposable glass pipettes is autoclaving combined with 70% ethanol.

Autoclaving uses: 121°C, 15 psi,15–20 minutes. This method destroys all microorganisms including spores.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 15-year-old girl presented with fatigue, chronic diarrhoea, weight loss, bone pain, and abdominal distension. Investigations revealed iron deficiency anemia and osteoporosis. Which of the following is the single best test to be done for her evaluation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. IgA tissue transglutaminase antibody

The presence of fatigue, chronic diarrhea, weight loss and abdominal distention along with investigations showing features of malabsorption (iron deficiency) lead to the diagnosis of celiac disease or gluten sensitive enteropathy. The single best test for which is checking serum for the presence of IgA tissue transglutaminase (anti-TTG) antibodies (Option D).

Celiac disease is a disorder characterized by an immunological response to gluten causing damage to the proximal intestinal mucosa (villous atrophy) and malabsorption of nutrients.

Symptoms usually begin 6 to 24 months from the introduction of gluten into diet, although most patients go undiagnosed.

The common manifestations are -  irritability, abdominal distention, chronic diarrhea, weight loss or muscle wasting and extra-intestinally, the symptoms observed are aphthous ulcers, delayed puberty, iron deficiency anemia and short stature.

Screening for celiac disease is by testing for tissue transglutaminase IgA, endomysial, and deamidated antigliadin antibodies. IgA levels in serum are measured to detect false-negative results because of IgA deficiency.

Small intestinal biopsy shows characteristic villus blunting, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes.

The treatment involves the exclusion of gluten-containing food from diet.

Long term complications observed are osteoporosis, anemia, infertility and malignancy (enteropathy related-T cell lymphoma is the most common association)

The Marsh classification is used to categorize celiac disease into different types and to quantify severity of disease involvement.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the role of the marked structure in the given image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Motor function

The marked structure is the subthalamic nucleus, which is a part of the basal ganglia and is concerned with motor function.

The basal ganglia refers to the mass of grey matter located within the cerebral white matter and is responsible for a number of coordinated functions including the control of extra-pyramidal pathways for motor coordination. There are two major pathways involved which are, the direct and indirect pathways.

The direct pathway stimulates the cortex to produce movement, whereas the indirect pathway inhibits it. The striatal activity in the direct pathway is mediated by D1 dopamine receptors and in the indirect pathway by D2 dopamine receptors. The subthalamic nucleus is a part of the indirect pathway. A lesion at subthalamic nuclei leads to loss of inhibitory effect of the indirect pathway resulting in dopaminergic overactivity responsible for features of hemiballismus.

Other Options:

Option B: Reward-punishment is associated with the prefrontal area and the dopaminergic connections linked to it from the ventral tegmental area.

Option C: Judgement is controlled by the frontal lobe.

Option D: Memory is controlled by the hippocampus.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Revised How much oxygen is given to a term infant with respiratory distress during resuscitation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 21%

Resuscitation in term infants is done by using 21% oxygen or room air.

In term infants with apnea, gasping or heart rate <100/min, positive pressure ventilation (PPV) is given by bag-mask device in room air with 21% oxygen. Room air in term infants is effective and may reduce the risk of hyperoxia, reduced cerebral blood flow and generation of free radicals.

If there is no improvement in 30 seconds, ventilative corrective steps should be taken and then oxygen concentration titrated as needed to obtain the expected saturation. If the heart rate falls below 60 then chest compressions are started, intubated and FIO2 is increased to 100%.

Resuscitation of most preterm infants can be initiated with a slightly higher fraction of inspired oxygen (21–30%) and titrated as needed.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the term used for a communication format in which 4–8 participants discuss a given topic informally in front of a large audience, without a fixed agenda, prepared speeches, or a predetermined speaking order, and later engage with the audience?
questions.explanation: The description provided matches the specific format of a Panel Discussion. In this mode, a small group of experts (4 to 8) sit in front of an audience and discuss a topic conversationally. Unlike other formats, there are no formal speeches or fixed order; the moderator guides a spontaneous exchange of ideas, and the session concludes with audience questions. A Symposium (Option B) involves formal, pre-prepared speeches by each expert on different aspects of a topic. A Workshop (Option C) is focused on practical learning and skill acquisition through active participation. A Seminar (Option D) is a more academic setting where a lead speaker presents a paper followed by group discussion. Therefore, the informal, conversational, and audience-interactive nature of the experts defines the Panel Discussion format
questions.learning: The description provided matches the specific format of a Panel Discussion. In this mode, a small group of experts (4 to 8) sit in front of an audience and discuss a topic conversationally.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 24-yr-old man presents with an excessive desire for sexual intercourse. What is this called?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Satyriasis

An excess desire for sexual intercourse in males is called satyriasis.

Satyriasis is also known as Don Juanism. In some men, sexual activity is a means to mask their deep feelings of inferiority. Some have unconscious homosexual impulses, which they deny by compulsive sexual contact with women. Many of them are no longer interested in the women after sex.

Other options

* Nymphomania: An excess desire for sexual intercourse in females

* Frotteurism: Sexual gratification achieved by touching or rubbing against a nonconsenting person.

* Masochism: The tendency to derive sexual gratification from one's own pain or humiliation.

Note: Don Juanism represents hypersexuality in males.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a road traffic accident. On examination, he has multiple injuries and is diagnosed with class III hemorrhagic shock. What is the approximate percentage range of blood loss in this condition?
questions.explanation: Hemorrhagic shock is categorized into four classes based on the volume of blood lost. In Class III shock, the blood loss is estimated to be between 30% and 40% of total blood volume. This stage is characterized by marked hypotension, a heart rate between 120–140 bpm, tachypnea, and significantly decreased urine output (5–15 ml/hour). Class I shock (Option A) involves up to 15% loss with normal vital signs. Class II shock (Option D) involves 15–30% loss, often presenting with tachycardia and narrowed pulse pressure. Class IV shock (Option C) involves more than 40% loss and is a life-threatening emergency with profound hypotension and lethargy. Identifying the class of shock is vital for determining the necessity of blood transfusions versus crystalloid resuscitation. Therefore, 30–40% loss is the definitive range for Class III
questions.learning: Hemorrhagic shock is categorized into four classes based on the volume of blood lost. In Class III shock, the blood loss is estimated to be between 30% and 40% of total blood volume.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 70-year-old woman, admitted for right leg cellulitis, develops diarrhea, abdominal pain, and fever three days into her hospital stay. Laboratory tests show a significantly elevated C-reactive protein (160 mg/L). Which pathogen is most likely causing her current symptoms?
questions.explanation: (Note: There is a nomenclature error in the source options; the intended answer is Clostridium difficile, which causes pseudomembranous colitis. "C. coli" is not a standard pathogen in this context.) The patient's development of diarrhea, fever, and abdominal pain three days after admission for a different infection (cellulitis) is the classic presentation of healthcare-associated (nosocomial) diarrhea. The primary culprit is Clostridium difficile, which typically occurs after antibiotic therapy for a primary infection (like cellulitis) disrupts the normal gut flora. E. coli (Option B) is more common in community-acquired diarrhea or food poisoning. Norovirus (Option C) and Rotavirus (Option D) are viral causes that usually present in outbreaks or specific age groups (infants) and would not be as strongly linked to a hospital admission for cellulitis. C. difficile toxins cause significant inflammation, explaining the high CRP of 160 mg/L. Therefore, antibiotic-associated colitis from Clostridium is the definitive clinical diagnosis

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presents with inability to extend his wrist and fingers. O/E, he exhibits a wrist drop with loss of sensation over the lateral aspect of the dorsum of the hand. Triceps muscle strength is fully intact and there is no sensory loss over the posterior arm. Elbow flexion in the mid-prone position is weak, and the brachioradialis tendon is not palpable on resisted flexion. Based on these findings, at which level is the radial nerve likely injured?
options: Posterior interosseous nerve at the forearm
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. At the spiral groove

Reasoning from the localising signs

| Finding | What it tells you

| ------- | -----------------

| Wrist drop (loss of wrist + finger extension) | Radial nerve affected proximal to the extensor compartment supply

| Triceps fully intact | Branches to triceps arise in/proximal to the spiral groove → lesion is at or below the groove, not in the axilla

| No sensory loss over posterior arm | Posterior cutaneous nerve of arm arises in the axilla → intact ⇒ excludes an axillary lesion

| Sensory loss over lateral dorsum of hand | Superficial branch of radial nerve is involved ⇒ excludes a pure PIN lesion (PIN is purely motor)

→ Below axilla + sensory branch involved = spiral groove (radial groove of humerus)

Other options:

| Option | Why it fails

| ------ | ------------

| A. Axilla | Would cause triceps paralysis (loss of elbow extension) + sensory loss over posterior arm. Both are explicitly negative — the classic "crutch palsy" pattern.

| B. Spiral groove | Triceps spared, posterior cutaneous n. of arm spared, superficial radial involved. Textbook Saturday-night / honeymoon palsy.

| C. Lateral epicondyle | Radial divides here into superficial + deep branches. Would give wrist drop + sensory loss — but brachioradialis and ECRL would be spared, and wrist drop is typically incomplete/with radial deviation.

| D. PIN in forearm | Purely motor → finger drop (loss of MCP extension) with preserved wrist extension in radial deviation and NO sensory loss. The stem's sensory deficit rules this out outright.

questions.text: A 45-year-old male with a history of heart surgery now presents with the chest X-ray shown below. What is the finding indicated by the '?' on the X-ray?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Prosthetic mitral valve

The structure marked in the image shows a prosthetic mitral valve and a pacemaker also in place.

Prosthetic heart valves are common. The most commonly replaced are aortic and mitral valves.

Replacements may be tissue or metallic valves.

In recent times, aortic valves in select circumstances are being replaced via a transcatheter approach, called transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) from a femoral artery approach.

Prosthetic valves are subdivided into two categories -mechanical and bioprosthetic

* Mechanical valves

* ball cage valves

* tilting disk valves

* Bioprosthetic valves

* homografts

* heterografts

* stented

* stentless

Transesophageal echocardiography is the modality of choice to assess the status of a prosthetic heart valve after placement of a valve.

Complications:

* Obstruction

* maybe due to thrombus or pannus

* Infective endocarditis

* with or without valvular vegetation or paravalvular abscess

* Paravalvular regurgitation

* Valve failure

* mechanical failure in mechanical valves

* degeneration of a biological valve

* Hemolytic anemia

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A young adult presents to the outpatient department with a testicular mass. Following orchidectomy, which type of testicular tumor is associated with the most favorable prognosis?
questions.explanation: Among germ cell tumors of the testis, seminoma carries the most favorable prognosis primarily due to its extreme radiosensitivity and high sensitivity to cisplatin-based chemotherapy. Seminomas tend to remain localized for a longer duration and spread predictably via the lymphatic system to retroperitoneal nodes, making them easier to target than Non-Seminomatous Germ Cell Tumors (NSGCTs). Teratomas (Option B) are often resistant to radiotherapy and chemotherapy, requiring surgical excision, and can undergo malignant transformation. Yolk sac tumors (Option C) are the most common testicular tumors in infants and young children, but in adults, they often present as part of a mixed germ cell tumor with a more aggressive course. Leydig cell tumors (Option D) are non-germ cell tumors; while often benign, they do not share the same systematic treatment success rates as pure seminomas. Consequently, with modern multimodal therapy, the five-year survival rate for early-stage seminoma exceeds 95%, solidifying its status as having the best clinical outlook among malignant testicular neoplasms
