questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: All of the following statements about gap junctions are true except:
options: They are composed of connexin proteins arranged into connexons
They allow direct passage of ions and small molecules (<1 kDa) between adjacent cells
They are present in cardiac muscle and are responsible for electrical coupling at intercalated discs
They require ATP hydrolysis to actively transport molecules between cells
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. They require ATP hydrolysis to actively transport molecules between cells

• Gap junctions are channels of passive, non-ATP-dependent diffusion — they allow direct intercellular passage of ions, second messengers, and small molecules (generally <1 kDa) down their electrochemical or concentration gradients, without requiring energy expenditure.
• Each gap junction channel is formed by the alignment of two connexons (hemichannels), each composed of six connexin subunits, from adjacent cells.
• They are essential for electrical coupling and synchronized contraction in cardiac muscle (at intercalated discs) and smooth muscle, as well as in other tissues like the lens, liver, and neurons (electrical synapses).
• The statement that they require ATP hydrolysis for transport is false — this describes active transport mechanisms (e.g., ATPase pumps), not gap junction-mediated diffusion.

Quick reference — Gap Junction Essentials:

| Feature | Detail

| ------- | ------

| Structural protein | Connexin (6 connexins → 1 connexon/hemichannel; 2 connexons → 1 complete channel)

| Transport mechanism | Passive diffusion (no ATP required)

| Size limit | Permits molecules <1 kDa (ions, cAMP, IP3, small metabolites)

| Key locations | Cardiac muscle (intercalated discs), smooth muscle, lens fibers, hepatocytes, neurons (electrical synapses), beta cells of pancreas

| Functional role | Electrical coupling, metabolic coupling, synchronized contraction

| Regulation | Closed by ↑intracellular Ca²⁺, ↓pH (acidosis); important in limiting injury spread after cell damage
questions.learning: They require ATP hydrolysis to actively transport molecules between cells • Gap junctions are channels of passive, non-ATP-dependent diffusion — they allow direct intercellular passage of ions, second messengers, and small molecules (generally <1 kDa) down…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the eye manifestation seen in HLA B27- positive patients with ulcerative colitis?
questions.explanation: Patients with HLA-B27-positive inflammatory bowel disease, such as ulcerative colitis, have a significantly increased risk for extraintestinal autoimmune manifestations. The most classic ocular complication is acute anterior uveitis. It typically presents with sudden eye pain, redness (ciliary flush), photophobia, and blurred vision. Conjunctivitis (Option B) is more common in reactive arthritis and involves a more superficial inflammation. Scleritis (Option C) presents with deep, boring pain and is more often linked to systemic diseases like rheumatoid arthritis. While iridocyclitis (Option D) is a subset of anterior uveitis, the general and clinically preferred term for this broad extraintestinal manifestation in IBD is uveitis. Therefore, uveitis is the standard diagnostic answer for this autoimmune link
questions.learning: Patients with HLA-B27-positive inflammatory bowel disease, such as ulcerative colitis, have a significantly increased risk for extraintestinal autoimmune manifestations.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A patient whose diet predominantly consists of rice and pulses presents with bowed legs (stick deformity). Deficiency of which vitamin could have been prevented to avoid this condition?
questions.explanation: Bowed legs, also known as a "stick deformity," in a patient with a restricted diet are a classic sign of rickets, a disease caused by Vitamin D deficiency in children. Vitamin D is critical for the intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate; its absence leads to defective bone mineralization and soft, deformed bones. Pulses and rice are poor sources of Vitamin D compared to fortified dairy or fish liver oils. Vitamin A deficiency (Option A) leads to night blindness and xerophthalmia, not bone deformities. Vitamin B12 deficiency (Option B) causes megaloblastic anemia and neurological issues. Vitamin C deficiency (Option C) leads to scurvy, which causes bleeding gums and poor wound healing but not the characteristic bowing of the legs. Sunlight exposure is the primary natural source of Vitamin D via endogenous skin synthesis
questions.learning: Bowed legs, also known as a "stick deformity," in a patient with a restricted diet are a classic sign of rickets, a disease caused by Vitamin D deficiency in children.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A young patient presents with multiple dark brown to black macules on the lips and buccal mucosa. Colonoscopy reveals multiple hamartomatous polyps. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome

Presence of multiple dark brown to black macules on the lips and buccal mucosa with hamartomatous intestinal polyps is characteristic of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.

It is caused by mutation in the STK11 gene.

• Mucocutaneous pigmentation (lips, buccal mucosa, fingers) is an early clue
• Polyps are hamartomatous, commonly in small intestine
• Increased risk of multiple malignancies (GI, pancreas, breast, ovary)
• Inheritance is autosomal dominant

Why not others:

• Familial adenomatous polyposis has adenomatous polyps without pigmentation
• Gardner syndrome has osteomas, fibromas, and dental abnormalities
• Cronkhite-Canada syndrome is non-hereditary with alopecia, nail atrophy, and diarrhea
questions.learning: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome Presence of multiple dark brown to black macules on the lips and buccal mucosa with hamartomatous intestinal polyps is characteristic of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct regarding sutures in surgery? I. Barbed sutures have the advantage of eliminating the need for knots. II. Vertical mattress sutures help in eversion of wound edges. III. Aberdeen knot is used for continuous suturing. IV. Silk is preferred for subcuticular suturing. Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, II and III

An ideal surgical suture should provide adequate tensile strength, cause minimal tissue reaction, be easy to handle, and maintain wound approximation until healing occurs. Different suturing techniques and suture materials are selected according to the tissue involved and the desired wound healing characteristics. The following statements are true:

• I. Barbed sutures have the advantage of eliminating the need for knots: Barbed sutures contain unidirectional or bidirectional barbs that anchor the tissue, eliminating the need for knot tying, reducing operative time and distributing tension evenly.
• II. Vertical mattress sutures help in eversion of wound edges: The vertical mattress suture provides excellent wound edge eversion and distributes tension, making it useful for wounds under tension.
• III. Aberdeen knot is used for continuous suturing: The Aberdeen knot is a secure knot used to terminate continuous sutures, commonly in abdominal wall and skin closure.

Why is IV incorrect?

• IV. Silk is preferred for subcuticular suturing: Subcuticular suturing is usually performed with absorbable monofilament sutures such as Monocryl (poliglecaprone), Vicryl Rapide, or PDS for better cosmetic results. Silk, a braided non-absorbable suture, causes greater tissue reaction and is not preferred.
questions.learning: I, II and III — An ideal surgical suture should provide adequate tensile strength, cause minimal tissue reaction, be easy to handle, and maintain wound approximation until healing occurs.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which neurotransmitter is secreted by the SA node in response to increased blood pressure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Acetylcholine

Acetylcholine is released in response to increased blood pressure.

In response to raised BP, there is inhibition of sympathetic system and activation of parasympathetic system. Acetylcholine is the universal neurotransmitter of PNS.

Baroreceptors are stretch receptors located in the heart and the adventitia of the blood vessels. They are stimulated by the stretching of the walls of the blood vessels when there is an increased volume or blood pressure in the vessel. They are important in the immediate management of blood pressure. They are of two types: carotid sinus and aortic arch receptors (high-pressure regions) and cardiopulmonary receptors (low-pressure regions).

An increase in blood pressure stimulates the baroreceptors. These signals are transmitted through small Hering’s nerves to the glossopharyngeal nerves and then to the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) in the medulla. These signals release glutamate and activate the caudal ventrolateral medulla (CVLM). This in turn inhibits the rostral ventrolateral medulla (RVLM) considered the vasoconstrictor center for the brain and the heart.

Simultaneously, this pathway also excites the vagal parasympathetic center. The stimulation of the vagus results in a slowing of impulse generation in the SA node and a slowing of conduction velocity in the AV node.

These neural changes produce vasodilation, venodilation, hypotension, bradycardia, and a decrease in cardiac output.

• NTS: Nucleus Tractus Solitarius
• CVLM: Caudal Ventrolateral Medulla
• RVLM : Rostral Ventrolateral Medulla (Vasomotor center)
• CVC : Cardiovagal center (Cardioinhibitory center)
• IML: intermediolateral nucleus
questions.learning: Acetylcholine Acetylcholine is released in response to increased blood pressure. In response to raised BP, there is inhibition of sympathetic system and activation of parasympathetic system.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Macula densa is made of specialized cells located at:
options: Junction of thick descending limb and DCT
Junction of thick descending limb and PCT
Junction of thick ascending limb and DCT
Junction of DCT and collecting duct
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Junction of thick ascending limb and DCT

Macula densa are the specialized cells present at the distal end of the thick ascending loop of Henle, where it reaches the glomerulus. Distal convoluted tubule starts from macula densa.

Macula forms the part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus.

Signals from the renal tubules affect filtration in its glomerulus. As the rate of flow through the ascending limb of the loop of Henle and the first part of the distal tubule increases, glomerular filtration in the same nephron decreases, and vice versa. This is known as tubuloglomerular feedback which maintains the constancy of the load delivered to the distal tubule.

The sensor is the macula densa. The Na+ and Cl− in the fluid enter the macula densa cells via theNa+–K–2Cl− cotransporter in their apical membranes. The increased Na+ increases the Na+-K+ ATPase activity causing ATP hydrolysis and the formation of adenosine. This acts on adenosine A1 receptors on the macula densa cells, causing the release of Ca2+ into the vascular smooth muscle in the afferent arterioles, leading to vasoconstriction and decreased GFR.
questions.learning: Junction of thick ascending limb and DCT Macula densa are the specialized cells present at the distal end of the thick ascending loop of Henle, where it reaches the glomerulus.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A patient presents to the emergency with signs of opioid overdose. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Naloxone

Naloxone is an opioid antagonist that rapidly reverses respiratory depression in opioid overdose. Naltrexone is for longterm dependence, fomepizole treats methanol poisoning, and flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines.
questions.learning: Naloxone Naloxone is an opioid antagonist that rapidly reverses respiratory depression in opioid overdose. Naltrexone is for longterm dependence, fomepizole treats methanol poisoning, and flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the vertebral level of the plane between the highest points of the iliac crests?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. L4-L5

The plane passing through the highest point of the iliac crest is called the supracristal plane.

Posteriorly, it corresponds to the level of the L4 body or L4/5 disc and its spinous process

Pearl PF0627: Abdominal planes and their landmarks

Planes that divide the abdomen into 9 regions

* Horizontal planes

* L3 - Subcostal plane (between 10th costal cartilages). Corresponds to the 3rd part of the duodenum

* L5 - Transtubercular plane (between tubercles of iliac crests). Corresponds to the origin of Inferior vena cava.

* Vertical planes (Paramedian or lateral planes)

* Mid-clavicular point to mid-inguinal point on both sides

The nine regions of the abdomen include:

* Left hypochondriac, Epigastric, Right hypochondriac

* Left lumbar, Umbilical (Central), Right lumbar

* Left iliac, Hypogastric (Suprapubic), Right iliac

Other planes and angles in the abdomen

* Transpyloric (Addison's) plane passes midway between the suprasternal notch and the upper border of the pubic symphysis.

* The supracristal plane passing through the highest point of the iliac crest on both sides. Posteriorly, it corresponds to the level of the L4 body or L4/5 disc and its spinous process. It is an important landmark when performing a lumbar puncture or spinal injection. The bifurcation of the abdominal aorta lies approximately in this plane.

* The plane of the pubic crest passes through the upper border of the pubic symphysis. When supine, this plane intersects the tip of the coccyx and the femoral head.

* Renal angle is the angle between the 12th rib and the outer border of Erector spinae muscle. The lower border of normal kidneys may occasionally be felt here.

* Lumbar triangle (of Petit) is marked below by the iliac crest, anteriorly by external oblique and posteriorly by latissimus dorsi. Lumbar herniation can occur here.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following options can be employed for the treatment of Kesari dal toxicity?
questions.explanation: Kesari dal (Lathyrus sativus) consumption leads to neurolathyrism, a crippling spastic paraplegia caused by the neurotoxin BOAA. Studies and clinical observations have suggested that Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) may offer protective effects or act as an adjunct in management. Vitamin C is thought to help by reducing oxidative stress or potentially influencing the absorption and metabolism of the toxin. Sodium bicarbonate (Option A) is used for metabolic acidosis. Vitamin A (Option B) is used for ocular deficiencies. IV immunoglobulin (Option D) is used for autoimmune neuromuscular disorders like GBS. While the primary prevention is the avoidance of the dal or specialized soaking techniques to leach the toxin, Vitamin C remains the standard "medical" adjunct mentioned in this context. Therefore, Vitamin C is the only correct pharmacological option listed for addressing the toxicity associated with chronic Kesari dal ingestion

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 72-year-old patient with a confirmed diagnosis of mild to moderate Alzheimer's dementia has shown aversion and non-compliance to oral medications. The patient's caregiver reports difficulty in administering the oral drugs due to the patient's refusal to swallow pills. Considering the need for continued treatment, which of the following medications could be prescribed in a form that does not require oral administration?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rivastigmine

Core issue: ↓ Acetylcholine in brain (basal forebrain degeneration)

Strategy: Increase cholinergic transmission

| Class | Drugs

| ----- | -----

| Cholinesterase inhibitors | Donepezil, Rivastigmine, Galantamine

| NMDA antagonist | Memantine

Rivastigmine is available as a transdermal patch, making it suitable for patients who cannot take oral medications.

It is a cholinesterase inhibitor used in mild to moderate Alzheimer’s dementia.

The patch provides steady drug delivery and improves compliance.

Memantine, donepezil, and galantamine are primarily administered orally.

| Drug | Class | Route | Special Feature

| ---- | ----- | ----- | ---------------

| Rivastigmine | AChE inhibitor |  Patch | Non-oral option

| Donepezil | AChE inhibitor | Oral | Once daily

| Galantamine | AChE inhibitor | Oral | Dual action

Patch Advantage

• Steady drug delivery

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Identify the finding that is seen in antemortem drowning?
questions.explanation: The image shows a hand tightly clutching grass/weeds, which is a classic sign of cadaveric spasm. This occurs at the moment of death, where muscles undergo instantaneous stiffening without relaxation. It is a strong indicator of antemortem drowning, as the victim grasps surrounding objects (like aquatic plants) during the struggle. Why this is important : Cadaveric spasm suggests the person was alive at the time of entering water, making it a key forensic sign of antemortem drowning. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Pugilistic attitude: Seen in burn victims due to heat-induced muscle contraction, not drowning. (C) Washerwoman hand: Skin wrinkling due to prolonged immersion; occurs both ante- and postmortem, so not specific. (D) Emphysema aquosum: Refers to overdistended lungs in drowning, but it is not depicted in this image. The gripping of objects clearly indicates cadaveric spasm, confirming antemortem drowning
questions.learning: The image shows a hand tightly clutching grass/weeds, which is a classic sign of cadaveric spasm. This occurs at the moment of death, where muscles undergo instantaneous stiffening without relaxation.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Identify the chromosomal abnormality from the karyotyping shown below :
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Trisomy 18

The given karyotype is Trisomy 18- Edward's syndrome.

Edward's syndrome: Trisomy 18 results in Edward’s syndrome, in which a complete extra copy of chromosome 18 is inherited as a result of meiotic nondisjunction. The clinical features include micrognathia, low-set ears, prominent occiput, and rocker bottom feet Prenatal ultrasound reveals fetal growth restriction.

The craniofacial features include dolichocephaly, short palpebral fissures, micrognathia, external anomalies of the ears, and redundant skin at the back of the neck.

Other features include a clenched fist with overriding fingers, i.e. index finger overlapping the third and 5th finger overlapping the 4th, small fingernails, underdeveloped thumbs, short sternum, and club feet.

Heart defects are the most common structural malformations seen in Edwards syndrome. It includes defects of septum, patent ductus arteriosus, valvular defects. Other structural malformations associated with other systems(in decreasing order) are,

* Renal: Horseshoe kidney

* GIT: Omphalocele, esophageal atresia with tracheo-oesophageal fistula, pyloric stenosis.

* CNS: Spina bifida, cerebellar hypoplasia, corpus callosum agenesis

* Eye: Microphthalmia, cataract, corneal opacities

* Limb: Radial aplasia/hypoplasia

Other options :

Option A: Trisomy 13 - Patau Syndrome

* It is characterized by forebrain and midline facial abnormalities.

* Patients can develop holoprosencephaly, which is characterized by fused frontal lobes and a single ventricle. Olfactory bulbs are also absent.

* The midline facial abnormalities that are seen with trisomy 13 include cleft lip, cleft palate, nasal defects, and a single central eye (“cyclops”).

* Other defects associated with Patau’s syndrome include polydactyly, rocker-bottom feet, and congenital heart diseases.

The image below shows the facial abnormalities seen in Patau syndrome:

Option B: Trisomy 21: Down's Syndrome

* It is the most common chromosomal abnormality.

* Children with Down’s syndrome have severe mental retardation, which progressively declines with advancing age.

* Patients have characteristic facial features that include a flat facial profile, oblique palpebral fissures, and epicanthal folds.

* There is a horizontal palmar crease, and muscle tone at birth is decreased, which leads to a “floppy baby".

Option D: Trisomy 11 is extremely rare and often leads to miscarriage in early pregnancy.
questions.learning: Trisomy 18 — The given karyotype is Trisomy 18- Edward's syndrome. Edward's syndrome: Trisomy 18 results in Edward’s syndrome, in which a complete extra copy of chromosome 18 is inherited as a result of meiotic nondisjunction.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 54-year-old woman with a history of rheumatic heart disease and prosthetic valve replacement six months ago presents with fever, fatigue, and progressively worsening shortness of breath. Examination reveals a new heart murmur and splinter hemorrhages on the nail beds, suggestive of infective endocarditis. Considering her prosthetic valve and current presentation, which organism is most likely responsible for her infective endocarditis?
questions.explanation: Infective endocarditis (IE) following prosthetic valve replacement is categorized by timing. "Early" prosthetic valve endocarditis occurs within one year of surgery and is most commonly caused by Staphylococcus epidermidis, a coagulase-negative staphylococcus (CoNS) that is part of the normal skin flora. This organism is highly adept at forming biofilms on foreign materials like prosthetic valves. While Option D (Coagulase-negative Staphylococci) is technically the broader group, standard medical examinations usually look for the specific species Staphylococcus epidermidis in this clinical context. Streptococcus viridans (Option B) is the most common cause of subacute IE on native, damaged valves, usually following dental procedures. Enterococcus faecalis (Option C) often causes endocarditis following gastrointestinal or genitourinary manipulations. Because this patient’s symptoms appeared within the 6-12 month post-operative window, S. epidermidis—introduced during the surgical procedure or through postoperative seeding—is the most statistically probable and classic answer for this board-style question

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: You are suturing a laceration in the ER using the interrupted suturing technique. What is the angle of needle placement?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 90 degrees

In the interrupted suture technique, the needle is placed at an angle of 90 degrees (at right angles).

Interrupted sutures:

The needle should be inserted and exit the skin at right angles. It should be rotated through the tissue rather than dragged to prevent unnecessary enlargement of the needle hole. The distance from the suture entry point to the wound edge should be approximately equal to the depth of the sutured tissue. There should be twice this distance between two consecutive sutures.

The image below shows interrupted suture:

Other suturing techniques:

Continuous Suture: The first suture is inserted in a manner identical to that in an interrupted suture. The remaining sutures are inserted in a continuous manner until the far end of the wound is reached. Care should be taken to maintain the tension of the suture to avoid excessive tension or leaving it too slack; hence, the use of an assistant is warranted. An Aberdeen knot is used to secure the end of the suture.

Mattress sutures - They can be vertical or horizontal and are used to create either an eversion or inversion of the wound edges. The initial suture is inserted in the same way as an interrupted suture, but then, the needle either moves horizontally or vertically and traverses both edges of the wound once again, as seen in the image below. The main advantage of the mattress suture is that it produces an accurate approximation of wound edges, especially in settings where the edges are not easily approximated.

Subcuticular sutures: It is used for a better cosmetic appearance. It is also employed in situations where the edges of the wound are easily approximated. In this technique, small bites of the subcuticular tissues are taken on alternate sites of the wound, and then, they are gently pulled together. This causes an approximation of the wound edges without the risk of the cross-hatched markings of interrupted sutures.
questions.learning: 90 degrees In the interrupted suture technique, the needle is placed at an angle of 90 degrees (at right angles). Interrupted sutures: The needle should be inserted and exit the skin at right angles.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is considered harmful to a newborn baby in the immediate postnatal period?
options: Cleaning the eyes with a wet sterile swab
Giving a bath immediately after birth
Placing the baby on the mother's chest
questions.explanation: Bathing a newborn immediately after birth is considered harmful as it can cause rapid heat loss, leading to life-threatening hypothermia. Immediate bathing also removes the vernix caseosa, a naturally occurring coating that provides essential antimicrobial protection and moisturizing properties to the neonatal skin. Furthermore, it interrupts critical early bonding and delays the initiation of breastfeeding, which should ideally occur within the first hour of life. World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines mandate delaying the first bath for at least 24 hours, or a minimum of 6 hours if cultural factors intervene. Cleaning the eyes with sterile swabs (Option A) is a safe practice to prevent neonatal ophthalmia. Placing the infant on the mother’s chest (Option D) is a recommended practice to encourage warmth and early feeding. Thus, immediate bathing is the only harmful practice among the choices

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following is true regarding De Quervain’s tenosynovitis?
options: Fingers are held in mild extension
Most common involvement is index finger
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It affects APL and EPB

De Quervain's disease is a stenosing tenosynovitis of the extensor tendons of the first dorsal compartment, namely extensor pollicis brevis (EPB) and abductor pollicis longus (APL).

It is prominent among females, especially pregnant women. Most commonly thumb is involved.

Finkelstein's test: On grasping the patient’s thumb and quickly abducting the hand ulnar ward, the pain over the radial styloid tip is excruciating. It’s the most pathognomonic objective sign but is also seen in other conditions like radial nerve entrapment and arthritis.

Treatment:

• Majority of the patients are treated medically
• Only few require the release of the 1st dorsal compartment which houses the APL and EPB tendons.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: What causes decrease in GFR?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Decrease in glomerular coefficient

Decrease in glomerular coefficient causes decrease in GFR.

The glomerular filtration coefficient (Kf) is a measure of how efficiently the glomerulus filters blood into the kidney tubules. It depends on two key factors:

• Surface Area for Filtration: Greater surface area means higher filtration.
• Permeability of the Glomerular Membrane: Higher permeability leads to greater filtration.

Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is the volume of fluid filtered from the renal glomerular capillaries into the Bowman's capsule per unit time.

The GFR is determined by the sum of the hydrostatic and colloid osmotic forces across the glomerular membrane, which gives the net filtration pressure. It is dependent on Glomerular Kf (glomerular ultrafiltration coefficient) also.

Mathematically, it can be expressed as follows:

GFR= Kf [PG + πB -PB- πG]

Forces favoring Filtration

• PG: Glomerular hydrostatic pressure (Option C)
• πB: Bowman’s capsule oncotic pressure

Forces opposing Filtration

• PB: Bowman’s capsule hydrostatic pressure (Option D)
• πG: Glomerular capillary oncotic pressure (Option B)

The formula for glomerular filtration rate (GFR) incorporates Kf:

• A high Kf means efficient filtration (e.g., in healthy kidneys)-indicates high GFR
• A low Kf {occurs when the surface area is reduced (e.g., due to glomerular damage) or the membrane becomes less permeable (e.g., in diabetic nephropathy)}- indicates low GFR.

Kf is essential for maintaining proper kidney function, as it directly affects how well the kidneys filter blood to form urine.
questions.learning: Decrease in glomerular coefficient Decrease in glomerular coefficient causes decrease in GFR. The glomerular filtration coefficient (Kf) is a measure of how efficiently the glomerulus filters blood into the kidney tubules.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: According to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) set for 2030, what is the target for reducing the maternal mortality rate?
questions.explanation: The United Nations Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 3.1 sets a global target to reduce the Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) to less than 70 per 100,000 live births by the year 2030. This goal aims to eliminate preventable maternal deaths worldwide and improve maternal health outcomes. Options A, C, and D represent other numerical thresholds but do not correspond to the officially adopted SDG target. MMR is defined as the number of maternal deaths per 100,000 live births resulting from complications related to pregnancy, childbirth, or its management, excluding accidental or incidental causes. India has made notable progress in reducing MMR through initiatives such as Janani Suraksha Yojana, promotion of institutional deliveries, improved access to antenatal and postnatal care, and strengthening of emergency obstetric services. Monitoring of progress is carried out through national data sources such as the Sample Registration System (SRS) and National Family Health Surveys (NFHS). Achieving the SDG 3.1 target requires universal access to quality maternal healthcare, skilled birth attendance, and timely referral services. Reducing MMR is a key indicator of health system performance, women’s health, and gender equality
questions.learning: The United Nations Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 3.1 sets a global target to reduce the Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR) to less than 70 per 100,000 live births by the year 2030.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The patient came to the ER with pain on the left side of the chest radiating to the left arm and shoulder for the last 40 minutes. ECG shows ST depression in precordial leads. What is the next best step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Low dose aspirin + clopidogrel

The given clinical scenario of a patient coming to the ER with pain on the left side of the chest radiating to the left arm and shoulder for the last 40 minutes. ECG showing ST depression in precordial leads is suggestive of NSTEMI(Non-ST elevation Myocardial infarction) and the next best step in management is low-dose aspirin with clopidogrel.

Acute coronary syndrome is classified into 2 groups:

* ST-segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI).

* NSTE-ACS.

NSTE-ACS further includes:

* NSTEMI (myocyte necrosis present and cardiac troponins elevated).

* Unstable Angina (myocyte necrosis absent and cardiac troponins not elevated).

The diagnosis of NSTE-ACS is based on the following:

Severe chest discomfort with at least one of 3 features:

* Occurring at rest or minimal exertion and lasting for more than 10 minutes

* Recent onset

* Crescendo pattern

ECG showing:

* ST segment depression

* T wave inversion

Elevated cardiac troponins in case of NSTEMI.

Management of NSTE-ACS:

To provide relief of pain and discomfort, initial treatment includes bed rest, nitrates, beta-blockers, and inhaled oxygen (only if arterial O2 saturation <90%).

Antithrombotic therapy consisting of antiplatelet and anticoagulant drugs:

* Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT): Aspirin (162-325 mg) AND one ADP receptor inhibitor (Ticagrelor, clopidogrel or prasugrel).

* Anticoagulation: Enoxaparin, unfractionated heparin, fondaparinux or bivalirudin.

* An early invasive strategy including diagnostic coronary angiography (within 2–72 hours of presentation) followed by revascularization. (percutaneous coronary intervention/ coronary artery bypass grafting) is indicated for stabilized patients who are at high risk of coronary events (Based on TIMI, GRACE or HEART score).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child in your unit is diagnosed with severe acute malnutrition (SAM). According to the WHO criteria, SAM is defined best by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Weight for height less than - 3SD

Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) is best defined as weight for height less than median minus -3SD

Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) in children of ages 6 to 59 months is defined by the WHO as any of the following:

1. Weight-for-length (or height) below −3 SD of the median WHO child growth standards.
2. Presence of bipedal edema
3. Mid-upper arm circumference <11.5 cm

Once the child is diagnosed with severe acute malnutrition, the doctor must assess for severe edema (+++); low appetite (failed appetite test); medical complications (severe anemia, pneumonia, diarrhea, dehydration, cerebral palsy, tuberculosis, HIV, heart disease, etc.) and one or more danger signs as per IMNCI

If any of the complications are present, the child is diagnosed with complicated SAM and is managed inpatient in the facility.

If the above-mentioned signs are absent, the child is diagnosed with uncomplicated SAM and supervised management at home is given.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text:
Which of the following is required for the cannulation of a newborn?

1. 22G needle
2. 24G needle
3. 5-mL syringe
4. Adhesive tape
5. Normal saline
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2,3,4,5

For cannulation in newborns, we would require a 24G needle, 5 mL syringe, adhesive tape, and normal saline.

Also, for a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC), we use a 24G needle for >1 kg neonate, and for <1 kg neonate, we use a 28G needle. We need to avoid using 1 mL syringes for flushing as it may lead to catheter rupture; preferably, use 5 or 10 mL syringes. Flushing of the cannulation is done using 0.9% sodium chloride or so-called normal saline (NS).

Dressing change: We change PICC line dressing only when visibly soiled, damp, or loosened. For making it easier and sterile, two persons should perform a dressing change.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 30-year-old female developed a tumor at the knee joint. Biopsy-image is given below and shows multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells.What is the most likely condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Giant cell tumour

The biopsy image shows characteristic multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells, with nuclei having a similar appearance to the surrounding mononuclear cells, suggestive of giant cell tumour.

Giant cell tumours are benign but locally aggressive tumours of bone and consist of a proliferation of mononuclear cells with scattered macrophages. They are most commonly seen between 20-45 years of age. GCTs can occasionally be associated with Paget’s disease of bone and focal dermal hypoplasia (Goltz syndrome).

They typically affect the metaphyses of long bones, more commonly the distal femur, proximal tibia, distal radius and proximal humerus. Patients present with pain and a mass.

A GCT is typically seen on X-ray as an eccentric, lobulated, lytic lesion with non-sclerotic borders, giving a soap bubble appearance. They usually have little or no matrix calcification, new bone formation or periosteal reaction. Tumours that extend into the soft tissues are seen as soft-tissue masses which may be covered by a thin layer of sclerosis. They are usually within the metaphysis but may involve the physis and subchondral plate. If malignant, the tumour appears as a lytic lesion with a sclerosing destructive tumour adjacent to it.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Suction and evacuation is a commonly performed procedure for termination of pregnancy or management of miscarriage, and its safety and effectiveness depend on appropriate timing. At what gestational age is suction and evacuation best performed?
questions.explanation: Suction and evacuation (S&E) is the preferred surgical method for the medical termination of pregnancy or the management of early miscarriage during the first trimester, typically up to 12 weeks of gestation. At this stage, the fetal tissue and placenta can be safely and effectively removed using a vacuum cannula with minimal risk of uterine injury or significant hemorrhage. While it can be performed as early as 6 weeks (Option C), the procedure is most commonly standardized and technically easiest around 10-12 weeks when the gestational sac is well-defined. Beyond 12 weeks, such as at 15 weeks (Option B) or 18 weeks (Option D), the procedure is classified as "dilatation and evacuation" (D&E), which involves larger instruments and higher risks due to the increased size of fetal parts and increased uterine vascularity. S&E remains a cornerstone of reproductive healthcare, offering a rapid and highly effective alternative to medical management, provided it is performed within the established first-trimester safety window
questions.learning: Suction and evacuation (S&E) is the preferred surgical method for the medical termination of pregnancy or the management of early miscarriage during the first trimester, typically up to 12 weeks of gestation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In the context of contraceptive effectiveness, the Pearl Index is utilized to evaluate:
questions.explanation: The Pearl Index is the standard statistical measure used to describe the clinical effectiveness of a contraceptive method. It specifically calculates the number of accidental pregnancies (Option A) that occur per 100 woman-years of exposure to the method. A lower Pearl Index indicates a more effective and reliable contraceptive. It does not measure population size (Option B), the general fertility rate (Option C) of a region, or the number of abortions (Option D) . The formula for the index is: . This index is essential for clinicians to counsel patients on the "failure rate" of various methods, such as comparing the high effectiveness of IUCDs to the lower effectiveness of barrier methods. Therefore, the Pearl Index is uniquely and strictly associated with evaluating accidental pregnancies in family planning studies
questions.learning: The Pearl Index is the standard statistical measure used to describe the clinical effectiveness of a contraceptive method. It specifically calculates the number of accidental pregnancies (Option A) that occur per 100 woman-years of exposure to the method.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A young male patient presents to ER with complaints of daytime somnolence and repeated awakening at night from sleep and his partner gives history of snoring in bed. All of the following are true except?
options: Apnea is due to fall in oxygen saturation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Pharngeal muscle tone increases

Pharyngeal muscle tone decreases during snoring.

Pharyngeal muscles are relaxed during sleep and cause partial obstruction. Breathing against obstruction causes vibrations of soft palate, tonsillar pillars and base of tongue producing sound.

Types of snoring:

• Primary snoring: without association with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). Primary snoring is not associated with excessive daytime sleepiness and has apnea—hypnoea index of less than five.
• Complicated snoring: associated with OSA.

Obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome (OSAHS) is diagnosed if the patient has either symptoms of nocturnal breathing disturbances or daytime sleepiness, and ≥5 episodes of obstructive apnea or hypopnea per hour of sleep. Each such episode should last for at least 10 seconds, resulting in ≥3% drop in oxygen saturation or a brain cortical arousal. OSA is diagnosed by overnight polysomnogram (PSG).

OSAHS is characterized by recurrent episodes of upper airway obstruction during sleep, leading to intermittent hypoxia and sleep fragmentation

Usually, there is a decline in neuromuscular output to pharyngeal dilator muscles during sleep. In predisposed individuals, this results in complete (apnea) or partial (hypopnea) pharyngeal collapse.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements is false regarding rectal carcinoma?
options: Hartmann’s operation is done in elderly debilitated patients
Adenocarcinoma is a rare variant of rectal carcinoma
Early morning spurious diarrhoea and tenesmus can occur
Growth confined to the rectal mucosa is stage A of modified Duke’s staging
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Adenocarcinoma is a rare variant of rectal carcinoma

Adenocarcinoma is the most common variant of rectal carcinoma.

Colorectal cancer is:

1. The second most common malignancy globally
2. The second most common cancer in women
3. The third most common cancer in men
4. The fourth most common cause of death due to cancer.

Symptoms of rectal carcinoma include:

1. Painless bleeding - earliest and most common
2. Alteration of bowel habits - change in frequency and consistency of the stool
3. Tenesmus - unable to pass a motion even when there is the sensation of needing to evacuate the bowel. It is suggestive of a tumor of the lower half of the rectum
4. Early morning bloody diarrhea (option C) - passage of blood and mucus in addition to feces. Pain and weight loss are usually late symptoms

Abdominal examination and digital rectal examination are used for the primary evaluation. Rigid sigmoidoscopy is performed to obtain a biopsy. A synchronous tumor (primary tumor with a different origin than the one currently investigated) is excluded by performing a colonoscopy.

Modified Duke’s classification:

A

Growth limited up to the rectal mucosa (option D)

B

B1: Tumor invading muscularis propria, no lymph node invasion.

B2: Tumors invading into or through serosa, no lymph node invasion.

C

C1: The tumour did not exceed the bowel wall, lymph node metastasis.

C2: Tumour exceeded the intestinal wall and lymph node metastasis.

D

Distant metastasis

Surgery is the mainstay of management for rectal carcinoma. Non-operative management is offered to only those patients who have a complete clinical response to neoadjuvant.

The type of surgery depends on multiple factors (size, location, age of the patient, etc). However, the general consensus is:

1. Early cancer (T1 and a few T2) is locally excised via the transanal approach.
2. Most rectal cancer is treated by anterior resection and colorectal/coloanal anastomosis.
3. Low extensive tumors are treated by laparoscopic abdominoperineal resection(APR) and permanent colostomy.
4. Hartmann’s operation (option A) is preferred in old and frail patients due to poor anal sphincter and postoperative incontinence.
questions.learning: Adenocarcinoma is a rare variant of rectal carcinoma Adenocarcinoma is the most common variant of rectal carcinoma. The second most common malignancy globally 2.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In patients with acute ischemic stroke, the ABCD² score is commonly used to predict the risk of stroke recurrence. Which of the following factors is NOT included in this stroke risk assessment tool?
questions.explanation: The ABCD2 score is a clinical tool used primarily to predict the short-term risk of a full stroke following a Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA). The components of the score are Age (60 years), Blood pressure (systolic 140 or diastolic 90 mmHg), Clinical features (unilateral weakness or speech impairment), Duration of symptoms (minutes), and Diabetes Mellitus. While a History of Stroke is a significant risk factor for future neurological events, it is notably absent from the standardized ABCD2 scoring criteria. Hypertension (Option B) is represented by the "B" in the acronym, Age (Option A) by "A", and Diabetes (Option D) by "D". The scoring helps clinicians decide on the urgency of hospital admission and the intensity of secondary prevention strategies. Scores ranging from 6 to 7 indicate a high risk of stroke within two days. Accurate application of this tool ensures that high-risk individuals receive timely intervention to prevent permanent neurological deficits and improve overall clinical outcomes

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A young male patient, who has a family history of bipolar disorder on his paternal side, has come to your OPD with 3 episodes of mania. Which of the following mood stabilizers can be given to him as the most effective treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lithium

Lithium is the drug of choice for maintenance therapy or prophylaxis of bipolar disorder. It is also the most effective long-term treatment for bipolar disorder.

Pearl PF1274: Treatment of acute manic episode

There is no single drug of choice for the treatment of acute mania.

If the patient is on anti-depressants: Stop antidepressants.

If the patient is already on anti-manic medication:

* If already on lithium or valproate: increase the dose of lithium or valproate and consider adding an antipsychotic.

* Consider adding short-term benzodiazepines for all patients.

If the patient is not on anti-manic medication:

* Consider an antipsychotic if symptoms are severe and behavior is disturbed (or)

* Consider valproate, but avoid in women of reproductive age (or)

* Consider lithium if future adherence is likely

* Consider adding short-term benzodiazepines for all patients.
questions.learning: Lithium Lithium is the drug of choice for maintenance therapy or prophylaxis of bipolar disorder. It is also the most effective long-term treatment for bipolar disorder.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 6-year-old boy came with a history of recurrent urinary tract infections. Imaging was done and is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Vesicoureteric reflux

In the given scenario of a 6-year-old boy with recurrent urinary tract infections and the micturating cystourethrogram showing a dilated ureter, the likely diagnosis is vesicoureteric reflux.

Vesicoureteric or vesicoureteral reflux (VUR) is a condition in which there is a retrograde urinary flow from the bladder to the ureter and kidney. It is usually congenital.

VUR can cause urinary stasis and lead to urinary tract infection (UTI). It also predisposes to pyelonephritis, which can lead to renal scarring due to parenchymal inflammation. This is known as reflux nephropathy.

Micturating cystogram is used to confirm the VUR. VUR can be graded based on the appearance of the urinary tract on the micturating cystogram. It is as follows:

Grade 1- reflux into the ureter

Grade 2- reflux into the ureter and renal pelvis

Grade 3- mild to moderate dilatation on IVU along with reflux and mild blunting of calices

Grade 4- blunting of fornices

Grade 5- absent papillary impressions

Grades 1-3 resolve spontaneously. Surgical management is done when acute pyelonephritis recurs in spite of antibiotic therapy or if severe reflux is associated with a defect that can be corrected surgically.

Other options:

Option B: Urinary bladder diverticula occurs due to pressure changes in the bladder leading to the formation of saccules that may protrude through the bladder wall. It is more common in elderly males >50 years and is usually asymptomatic or not infected. Symptoms may occur due to associated urinary obstruction, recurrent infection, or pyelonephritis. They are diagnosed incidentally on cystoscopy or ultrasonography.

Option C: Urinary bladder hernia is an uncommon condition characterized by herniation of the urinary bladder or ureter into the inguinal canal, scrotum, or femoral canal. Urinary symptoms such as dysuria, frequency, urgency, nocturia, and hematuria can be seen. Retrograde cystography is the best technique to image a bladder hernia.

Option D: Vesicocolic fistula is an abnormal communication between the bladder and the colon. As a result of this, the fecal matter may enter the bladder. Diverticulitis is the most common cause. Bubbles in the urine, pain, hematuria, and recurrent UTI can occur. Cystoscopy reveals edema and gas bubbles. The fistula can be seen in a cystogram.
questions.learning: Vesicoureteric reflux — In the given scenario of a 6-year-old boy with recurrent urinary tract infections and the micturating cystourethrogram showing a dilated ureter, the likely diagnosis is vesicoureteric reflux.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young male patient presents with a history of high-grade fever for the last 5 days. When his hands were examined, the following lesions were seen which were painless and a new regurgitant murmur is heard. Echocardiogram shows the presence of a mass on the mitral valve. Which of the following abdomen finding will be present here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Splenomegaly

In the above clinical scenario of a patient presenting with high-grade fever, new-onset murmur, and faint, red, painless macules on palms and soles (called as Janeway lesions), the most probable diagnosis for this patient would be infective endocarditis (IE). The most common abdominal finding is splenomegaly..

Infective endocarditis is characterized by the presence of large, friable, irregular vegetations on heart valves. Patients with infective endocarditis can have cardiac or non-cardiac manifestations.

Cardiac manifestations of IE:

* Presence of new regurgitant murmurs

* Congestive heart failure due to valve dysfunction

* Perivalvular abscesses and intracardiac fistulae- This is caused due to the extension of infection beyond the valves and into the adjacent myocardial tissue

* Conduction system defects- due to the damage of the interventricular septum by the abscess.

* Embolization of coronary arteries

Noncardiac manifestations of IE are:

* Arterial emboli- causing pain of ischemia of the organs

* Roth's spots- retinal hemorrhages with a pale center

* Janeway lesions- In contrast to Osler's nodes, these are faint, red, painless macules on palms and soles. They occur as a result of septic embolization and are commonly associated with staphylococcal IE.

* Glomerulonephritis

* Positivity for rheumatoid factor

* Petechiae on the oral and conjunctival mucosa

* Splinter subungual hemorrhages-painless, dark red lines in the nailbed.

* Mycotic aneurysms

* Splenomegaly

* Osler’s nodes (shown in the image below) are tender, red nodules that typically appear on the pads of the fingers and toes. Occurs due to immune complex deposition and vasculitis.

Image given below shows Roth spots.

Pearl PF0379: Modified Duke's criteria for diagnosis of infective endocarditis

Diagnosis of Infective endocarditis is by Duke's Criteria, which requires either:

* Clinical criteria

* Pathologic criteria

If clinical criteria are used, definitive endocarditis is defined by the presence of 2 major or 1 major + 3 minor or 5 minor criteria.

Presence of single pathological criteria is definitive of infective endocarditis.

Clinical Criteria

Major Criteria

1. Positive blood culture

Typical microorganism for IE from 2 separate blood cultures.

(or)

Persistently positive blood culture of an organism consistent with IE from:

• Blood cultures drawn >12 h apart.
• All of 3 or a majority of ≥4 separate blood cultures, with first and last drawn at least 1 h apart.

(or)

Single positive blood culture for Coxiella burnetti or phase I IgG antibody titer of >1:800.

2. Evidence of endocardial involvement

Echocardiographic identification of oscillating intracardiac mass on valve or implant or in the path of regurgitant jets

(or)

New Valvular regurgitation

Minor Criteria

1. Predisposing heart lesion or intravenous drug use

2. Fever ≥38.0°C (≥100.4°F)

3. Vascular lesions: Major arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial hemorrhage, conjunctival hemorrhages, Janeway lesions.

4. Immunological evidence: Glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots, rheumatoid factor.

5. Microbiologic evidence: Positive blood culture but not meeting the major criterion, or serologic evidence of active infection with an organism consistent with infective endocarditis.

Pathological Criteria

1. Microorganisms demonstrated by culture or histologic examination, in vegetation, embolus from vegetation, or intracardiac abscess

(or)

2. Histologic confirmation of active endocarditis in vegetation or intracardiac abscess

Note: The diagnosis of endocarditis is rejected if an alternative diagnosis is established, if symptoms resolve and do not recur with ≤4 days of antibiotic therapy, or if surgery or autopsy after ≤4 days of antimicrobial therapy yields no histologic evidence of endocarditis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 46-year-old nulliparous woman is found to have an endometrial thickness of 16 mm on TVS. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Endometrial biopsy

A thickened endometrium in a perimenopausal woman raises suspicion for:

• Endometrial Hyperplasia
• Endometrial Carcinoma

Risk factors present in this patient:

| Risk Factor | Significance

| ----------- | ------------

| Age >45 years | Higher malignancy risk

| Nulliparity | More lifetime estrogen exposure

| Thick endometrium (16 mm) | Abnormal finding

Therefore histological confirmation is required.

Typical findings:

| Group | Endometrial Thickness

| ----- | ---------------------

| Premenopausal proliferative phase | 5–7 mm

| Secretory phase | up to 12–14 mm

| Postmenopausal | <4 mm

In a 46-year-old woman, 16 mm is abnormally thick, so tissue diagnosis is required.

Endometrial Biopsy is the first-line diagnostic test.

Common method: Pipelle biopsy

Purpose:

• Detect hyperplasia
• Diagnose endometrial cancer

B) Hysterectomy

Too aggressive without histological diagnosis.

Risk Factors for Endometrial Cancer

| Risk Factor | Mechanism

| ----------- | ---------

| Nulliparity | Continuous estrogen exposure

| Obesity | Peripheral estrogen production

| PCOS | Chronic anovulation

| Diabetes | Metabolic risk

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following abnormalities occur from vitamin D deficiency in children? 1. Craniotabes 2. Bossing of frontal and parietal bones 3. Muscle hypotonia 4. Shrinking of epiphysis at the lower end of radius Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 2 and 3

Vitamin D deficiency in children causes rickets, characterized by defective mineralization of the growing bone. Clinical features include craniotabes, frontal/parietal bossing, muscle hypotonia, widening of wrists, rachitic rosary, bow legs, and delayed closure of fontanelles.

Why not the other option?

• 4. Shrinking of epiphysis at the lower end of radius: Incorrect. Rickets causes widening, cupping, fraying, and splaying of the metaphysis at the distal radius, not shrinking of the epiphysis.

questions.text: A 16-year-old female patient presents with an ovarian mass. On further evaluation, her serum biomarkers are found to be normal except for LDH, which is found to be elevated. The most likely diagnosis is:

Correct answer: A. Dysgerminoma

The given clinical history of a 16-year-old female presenting with an ovarian mass and raised LDH, points towards the diagnosis of dysgerminoma.

Dysgerminoma corresponds to the seminoma of the testis and accounts for 3-5% of all ovarian tumors. It usually arises in young girls or in children, with an average age of 20 years. It is the most common malignant tumor of the ovary. It is usually unilateral, but they are the only germ cell malignancy with a significant rate of bilateral ovarian involvement (15-20%) and can be found at gonadal or extragonadal sites.

Genetics:

• Express OCT-3, OCT-4 and NANOG
• Activating mutations in the KIT gene in one-third of cases

Pathology:

• Solid neoplasm with areas of softening due to degeneration with fleshy consistency
• Mimics the pattern of the primitive gonad, lymphocytic infiltration is seen

It presents with abdominal pain, distension, a palpable mass and ascites. Some tumors occur in patients with gonadal dysgenesis, including pseudohermaphroditism. It secretes placental alkaline phosphatase, lactate dehydrogenase and beta-HCG, but no sex hormones.

Morphology and histology:

• Most dysgerminomas (80% to 90%) are unilateral tumors ranging in size from barely visible nodules to masses that virtually fill the abdomen.
• On cut surfaces, they have a solid yellow-white to gray-pink appearance and are often soft and fleshy.
• Like seminoma, it is composed of large vesicular cells with clear cytoplasm, well-defined cell boundaries, and centrally placed regular nuclei.
• The tumor cells grow in sheets or cords separated by scant fibrous stroma, which is infiltrated by lymphocytes and may contain noncaseating granulomas

The image below shows the histopathology of a dysgerminoma, characterized by uniform cells resembling primordial germ cells separated by fibrous septa with lymphocytes.

Management:

• Though dysgerminomas are radiosensitive, they are contraindicated due to ovarian destruction in young girls. It is employed only for residual and recurrent tumors.
• Treatment includes surgical removal and postoperative chemotherapy.

Chemotherapy comprises of

• Injection bleomycin 15 mg i.v (or) i.m weekly for 12 weeks
• Injection etoposide 100mg/m2 1-5 days every 3 weeks
• Injection cisplatin 20 mg/m2 1-5 days 3 weeks

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A hypertensive patient presents with an irregularly irregular pulse and a loud P2 on auscultation. Upon examination of the Jugular Venous Pressure (JVP), which finding is most likely to be observed in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Absent a wave

An irregularly irregular pulse indicates atrial fibrillation.

| Wave | Cause

| ---- | -----

| a wave | Atrial contraction

| c wave | Tricuspid valve bulging

| v wave | Venous filling of atrium

| x descent | Atrial relaxation

| y descent | Ventricular filling

In AF, atrial contraction is absent, leading to loss of the ‘a’ wave in JVP.

A loud P2 suggests associated pulmonary hypertension.

Cannon waves occur with AV dissociation, not atrial fibrillation.

B) Cannon a wave

Occurs when atria contract against a closed tricuspid valve.

Seen in:

• Complete heart block
• AV dissociation

C) Rapid x descent

Seen in conditions like cardiac tamponade.

D) Rapid y descent

Seen in constrictive pericarditis.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 26-year-old man presents with a chronic skin lesion that has a rough, scaly surface. Skin biopsy shows marked hyperkeratosis. Based on these clinical and histopathological findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical description of a scaly, rough skin lesion in a young adult is highly suggestive of Psoriasis (Option B). The histopathological finding of marked hyperkeratosis (thickening of the stratum corneum) is a classic feature of psoriasis, along with parakeratosis and acanthosis. Atopic dermatitis (Option A) typically presents as itchy, poorly defined eczematous patches in the flexures, often with a different histological pattern. Pemphigus vulgaris (Option C) and Pemphigus foliaceus (Option D) are autoimmune blistering diseases; they present with fluid-filled vesicles or erosions rather than primary thick scaly plaques. Pemphigus vulgaris specifically involves painful mucosal erosions and deep blisters. Therefore, the specific combination of a chronic scaly plaque and hyperkeratosis on biopsy makes psoriasis the most probable and accurate diagnosis. Psoriasis lesions are typically well-demarcated with silvery scales

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A male patient presents with nasal obstruction, foul-smelling nasal discharge, and loss of smell. Endoscopic findings are shown in the image below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Atrophic rhinitis

The clinical vignette of anosmia, foul-smelling discharge, and the endoscopic findings points to a diagnosis of atrophic rhinitis.

Atrophic rhinitis is a chronic inflammation of the nose characterized by atrophy of nasal mucosa and turbinate bones. The exact etiology of this condition is not known. It is more common in females and starts around puberty.

Clinically patients present with nasal obstruction, foul odor, and merciful anosmia. Merciful anosmia is when the patient has marked anosmia and is unable to smell the foul odor coming from their nose.

On examination of the nose, greenish or greyish crusting of the nasal passage, pale nasal mucosa, atrophied nasal turbinates, and epistaxis following the removal of the crusts. The roomy nasal cavity is seen due to the resorption of bones of the turbinates.

Treatment:

* Nasal irrigation - using warm saline or an alkaline solution composed of sodium bicarbonate 1 part, sodium biborate 1 part, sodium chloride 2 parts in 280 mL of water.

* Local antibiotics - Kemicetine antiozena solution containing chloromycetin, estradiol, and vitamin D2.

* 25% glucose in glycerine, estradiol spray, systemic use of streptomycin, potassium iodide, placental extract.

* Surgical management:

* Young's operation: In this procedure, flaps are raised within the nasal vestibule and both the nostrils are completely closed and are opened after 6 months. During this time, the mucosa may revert to normal and the crusting is reduced.

* Modified Young's operation: In this procedure, the nostrils are partially closed and thereby avoiding the discomfort of complete closure of the nostrils. The results are the same compared to Young's operation.

* Narrowing of the nasal cavity can be done by submucosal injection of Teflon paste, or by insertion of fat, cartilage, or Teflon strips under the mucoperiosteum.

Other options:

Option B: Nasal polyps are non-neoplastic masses of the edematous nasal or sinus mucosa. Nasal polyps can be antrochoanal polyps or ethmoidal polyps. They present with a polypoid mass in the nose.

Option C: Allergic rhinitis is associated with inferior turbinate hypertrophy and can cause chronic nasal obstruction. It is characterized by watery nasal discharge, sneezing, and itching in the nose.

Option D: Foreign body nose is commonly seen in children. The child presents with unilateral, foul-smelling nasal discharge.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A man presents with a history of dysuria and urethral discharge after having unprotected sexual intercourse. Gram-staining of the purulent discharge is seen in the following image. What is the treatment of choice for this infection?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ceftriaxone

This clinical scenario along with the microscopic findings of gram‐negative intracellular diplococci indicates infection with Neisseria gonorrhoeae. The treatment of choice for the infection is ceftriaxone.

Gonorrhea is a disease acquired by sexual contact. The first step in infection is the adhesion of gonococci to the urethra or other mucosal surfaces. The incubation period is 2-8 days. The major symptoms include purulent urethral discharge and dysuria.

In males, the disease starts as acute urethritis presenting with purulent discharge. The patients may also have penile lymphangitis when the soft tissue inflammation is extensive. This infection may extend along the urethra to involve the prostate, seminal vesicles, and epididymis.

In females, the initial infection involves the cervix uteri and urethra which may extend to Bartholin glands, endometrium, and fallopian tubes. Pelvic inflammatory disease and salpingitis may lead to sterility. Rarely peritonitis may develop with perihepatic inflammation (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome).

The discharge is collected and subjected to Gram stain, revealing gram‐negative intracellular diplococci within phagocytes. Stuart's transport medium is used. Cultures can be obtained from chocolate agar or Mueller-Hinton agar. Specifically, Thayer-Martin agar is used to isolate N. gonorrhoeae.

Single-agent therapy with ceftriaxone is preferred for the treatment of gonococcal infections.

According to CDC guidelines (2021), treatment of uncomplicated gonococcal infections is as follows:

• Weight <150 kg – Ceftriaxone 500 mg intramuscular (IM) in a single dose
• Weight ≥150 kg – Ceftriaxone 1 g IM in a single dose

The doses of ceftriaxone are higher than the previous guidelines as the gonococcal minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) are rising worldwide. The British BASHH guidelines also recommend a high dose of 1g.

Concurrent chlamydial infection must also be treated unless it has been excluded by molecular testing.

First-line drug administered is

• Oral doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days

Partner treatment is also required.

Other options:

Option A: Erythromycin: This is not the preferred treatment for gonorrhea, as it is less effective and has a higher rate of resistance compared to ceftriaxone.

Option B: Azithromycin: Although it can be used in combination with ceftriaxone for the treatment of gonorrhea, it is not the treatment of choice as a single agent.

Option D: Penicillin G: This was once a treatment option for gonorrhea, but it is no longer recommended due to widespread resistance.
questions.learning: Ceftriaxone — This clinical scenario along with the microscopic findings of gram‐negative intracellular diplococci indicates infection with Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Anti-D vaccine is not given in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Intrauterine transfusion at 28 weeks

The anti-D vaccine is not given in intrauterine transfusion at 28 weeks. Intrauterine transfusion is done in alloimmunized pregnancies, where the maternal immune system (Rh negative) has already been exposed to the fetal blood (Rh positive).

The purpose of the anti-D vaccine is to prevent the development of maternal antibodies against fetal red cells, which is already occurring in alloimmunized pregnancies.

Anti-D vaccine is administered only in ICT-negative non-isoimmunized pregnancies.

Intrauterine transfusion is done when the peak systolic velocity of the middle cerebral artery (MCA) exceeds 1.5 multiples of the median or if hydrops develop or if the fetal hematocrit is <30%. This indicates that the mother already has antibodies against the fetus's red blood cells, making the administration of anti-D unnecessary.

The indications for administering anti-D are:

• Pregnancy loss: spontaneous or elective abortion (option D) and ectopic pregnancy.
• Fetal death: Regardless of the trimester.
• Procedures: Such as amniocentesis (option A), chorionic villus sampling, fetal blood sampling, and molar pregnancy evacuation.
• Other situations: Antepartum bleeding (including threatened abortion), delivery (vaginal or cesarean), external cephalic version, placental abruption, manual removal of placenta (option B), and trauma to the abdomen during pregnancy.

All Rh D-negative women should be given a single dose of 300 mcg of anti-D at 28 weeks of pregnancy (ICT should be negative).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are local complications of acute pancreatitis? 1. Pseudocyst 2. Pleural effusion 3. Ileus 4. Acute fluid collection Select the correct answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2 and 4

Complications of acute pancreatitis are classified into local and systemic complications according to the Revised Atlanta Classification (2012). Local complications arise from inflammation or necrosis within and around the pancreas, whereas systemic complications involve distant organ dysfunction.

Why is C correct?

• 1. Pseudocyst ✅

• A pancreatic pseudocyst is a late local complication that usually develops ≥4 weeks after interstitial edematous pancreatitis and contains enzyme-rich fluid enclosed by a fibrous wall.

• 2. Pleural effusion ✅

• Pleural effusion, especially left-sided, is a recognized local extrapancreatic complication due to the spread of pancreatic inflammation or pancreaticopleural fistula.

• 3. Ileus ❌

• Ileus is considered a systemic manifestation of acute pancreatitis resulting from severe inflammation and electrolyte disturbances, rather than a local pancreatic complication.

• 4. Acute fluid collection ✅

• Acute peripancreatic fluid collection (APFC) develops within the first 4 weeks of interstitial edematous pancreatitis and is one of the earliest local complications.
questions.learning: 1, 2 and 4 Complications of acute pancreatitis are classified into local and systemic complications according to the Revised Atlanta Classification (2012).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which one of the following is a common pathology associated with ureteric injury while performing surgical procedure of abdominal hysterectomy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Pelvic endometriosis

Ureteric injury is a recognized complication of abdominal hysterectomy, particularly in the presence of distorted pelvic anatomy. Pelvic endometriosis is one of the most common pathological conditions predisposing to ureteric injury because it causes dense fibrosis, adhesions, and distortion of normal tissue planes, making ureteric identification difficult.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Adenomyosis: Adenomyosis enlarges the uterus but does not usually distort the ureteric course to the same extent as pelvic endometriosis.
• C. Hydrosalpinx: Although it may cause adnexal enlargement, it is less commonly associated with ureteric injury.
• D. Ovarian teratoma: A benign ovarian teratoma rarely causes extensive pelvic fibrosis or ureteric distortion.
questions.learning: Pelvic endometriosis Ureteric injury is a recognized complication of abdominal hysterectomy, particularly in the presence of distorted pelvic anatomy.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Open pre-peritoneal large mesh repair for complex inguinal hernia is associated with which of the following procedures? (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Stoppa operation

The Stoppa operation is the open pre-peritoneal large mesh repair technique for complex inguinal hernias. This procedure involves placing a large prosthetic mesh in the pre-peritoneal space that covers the entire myopectineal orifice bilaterally. It's specifically designed for complex, recurrent, or bilateral inguinal hernias. The Stoppa approach provides excellent coverage of all potential hernia sites while avoiding direct contact with nerves in the inguinal canal, reducing the risk of chronic pain.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the smallest pelvic diameter at the brim?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Obstetric conjugate

The obstetric conjugate is the smallest pelvic diameter at the brim.

It is the distance between the midpoint of the sacral promontory to the prominent bony projection in the midline on the inner surface of the symphysis pubis. It is the shortest anteroposterior diameter in the anteroposterior plane of the inlet and measures 10 cm. It represents the narrowest fixed diameter of the pelvic inlet that the fetal head must navigate. It cannot be measured directly during a pelvic exam but is estimated using the diagonal conjugate.

Other Options:

Option B: Diagonal Conjugate:  It is the distance between the lower border of the symphysis pubis to the midpoint on the sacral promontory. It measures 12 cm. Obstetric conjugate is derived by subtracting 1.5–2 cm from the diagonal conjugate depending upon the height, thickness and inclination of the symphysis pubis.

Option C and D : True conjugate: Also called anatomical conjugate, is the distance between the midpoint of the sacral promontory to the inner margin of the upper border of the symphysis pubis and measures 11 cm.
questions.learning: Obstetric conjugate — The obstetric conjugate is the smallest pelvic diameter at the brim. It is the distance between the midpoint of the sacral promontory to the prominent bony projection in the midline on the inner surface of the symphysis pubis.

The plant shown above is the Cerbera Thevetia.

Thevetin is a cardiac poison derived from the plant Cerbera Thevetia (yellow oleander). All parts of the plant are poisonous. Cardiovascular signs include a weak and irregular pulse rate with hypotension. Possible complications are heart block and cardiorespiratory failure.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The following appearance in IVP is caused by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ureterocoele

The given intravenous pyelography (IVP) depicts the cobra head or adder head deformity or spring onion sign seen in bilateral ureterocele. These signs refer to a dilated, contrast-filled distal ureter surrounded by a thin rim of the ureteric wall and bladder mucosa.

Ureterocoele is a cystic enlargement of the intramural portion of the ureter, more commonly seen in females than males. It is thought to be caused due to ureteric orifice atresia. They are similar to ectopic ureters, which typically drain the upper pole of the kidney and are associated with dysplastic or non-functional renal tissue.

If they present clinically, ureteroceles often manifest with urinary tract infections (UTIs) in children, while in adults, they are more likely to present with stones in the lower ureter. Ureterocoeles can enlarge and obstruct the bladder neck or the contralateral ureteric orifice.

The classic sign of a ureterocele on intravenous urography is a ‘cobra head’, ‘adder head’, or 'spring onion sign'.  On ultrasonography, it can be seen as a fluid-filled cystic mass in the bladder.

The treatment of simple ureteroceles is surgical excision with re-implantation of the ureter.
questions.learning: Ureterocoele — The given intravenous pyelography (IVP) depicts the cobra head or adder head deformity or spring onion sign seen in bilateral ureterocele.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following statements about Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA) is incorrect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Biopsy done under L/A

JNA is a benign but locally aggressive vascular tumor arising near the sphenopalatine foramen. It is classically seen in adolescent males due to androgen dependence.

·         Recurrent, profuse epistaxis due to high vascularity

·         Progressive unilateral nasal obstruction

·         May extend to pterygopalatine fossa, orbit, or intracranial cavity

Biopsy is not performed in suspected JNA because:

·         Tumor is highly vascular

·         Attempting biopsy can cause life-threatening hemorrhage

Diagnosis is made by:

·         Clinical presentation

·         Imaging (contrast CT/MRI)

·         Angiography showing feeding vessels

Management principle: Preoperative embolization followed by surgical excision is the standard treatment.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A husband and wife presented to the outpatient department with complaints of the husband's premature ejaculation, which is leading to frequent conflicts between them. Which of the following non-pharmacological techniques is most appropriate for treatment?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Squeeze Technique

Premature ejaculation (PE) is commonly managed with behavioral (non-pharmacological) techniques, especially when relationship distress is present.

The squeeze technique, developed by Masters and Johnson, is a classic behavioral therapy for PE.

How it works:

• During sexual stimulation, when the man feels he is about to ejaculate,
• The partner squeezes the penis just below the glans (corona) for a few seconds.
• This reduces arousal and delays ejaculation.
• The process is repeated multiple times during intercourse to improve ejaculatory control.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Sensate focus technique: Used mainly for performance anxiety and erectile dysfunction, focusing on non-demand sensual touching.
• Exposure and Response Prevention: Used in Obsessive–Compulsive Disorder (OCD).
• Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT): Helpful for psychological issues but not the primary behavioral technique for PE.
questions.learning: Squeeze Technique Premature ejaculation (PE) is commonly managed with behavioral (non-pharmacological) techniques, especially when relationship distress is present.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Most important prognostic factor for Carcinoma Breast is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Axillary lymph node status

Option A: Axillary lymph node status

It reflects the extent of disease spread beyond the primary tumor.

• The number of involved lymph nodes strongly correlates with:

• Risk of recurrence
• Overall survival

• It is a key component of staging (TNM system).

Option B: Tumor size → Important for staging, but less predictive than nodal involvement.

Option C: Distant metastasis → Indicates advanced disease (Stage IV), but among early-stage cases, lymph nodes guide prognosis more precisely.

Option D: Hormonal status (ER/PR, HER2) → Important for treatment decisions, but not the single strongest prognostic factor.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following techniques is based on RNA?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. RT PCR

RT PCR is a RNA-based technique.

RT PCR is a method used to quantitate mRNA levels that relies upon the first step of cDNA copying of mRNAs catalyzed by reverse transcriptase prior to PCR amplification and quantitation.

Other techniques:

• Sanger's technique and Southern blot: DNA
• Western blot: protein
• Northern blot: RNA
• Next-generation DNA sequencing technologies include Illumina (Solexa) sequencing, Roche 454 sequencing, Ion torrent: Proton/PGM sequencing, SOLID sequencing.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following heart sounds would be normal in pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. S3

Among the given options, the presence of third heart sound (S3) is normal in pregnancy.

The third heart sound (S3) occurs due to rapid diastolic filling that is seen secondary to the physiological hypervolemia that occurs during the pregnancy.

Other normal auscultatory findings include:

• First heart sound is loud with an exaggerated split
• Second heart is loud but normal
• Third heart sound is loud and easily heard
• Systolic murmur of grade<3/6
• Mammary murumur or continous machinery murmur
• Apex beat shifted to 4th intercostal space
