questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Frontline health workers are employed to record the births and deaths in countries which have made slow progress in the development of a comprehensive vital registration system. This approach is known as:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lay reporting

Lay reporting is a method of collecting birth and death data in areas where a complete Civil Registration and Vital Statistics (CRVS) system is not yet fully developed. In this approach, frontline health workers, teachers, village volunteers, or other community-based workers record vital events and report them to the health system.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A.  Registration of vital events: Refers to the official, continuous, compulsory, and permanent registration of births, deaths, marriages, etc., under the Civil Registration System (CRS).
• C. Sample Registration System (SRS) ✗

• India’s Sample Registration System is a dual-record system involving:

• Continuous enumeration by a resident part-time enumerator.
• Independent six-monthly survey by a supervisor.

• It is not based solely on frontline health workers.

• D. Census: Census is conducted once every 10 years and provides demographic information but does not continuously record births and deaths.
questions.learning: Lay reporting Lay reporting is a method of collecting birth and death data in areas where a complete Civil Registration and Vital Statistics (CRVS) system is not yet fully developed.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which type of hysterectomy is done in a case of carcinoma cervix stage I B?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Type 3 hysterectomy

Type 3 hysterectomy/Radical hysterectomy is the treatment of choice in carcinoma cervix stage 1 B.

Stage IB lesions are defined as those with the deepest invasion ≥ 5mm yet still confined to the cervix. The stage is subcategorized either as IB1 if tumors measure <2cm or as IB2 if they measure 2cm to <4cm or as IB3 if the invasion is ≥4cm in greatest dimension.

Radical hysterectomy and pelvic lymphadenectomy for stage IB are usually chosen for premenopausal women who wish to preserve ovarian function. Oophorectomy is avoided in younger women who wish to preserve fertility.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which contraceptive device has the longest duration of effectiveness?
questions.explanation: The Copper T 380 A (Option B) is one of the most effective and long-lasting forms of reversible contraception. It is FDA-approved for 10 years of continuous protection, which is the longest duration among the devices listed. Progestasert (Option A) was an early progesterone-releasing IUD that required replacement every year. Mirena (Option C), a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG-IUS), is approved for 5 to 8 years of use depending on the specific clinical indication and regional guidelines. The Nova T (Option D) is a copper-containing IUD with a typical effective duration of 5 years. Because the CuT 380 A contains a larger amount of copper wire and sleeves (380 ) than other models, it provides the most durable long-term prevention of pregnancy, making it a highly cost-effective option for women seeking long-term birth control
questions.learning: The Copper T 380 — A (Option B) is one of the most effective and long-lasting forms of reversible contraception. It is FDA-approved for 10 years of continuous protection, which is the longest duration among the devices listed.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the liver segment marked in the image below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. V

The liver segment highlighted in green in this CT section is segment V. The section of the CT given is taken below the portal vein as the cross-section of the portal vein before its bifurcation can be viewed.

A horizontal plane known as the portal plane divides the liver where the portal vein bifurcates and becomes horizontal. This divides each section of the liver into superior and inferior segments:

• Left lateral section: segment II above and segment III below the portal plane
• Left medial section: segment IVa above and segment IVb below the portal plane
• Right anterior (or medial) section: segment VIII above and segment V below the portal plane
• Right posterior (or lateral) section: segment VII above and segment VI below the portal plane

Shown below is a section from below the portal plane.

Couinaud classification is the commonly used classification of the liver. It divides the liver is divided into eight segments. It is based on the distribution of portal venous branches in the liver parenchyma. Each segment has its own vascular supply, biliary drainage, and lymphatic drainage.

The Couinaud's liver segments are as follows:

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 12-year-old presented with fever and difficulty swallowing. He had swelling in the marked region and was advised to undergo surgery. Post-surgery the gauze continued to soak with blood. Which of the following vessels must have been injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Paratonsillar vein

The given image is a cadaveric specimen with the arrow pointing towards, the tonsillar fossa, and the given clinical vignette is suggestive of tonsillitis. Post tonsillectomy hemorrhage is commonly venous in origin, from the paratonsillar/ external palatine vein.

Torrential hemorrhage can be due to injury to an aberrantly large or aberrantly placed tonsillar arterial branch of the facial artery.

Blood supply of the tonsils:

Arterial supply:

• The tonsillar branch of the facial artery is the main supply.
• Ascending palatine branch of the facial artery.
• Ascending pharyngeal branch of the external carotid artery.
• Dorsal lingual branches of the lingual artery.
• Descending palatine branches of the maxillary artery.

Venous supply:

• Veins from the tonsils drain into paratonsillar vein which joins the common facial vein and pharyngeal venous plexus.

Types of Hemorrhage seen during/post tonsillectomy:

• Primary hemorrhage:

• Occurs during surgery due to injury to blood vessels.
• Can be controlled by pressure, ligation, or electrocoagulation of the bleeding vessels.

• Reactionary hemorrhage:

• It occurs within 24 hours of surgery.
• It may be due to dislodgement of the clot, slippage of ligature, or return of blood pressure to normal.
• It is managed by removal of clot and application of pressure or vasoconstrictor.
• If not controlled the patient is anesthetized and hemorrhage is managed by re-exploration.

• Secondary hemorrhage:

• It occurs between 24 hours to 10 days (most common between 5th to 8th postoperative days).
• It is due to sepsis and premature separation of the membrane.
• The patient is started on IV antibiotics and if not controlled, general anesthesia is given and the bleeding vessel is electrocoagulated or ligated.

The images below summarize the blood supply to the tonsils and the relations of the tonsillar bed respectively.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 22-year-old primigravida with a monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy at 22 weeks undergoes ultrasonography. One twin has severe polyhydramnios with signs of hydrops fetalis, while the co-twin has oligohydramnios. Which Quintero stage best describes this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Stage IV

Hydrops fetalis in either twin is the defining feature of Quintero Stage IV TTTS. TTTS occurs due to unbalanced placental vascular anastomoses in monochorionic twins, resulting in a hypovolemic donor twin and a hypervolemic recipient twin. The recipient may develop cardiac failure leading to hydrops.

Quintero Staging (High-Yield)

| Stage | Finding

| ----- | -------

| I | Oligohydramnios–polyhydramnios sequence; donor bladder visible

| II | Donor bladder not visualized

| III | Abnormal Doppler studies (AEDF/REDF in UA, reversed a-wave in DV, or pulsatile UV)

| IV | Hydrops fetalis in either twin

| V | Demise of one or both twins
questions.learning: Stage IV Hydrops fetalis in either twin is the defining feature of Quintero Stage IV TTTS. TTTS occurs due to unbalanced placental vascular anastomoses in monochorionic twins, resulting in a hypovolemic donor twin and a hypervolemic recipient twin.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following anti-diabetic drugs is associated with the increased risk of fractures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Canagliflozin

Canagliflozin is associated with an increased risk of fractures.

Canagliflozin is a sodium-glucose transporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitor. SGLT2 is a Na+-glucose cotransporter that is located in the proximal convoluted tubule. They reabsorb glucose and sodium from the tubular lumen back into the blood through the epithelial cells. SGLT2 inhibitors block the transport of glucose in the proximal tubule and promote glycosuria and hence, lowering blood glucose.

The currently available SGLT2 inhibitors are canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, and empagliflozin. Other than decreasing blood glucose they also decrease blood pressure and, cause weight loss of 2–4 kg. Empagliflozin and canagliflozin reduce the risk for major cardiovascular events.

The main side effect of SGLT2 inhibitors is an increase in lower urinary tract infections and genital mycotic infections. This is because of their glycosuric properties. A recent warning from the FDA says that SGLT2 inhibitors may increase the risk of fractures. They also affect circulating levels of parathyroid hormone, and 1,25-hydroxy vitamin D thereby affecting the mineral balance in bone.

Other options:

Option A: Rosiglitazone is a thiazolidinedione that acts as a peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ agonist in the adipose tissue which increases insulin sensitivity and adipose differentiation. Side effects are weight gain, edema, and increased risk of fractures. Compared to rosiglitazone, canagliflozin is commonly used in clinical practice. American diabetes association recommends canagliflozin as the first-line drug along with metformin, in patients with a high risk of cardiovascular disease, renal failure, and heart failure. Even when thiazolidinediones are required, clinicians prefer pioglitazone over rosiglitazone due to the higher risk of cardiovascular-related mortality in rosiglitazone. Therefore, canagliflozin would be a better option compared to rosiglitazone.

Option B: Liraglutide is a long-acting glucagon-like peptide-1 agonist. Nausea, diarrhea, and acute pancreatitis are some frequent side effects.

Option C: Voglibose reduces the intestinal absorption of starch, dextrin, and disaccharides by inhibiting the action of α-glucosidase in the intestinal brush border. The most prominent adverse effects are malabsorption, flatulence, diarrhea, and abdominal bloating.
questions.learning: Canagliflozin Canagliflozin is associated with an increased risk of fractures. Canagliflozin is a sodium-glucose transporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitor.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presented with nasal congestion and upon examination, nasal polyps were observed. A coronal CT scan finding of the patient is given below. Which of the following sinus drainage pathways is likely to be affected? CT - Computed Tomography
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Maxillary

In this patient with rhinosinusitis and nasal polyps, the CT scan indicates that the maxillary sinus is likely affected, as evidenced by the presence of a polyp in this sinus.

Antrochoanal polyp is a type of non-neoplastic nasal polypoidal masses of edematous nasal or sinus mucosa. It arises from the mucosa of the maxillary antrum near its accessory ostium, comes out of it, and grows in the choana and nasal cavity. It is usually single and unilateral which are more commonly seen in children and young adults.

It has 3 parts namely

* Thin antral stalk,

* Round and globular choanal part, and

* Flat nasal part.

The clinical features include unilateral nasal obstruction, mucoid nasal discharge, and a hyponasal voice.

Anterior rhinoscopy may miss the antrochoanal polyp when it starts to grow posteriorly. A large polyp may protrude from the nasal cavity and may appear pink and congested. It is soft and can be moved with a probe. Posterior rhinoscopy may reveal a globular mass filling the choana and hanging down behind the soft palate.

X-ray (lateral view) of soft tissue nasopharynx, reveals a globular swelling in the postnasal space, it is differentiated from angiofibroma by the presence of a column of air behind the polyp known as Dodd sign or crescent sign.

Diagnosis is made by radiograph of the paranasal sinuses reveals opacity of the involved antrum. Non-contrast CT scan reveals the extent of the polyp. Endoscopic examination reveals the antrochoanal polyp hidden posteriorly in the nasal cavity.

Endoscopic sinus surgery is the treatment of choice. Recurrence is uncommon after the complete removal of the polyp.
questions.learning: Maxillary — In this patient with rhinosinusitis and nasal polyps, the CT scan indicates that the maxillary sinus is likely affected, as evidenced by the presence of a polyp in this sinus.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old man who was found dead was brought in for autopsy. The doctor notices a greyish-white waxy layer over the body with preserved facial features. Which of the following statements is true concerning adipocere formation?
options: It occurs in hot and dry temperatures
It is a type of body preservation with saponification of fats
Occurs within few hours of death
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It is a type of body preservation with saponification of fats

The given scenario indicates adipocere formation, which is a late postmortem change where body fats undergo saponification through anaerobic hydrolysis and hydrogenation, resulting in a waxy substance. Therefore, the correct answer is that it is a type of body preservation with saponification of fats.

Adipocere formation or corpse wax, is a late sign of death, that occurs days to months after death. A wax-like organic substance is formed by the anaerobic hydrolysis or hydrogenation of fat in tissues. It has a greyish-white appearance with a distinctive offensive or sweetish smell.

Adipocere formation varies widely, taking as little as three weeks in temperate regions during summer, but typically requires several months for significant changes. In rare cases, the entire body may be affected, with complete conversion of an adult limb taking three to six months.

Medicolegal importance is as follows:

• It is the surest sign of death
• It gives a rough estimate of the time since death
• The cause of death can be identified.
• In the face, the features are well preserved and therefore used in identification.

Postmortem changes are classified based on time:

• Immediate signs of death (at the time of somatic or clinical death):

• Insensibility and loss of voluntary power
• Cessation of respiration
• Cessation of circulation

• Early signs of death (cellular death that is observed in the first 12 to 24 hours of death):

• Pallor and loss of elasticity of the skin
• Eye changes
• Primary flaccidity of muscles
• Algor mortis/Postmortem cooling
• Postmortem lividity/Suggillation
• Rigor mortis

• Late signs of death:

• Putrefaction
• Adipocere
• Mummification

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 6-year-old child presents with fever, sore throat, and dyspnea. On oral examination, a pseudomembrane is seen over the tonsils. What is the mechanism of action of the toxin produced by the causative organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Inhibition of elongation factor-2 (EF-2)

This child with pseudomembrane over tonsil has diphtheria, in which the toxin inactivates the elongation factor EF-2.

Diphtheria toxin is an exotoxin that consists of two fragments - A and B. It acts by inhibiting protein synthesis. Fragment B helps in binding the toxin to the cells while fragment A inactivates the elongation factor (EF-2) responsible for protein synthesis. Pseudomonas aeruginosa also produces toxins with a similar mechanism of action.

This infection presents as fever and sore throat, which progresses to dyspnea due to obstruction by the pseudomembrane. Bull's neck appearance is seen due to cervical lymphadenitis. Complications like damage to the heart (myocarditis), kidney (tubular necrosis), liver, and adrenal glands can develop due to the toxin.

Neisser's or Albert's stain will show the bacilli with metachromatic granules situated at the poles of the bacilli. Tellurite blood agar is the selective culture medium.
It is treated mainly by neutralizing with antitoxin and antibiotics to arrest more toxin production.

Pearl PF0802: Mechanism of action of various bacterial toxins

The mechanism of action of various bacterial toxins are as given below:

Increase in cAMP

* Bordetella pertusis

* Bacillus anthracis

* Vibrio cholerae - Cholera toxin

* Enterotoxigenic E.coli (ETEC) - heat labile toxin

Increase in cGMP

* Enterotoxigenic E.coli (ETEC) - heat stable toxin

Inhibition of protein synthesis

* Diptheria toxin: inhibit elongation factor-2 (EF-2)

* Pseudomonas: inhibit elongation factor-2 (EF-2)

* Clostridium difficile

* Enterohemorrhagic E.coli (EHEC)-Shiga-like toxin: inhibit 60S

* Shigella dysenteriae- Shiga toxin: inhibit 60S
questions.learning: Inhibition of elongation factor-2 (EF-2) — This child with pseudomembrane over tonsil has diphtheria, in which the toxin inactivates the elongation factor EF-2.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Question 198.Which of the following findings is usually not seen in patients who have received a massive blood transfusion?
questions.explanation: Massive blood transfusion is defined as replacing the patient's entire blood volume within 24 hours. The electrolyte imbalance that is characteristically absent is hypercalcemia; instead, patients frequently develop hypocalcemia (Option C). This occurs because the citrate used as an anticoagulant in stored blood binds to the patient's ionized calcium. Other options are common complications: DIC (Option A) can occur due to the underlying trauma and coagulopathy; febrile transfusion reactions (Option B) are common due to leukocytes in the blood; and dilutional thrombocytopenia (Option D) is a hallmark of massive transfusion as stored blood is deficient in functional platelets . Therefore, because citrate causes a reduction in serum calcium, hypercalcemia is not expected. Clinicians must often supplement calcium during massive protocols to prevent cardiac arrhythmias and further coagulation defects. Thus, "Hypercalcemia" is the correct "absent" finding for this clinical scenario
questions.learning: Massive blood transfusion is defined as replacing the patient's entire blood volume within 24 hours. The electrolyte imbalance that is characteristically absent is hypercalcemia; instead, patients frequently develop hypocalcemia (Option C).

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A patient with elevated calcium and normal alkaline phosphatase undergoes a skull X-ray. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of hypercalcemia (elevated calcium) and a normal alkaline phosphatase (ALP) level is highly characteristic of Multiple Myeloma. In this plasma cell malignancy, "punched-out" osteolytic lesions are created by increased osteoclast activity without an accompanying osteoblastic (bone-forming) response; therefore, ALP, which is a marker of osteoblast activity, remains normal. This contrasts with Paget's disease (Option B) or bone metastases from prostate cancer, where ALP is typically significantly elevated. Graves' disease (Option A) is a thyroid disorder and does not typically present with lytic skull lesions. Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML, Option D) primarily involves the bone marrow and blood counts, not focal osteolytic bone destruction. Skull X-rays in Multiple Myeloma classically show multiple, well-circumscribed lytic lesions. Diagnosis is further supported by the presence of an M-spike on protein electrophoresis and Bence-Jones proteinuria
questions.learning: The combination of hypercalcemia (elevated calcium) and a normal alkaline phosphatase (ALP) level is highly characteristic of Multiple Myeloma. In this plasma cell malignancy, "punched-out" osteolytic lesions are created by increased osteoclast activity…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 65-year-old female, a stone-cutter by occupation, had multiple well-circumscribed nodular opacities in upper and middle zones of a chest X-ray along with mediastinal lymph nodes showing egg-shell calcification. Which one of the following is the most likely etiology?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Silicosis

Silicosis is a pneumoconiosis caused by chronic inhalation of crystalline silica dust, commonly affecting stone-cutters, miners, sandblasters, quarry workers, and ceramic workers.

• Occupational history: Stone-cutting with prolonged silica exposure.
• Chest X-ray:

• Multiple small, well-circumscribed nodular opacities predominantly in the upper and middle lung zones.
• “Egg-shell” calcification of hilar/mediastinal lymph nodes is a classic radiological feature.

• Progressive disease may lead to progressive massive fibrosis (PMF).

Complications:

• Increased risk of tuberculosis (silicotuberculosis)
• COPD
• Pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale
• Lung cancer
• Increased risk of autoimmune diseases (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, systemic sclerosis)

Why not the other options?

• A. Byssinosis: Due to cotton dust exposure; causes chest tightness and obstructive airway disease, not nodular upper lobe fibrosis with egg-shell calcification.
• C. Berylliosis: Due to beryllium exposure (aerospace/electronics); causes granulomatous lung disease resembling sarcoidosis.
• D. Siderosis: Due to iron dust exposure (welders); usually a benign pneumoconiosis without egg-shell lymph node calcification.
questions.learning: Silicosis Silicosis is a pneumoconiosis caused by chronic inhalation of crystalline silica dust, commonly affecting stone-cutters, miners, sandblasters, quarry workers, and ceramic workers. • Occupational history: Stone-cutting with prolonged silica…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Low serum thyroglobulin levels are seen in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Thyrotoxicosis factitia

Serum thyroglobulin (Tg) is a protein produced exclusively by thyroid follicular cells and serves as a marker of endogenous thyroid hormone production. It is useful in differentiating the causes of thyrotoxicosis.

A. Thyrotoxicosis factitia ✓

• Caused by exogenous ingestion of thyroid hormone.
• Since the thyroid gland is suppressed and not actively producing hormone, serum thyroglobulin is low.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• B. Subacute thyroiditis ✗: Destruction of thyroid follicles releases stored thyroglobulin, resulting in high serum thyroglobulin.
• C. Graves’ disease ✗: Increased thyroid hormone synthesis and secretion cause elevated thyroglobulin.
• D. Toxic multinodular goitre ✗: Autonomous thyroid nodules produce excess hormone, leading to increased thyroglobulin.
questions.learning: Thyrotoxicosis factitia Serum thyroglobulin (Tg) is a protein produced exclusively by thyroid follicular cells and serves as a marker of endogenous thyroid hormone production.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Flipping of which molecule occurs during apoptosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Phosphatidylserine

Phosphatidylserine (PS) is the molecule that flips out during apoptosis.

Phosphatidylserine (PS) is a phospholipid and a key component of the inner leaflet of cell membranes, playing a critical role in cell structure and signalling. It is particularly abundant in the brain, where it contributes to neuronal function, synaptic activity, and maintenance of the blood-brain barrier.

Phosphatidylserine (PS) switching is the process where PS translocates from the inner to the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane, serving as an "eat-me" signal for apoptosis. This externalization is crucial for the recognition and clearance of apoptotic cells by phagocytes.

Other options:

Options B and D: Phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine remain predominantly in the inner leaflet during normal cell conditions.

Option C: Sphingomyelin is typically found in the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane and does not play a significant role in apoptotic signalling.
questions.learning: Phosphatidylserine Phosphatidylserine (PS) is the molecule that flips out during apoptosis. Phosphatidylserine (PS) is a phospholipid and a key component of the inner leaflet of cell membranes, playing a critical role in cell structure and signalling.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A professional singer presents with difficulty in raising the pitch of her voice. Which nerve is most likely injured?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. ELN

Inability to raise the pitch of voice indicates dysfunction of the cricothyroid muscle, which is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve (ELN).

·    Cricothyroid muscle:

o    Tenses and elongates vocal cords → produces high-pitched sounds

·  External laryngeal nerve (branch of superior laryngeal nerve):

o    Supplies cricothyroid muscle

·   Injury leads to:

o    Monotonous voice

o    Inability to sing high notes (important in professional voice users)

Why not other options:

·         Internal laryngeal nerve (ILN): Sensory above vocal cords, no role in pitch

·         Recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN): Supplies all other intrinsic muscles → causes hoarseness, not specifically loss of high pitch

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is the drug of choice for scrub typhus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Doxycycline

Doxycycline is the drug of choice for scrub typhus.

Azithromycin, chloramphenicol, or rifampin can be administered as alternatives in patients allergic to doxycycline and in pregnancy.
questions.learning: Doxycycline Doxycycline is the drug of choice for scrub typhus. Azithromycin, chloramphenicol, or rifampin can be administered as alternatives in patients allergic to doxycycline and in pregnancy.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: General Physiology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following junctions is/are calcium dependent? A. Desmosomes B. Tight junctions C. Adherens junctions D. Gap junctions
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A & C

Calcium-dependent cell junctions are those that use cadherins, which require Ca²⁺ for proper adhesion between cells.

Calcium-dependent junctions:

• Desmosomes → mediated by desmogleins and desmocollins (cadherins)
• Adherens junctions → mediated by E-cadherin

Calcium-independent junctions:

• Tight junctions → formed by claudins and occludins
• Gap junctions → formed by connexins (connexons) for cell-to-cell communication

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Identify the postmortem change shown in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tache noire

The image shows Tache noire.

If the eyelids remain open for a few hours after death, a layer of cell debris and mucus forms a yellow triangle on the sclera at either side adjacent to the iris. The base of the triangle is towards the margin of the cornea and the apex is towards the canthus of the eye. This debris turns brown when the dust settles on them. It appears within 3-4 hours of death.

Other postmortem changes occurring in the eye:

* Cornea: Dull, and opaque due to the lack of lacrimal moistening.

* Flaccidity of eyeballs occurs due to a fall in intraocular pressure.

* Pupils- Soon after death, pupils are slightly dilated due to the relaxation of the iris muscles. At the onset of rigor, the pupils become constricted.

* Increase in potassium concentration in the vitreous. It is helpful in determining the time since death.

* Kevorkian sign(Option C)- It is characterized by fragmentation of the blood column in the retinal vessels. It appears within minutes after death and lasts for about 1 hour.
questions.learning: Tache noire — The image shows Tache noire. If the eyelids remain open for a few hours after death, a layer of cell debris and mucus forms a yellow triangle on the sclera at either side adjacent to the iris.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient with schizophrenia developed acute muscular dystonia and was treated for it. He now presents with dry mouth, dizziness, and hypotension. Which drug is most likely responsible for these adverse effects?
questions.explanation: Acute muscular dystonia is a common extrapyramidal side effect (EPS) of antipsychotics like haloperidol. It is standardly treated with anticholinergic medications such as benztropine. Benztropine restores the neurotransmitter balance by blocking acetylcholine. The new symptoms—dry mouth, dizziness, and hypotension—are classic side effects of anticholinergic therapy. Dry mouth results from muscarinic receptor blockade in salivary glands. Risperidone (Option B) and Haloperidol (Option C) are antipsychotics that cause EPS rather than treat them. Propranolol (Option D) is a beta-blocker used for akathisia (restlessness) but does not cause a dry mouth. As the patient developed these symptoms after being treated for dystonia, benztropine is the only logical pharmacological cause
questions.learning: Acute muscular dystonia is a common extrapyramidal side effect (EPS) of antipsychotics like haloperidol. It is standardly treated with anticholinergic medications such as benztropine.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following statements regarding MgSO4 is false?
options: MgSO4 causes uterine relaxation, but is dose dependant
MgSO4 is continued upto 24 hours after delivery or last attack of seizure
It has inhibitory effect on cerebral cortex thereby preventing seizures and lowering the BP
In renal failure, MgSO4 loading dose can be given, but maintenence dose should be adjusted based on renal function
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. It has inhibitory effect on cerebral cortex thereby preventing seizures and lowering the BP

The false statement regarding MgSO4 (Magnesium sulfate) is option C. It has an inhibitory effect on the cerebral cortex, thereby preventing seizures, but this action is not responsible for lowering blood pressure.

MgSO4 is mainly used in preeclampsia due to its specific anticonvulsant action and neuroprotective action on the cortex. MgSO4 acts as a membrane stabilizer. It reduces motor endplate sensitivity to acetylcholine and blocks neuronal calcium influx. It is not used to treat hypertension, although it shows some hypotensive action by decreasing vascular response to vasopressors.

MgSO4 is used for the management of eclampsia and as prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia. The therapeutic level of magnesium in eclampsia is 4-7mEq/L. The two regimens commonly used are Pritchard and Sibai regimen.

Regimen
Loading Dose
Maintenance Dose

Intramuscular (Pritchard)
4g (20% solution) IV over 3-5 minute
followed by 10g (5O%), deep IM
(5 gm in each buttock)
5g (5O%) IM 4 hourly in alternate buttocks

Intravenous (Zuspan or Sibai)
4g IV slow over 15-20 minute
1-2g/h IV infusion

Other actions:

• Cerebral vasodilatation
• Uterine artery vasodilatation
• Uterine tocolytic i.e. inhibits uterine contractility
• Increased production of endothelial prostacyclin
• Inhibits platelet activation

Other options:

Option A: MgSO4 inhibits uterine contractility but is dose-dependent (only above serum values of 8-10 mEq/L).

Option B: MgSO4 has to be administered up to 24 hours after the last seizure (in postpartum seizure) or delivery, whichever is later. For recurrent seizures, 2 g IV bolus is given in the above regimen.

Option D: Magnesium is cleared almost exclusively by renal excretion. But, in renal failure, the initial 4-g loading dose of magnesium sulfate can be safely administered regardless of renal function. Only the maintenance dose needs to be altered according to the renal function. This is because the loading dose is responsible for reaching therapeutic levels, but the maintenance doses are responsible for maintaining steady states.
questions.learning: It has inhibitory effect on cerebral cortex thereby preventing seizures and lowering the BP The false statement regarding MgSO4 (Magnesium sulfate) is option C.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Under the National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme, which disease is being controlled by targeting the insect shown in the image as its vector?
questions.explanation: The insect shown in the image is a Culex mosquito, which can be identified by its brownish body, short palps, and resting position parallel to the skin surface. Under the National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme, control measures targeting Culex mosquitoes are primarily aimed at preventing Japanese encephalitis (JE), a viral disease caused by a flavivirus. The principal vector is Culex tritaeniorhynchus, which breeds in rice fields and stagnant water and transmits the infection from animal reservoirs like pigs and birds to humans. Other options are incorrect: (A) Chikungunya is transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes (Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus), not Culex. (B) Malayan filariasis can be transmitted by Culex species, but the primary disease targeted under NVBDCP with this vector image is Japanese encephalitis. (C) Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) is transmitted by sandflies (Phlebotomus), not mosquitoes. Thus, the mosquito shown is most closely associated with Japanese encephalitis control
questions.learning: The insect shown in the image is a Culex mosquito, which can be identified by its brownish body, short palps, and resting position parallel to the skin surface.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 25-year-old man undergoes an elective splenectomy for hereditary spherocytosis. While ligating the splenic vessels, the surgeon preserves an artery to maintain the blood supply to the stomach. Which artery is it?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Short gastric artery

During splenectomy, the splenic artery and vein are ligated. The short gastric arteries, which arise from the terminal part of the splenic artery, supply the fundus of the stomach. Care must be taken to preserve them whenever possible to prevent ischemia or necrosis of the gastric fundus, especially if collateral blood supply is limited.

Why not the other options?

• A. Splenic artery: Main artery to the spleen; it is ligated during splenectomy.
• B. Left gastroepiploic artery: Also arises from the splenic artery and supplies the greater curvature, but preservation of the short gastric arteries is specifically important for the gastric fundus.
• C. Left gastric artery: Arises from the celiac trunk and supplies the lesser curvature; it is not the vessel encountered at the splenic hilum.
questions.learning: Short gastric artery During splenectomy, the splenic artery and vein are ligated. The short gastric arteries, which arise from the terminal part of the splenic artery, supply the fundus of the stomach.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient undergoing surgery receives succinylcholine for muscle relaxation and later develops hyperthermia, rigidity, tremors, and tachycardia. What is the most appropriate treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dantrolene

The above clinical scenario is suggestive of malignant hyperthermia. The drug of choice for the condition is dantrolene.

Dantrolene is a direct-acting skeletal muscle relaxant that acts on the RyR1 (ryanodine receptor) calcium channels in the sarcoplasmic reticulum of skeletal muscles and inhibits calcium-induced calcium release. This results in the uncoupling of membrane depolarisation and muscle contraction, thus inhibiting muscle contraction.

Malignant hyperthermia is a genetic condition in which mutated RyR1 receptors are present in the skeletal muscles. In the presence of certain triggers, this mutated RyR1 causes severe dysfunction in the RyR1 channels. This leads to the accumulation of calcium ions in the skeletal muscle, resulting in sustained muscle contraction, rigidity, increased heat production, acidosis, hyperkalaemia, and increased end-tidal CO₂.

Drugs triggering malignant hyperthermia:

* Succinylcholine

* Halothane

* Isoflurane

* Sevoflurane

Susceptible patients:

* Patients with a positive family history. It can be inherited as an autosomal dominant trait.

* Patients with congenital myopathies.

Treatment:

Dantrolene sodium is the drug of choice for malignant hyperthermia. Once the diagnosis is made, the causative inhalational agent should be stopped immediately. Supportive treatment with rapid cooling, inhalation of 100% oxygen, control of acidosis, and treatment of hyperkalaemia should be given.
questions.learning: Dantrolene — The above clinical scenario is suggestive of malignant hyperthermia. The drug of choice for the condition is dantrolene.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: WHO defines blindness as visual acuity less than ______
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 3/60

According to WHO, 'Blindness' is defined as visual acuity of less than 3/60, or a corresponding visual field loss to less than 10°, in the better eye with the best possible correction.

Presenting visual acuity in the range of worse than 6/18 to 6/60 is defined as moderate visual impairment. Presenting visual acuities from 3/60 (including 3/60) to worse than 6/60 is classified as severe visual impairment.

Distance vision impairment:

* Mild –visual acuity worse than 6/12 to 6/18

* Moderate –visual acuity worse than 6/18 to 6/60

* Severe –visual acuity worse than 6/60 to 3/60

* Blindness –visual acuity worse than 3/60

National Programme for the Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment (NPCBVI). The levels of eye care, according to NPCBVI are:

* Primary level: Sub-district level hospitals, community health centers, mobile ophthalmic units, upgraded PHCs, link workers, Panchayats.

* Secondary level: District hospitals, NGO eye hospitals

* Tertiary levels: Regional institutes of Ophthalmology, medical colleges.

The goal is to reduce the prevalence of blindness to 0.3% by 2020.
questions.learning: 3/60 According to WHO, 'Blindness' is defined as visual acuity of less than 3/60, or a corresponding visual field loss to less than 10°, in the better eye with the best possible correction.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with sarcoidosis and multi-organ involvement is being evaluated for treatment options. Which of the following drugs is not commonly used in the management of sarcoidosis?
questions.explanation: Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous disease. Prednisone (Option D) is the gold-standard first-line therapy to control inflammation. In cases where steroids are insufficient or not tolerated, steroid-sparing agents such as Methotrexate (Option C) or antimalarials like Hydroxychloroquine (Option B, particularly for skin or hypercalcemia) are typically used . Fludrocortisone (Option A) is a mineralocorticoid used primarily for the management of adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) or orthostatic hypotension; it has no therapeutic role in treating the granulomatous inflammatory process of sarcoidosis. Because the other listed drugs are standard components of the sarcoidosis treatment ladder, Fludrocortisone is the correct "except" choice. Management of multi-organ sarcoidosis focuses on suppressing the immune-mediated formation of non-caseating granulomas to prevent permanent organ damage. Clinicians must balance the benefits of these immunosuppressants with their long-term side-effect profiles. Therefore, Fludrocortisone is the outlier in this list of sarcoidosis medications
questions.learning: Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous disease. Prednisone (Option D) is the gold-standard first-line therapy to control inflammation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 14-year-old girl is brought to the clinic because of cyclic lower abdominal pain occurring monthly for the past 6 months. She has not yet had menarche. She reports normal breast development and pubic hair growth. Physical examination reveals a firm, tender midline pelvic mass. External genital examination shows a bulging, bluish membrane at the vaginal introitus. Pelvic ultrasound demonstrates a distended vagina and uterus filled with fluid. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this patient’s condition?
options: Failure of resorption of the uterine septum
Failure of canalization of the vaginal plate
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Failure of canalization of the vaginal plate

Imperforate hymen results from failure of canalization of the vaginal plate, causing obstruction of menstrual outflow. Typical presentation:

• Primary amenorrhea
• Cyclic pelvic/abdominal pain
• Normal secondary sexual characteristics
• Pelvic mass due to retained menstrual blood

Characteristic findings:

• Bulging bluish hymenal membrane
• Hematocolpos (blood in vagina)
• Hematometra (blood in uterus)

Embryology:

• Upper vagina → Müllerian (paramesonephric) ducts
• Lower vagina → urogenital sinus (sinovaginal bulbs/vaginal plate)

Failure of vaginal plate canalization leads to imperforate hymen.

Key differentials:

• Müllerian agenesis → absent uterus with primary amenorrhea
• Septate uterus → recurrent pregnancy loss
• Failure of Müllerian fusion → bicornuate or didelphys uterus.
questions.learning: Failure of canalization of the vaginal plate Imperforate hymen results from failure of canalization of the vaginal plate, causing obstruction of menstrual outflow.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A newborn presents with conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, intrahepatic cholestasis, elevated alkaline phosphatase levels, and liver biopsy showing eosinophilic, PAS-positive cytoplasmic granules suggestive of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. What is the most common cause of jaundice in this condition?
questions.explanation: Neonatal hepatitis is a primary cause of liver dysfunction in newborns, presenting with jaundice, hepatomegaly, and conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. The specific biopsy finding of eosinophilic, PAS-positive cytoplasmic granules is highly suggestive of Alpha-1 Antitrypsin deficiency, which is a significant metabolic cause of neonatal hepatitis. Hypoplasia of the biliary tract (Option A) involves underdeveloped ducts and presents with cholestasis but is not the most common neonatal cause. A choledochal cyst (Option C) involves extrahepatic bile duct dilation and would typically be identified on imaging rather than by PAS-positive granules. Physiological jaundice (Option D) is a temporary condition that presents with unconjugated bilirubinemia, not the conjugated form seen here. Thus, the clinical constellation of cholestatic markers and specific histological inclusions confirms neonatal hepatitis
questions.learning: Neonatal hepatitis is a primary cause of liver dysfunction in newborns, presenting with jaundice, hepatomegaly, and conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. The specific biopsy finding of eosinophilic, PAS-positive cytoplasmic granules is highly suggestive of…

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A male child presented with arthralgia and abdominal pain. On examination, there was palpable purpura over the lower limbs. There is a past history of upper respiratory tract infection prior to the onset of presenting symptoms. Which of the following is the treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Glucocorticoids

IgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura) is a small-vessel vasculitis seen in children, typically following an upper respiratory infection, presenting with palpable purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain, and possible renal involvement.

• Classic tetrad:
• Palpable purpura (non-thrombocytopenic, mainly lower limbs)
• Arthralgia/arthritis
• Abdominal pain
• Renal involvement (hematuria/proteinuria)

Treatment: Usually self-limiting; supportive care is mainstay. Glucocorticoids are used in moderate to severe cases (significant abdominal pain, renal involvement)

Why others are incorrect:

• Azathioprine, methotrexate, cyclosporine are not first-line and used only in severe/refractory cases
questions.learning: Glucocorticoids IgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura) is a small-vessel vasculitis seen in children, typically following an upper respiratory infection, presenting with palpable purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain, and possible renal involvement. •…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A lot of patients presented to PHC OPD with edema, ocular problems, cardiac failure. Several deaths were reported too. There was a common history of buying oil from a local grocery store. Drug inspector will use the following test to detect adulteration.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Paper chromatography test

The clinical picture suggests epidemic dropsy, caused by adulteration of edible oil with argemone oil.

Detection of argemone oil adulteration is best done using paper chromatography, which separates and identifies toxic alkaloids such as sanguinarine.

Sanguinarine causes:

• Capillary dilation
• Increased vascular permeability
• Edema and organ damage

Simple chemical tests like nitric acid or sulphuric acid are screening methods, but chromatography provides confirmatory evidence for regulatory action.

A) Nitrate test

❌ Used to detect nitrate contamination, not argemone oil.

B) Phosphatase test

❌ Used in milk pasteurization testing, not oil adulteration.
questions.learning: Paper chromatography test — The clinical picture suggests epidemic dropsy, caused by adulteration of edible oil with argemone oil. Detection of argemone oil adulteration is best done using paper chromatography, which separates and identifies toxic…

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Long-term use of combined oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) provides protection against which of the following cancers except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Cervical

Long-term use of combined oral contraceptives increases the risk of cervical cancer, especially in women with persistent HPV infection, while offering protection against ovarian, endometrial, and colorectal cancers.

Mode of Action of Combined Oral Pills:

The primary mechanism of action of combined oral pills is to prevent the release of the ovum from the ovary by blocking pituitary secretion of gonadotropin required for ovulation. In addition, the progestogen component makes the cervical mucus thick and scanty, thereby inhibiting sperm penetration. Progestogens also reduce tubal motility and delay the transport of sperm and ovum to the uterine cavity.

Benefits of Combined Pills:

* Highly effective in preventing pregnancy when taken as prescribed (almost 100% effective).

* Protection against other diseases such as benign breast disorders, including fibrocystic disease and fibroadenoma, ovarian cysts, iron-deficiency anaemia, pelvic inflammatory disease, ectopic pregnancy.

* Can be safely used in large family planning programmes, making them important for population control efforts.

Adverse Effects of Combined Pills:

* Cardiovascular effects: Increased risk of myocardial infarction, cerebral thrombosis, and venous thrombosis, especially with advancing age and smoking.

* Metabolic effects: Elevation of blood pressure, changes in serum lipids (increase in LDL, decrease in HDL), altered carbohydrate metabolism with elevated blood glucose and insulin.

* Liver disorders: Risk of hepatocellular adenoma and gallbladder disease; cholestatic jaundice can occur in some users.

* Effects on lactation and fertility: Reduced breast milk quantity and premature cessation of lactation; slight delay in return of fertility after discontinuation.

* Other risks: Possible ectopic pregnancies with progestogen-only use, and potential concerns regarding foetal development if taken inadvertently during pregnancy.
questions.learning: Cervical Long-term use of combined oral contraceptives increases the risk of cervical cancer, especially in women with persistent HPV infection, while offering protection against ovarian, endometrial, and colorectal cancers.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
A patient presents with dull aching pain in both legs. He gives a history of prolonged standing and tortuous veins in the legs. Which of the following tests are done for saphenofemoral incompetence?

1. Brodie Trendelenburg Test
2. Morrissey's test
3. Fegan's test
4. Modified Perthes test
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2

Brodie Trendelenburg test and Morrissey's test are performed to test the incompetence of the saphenofemoral valve. Fegan’s method is used to detect perforator incompetence while Modified Perthe’s test is a test for deep vein thrombosis (DVT).

Brodie Trendelenburg test - Lay the patient down and elevate the leg. Empty the vessels and tie a tourniquet below the SFJ. Ask the patient to stand up:

• Trendelenburg’s test part l - Here the tourniquet is released. A rapid filling from above shows saphenofemoral incompetence.
• Trendelenburg’s test part ll - Here the tourniquet is not released. A gradual filling from below to upwards indicates perforator incompetence.

Morrissey’s cough impulse test - The limb is elevated to empty the varicose veins. Now it is put to bed and the patient is asked to cough forcibly. An expansile cough impulse is felt at the saphenous opening if the saphenofemoral valve is incompetent. Similarly, a bruit may be heard on auscultation. The patient is asked to cough. A cough impulse at the saphenofemoral junction indicates SFJ incompetence.

Fegan’s method - Mark the places of excessive bulges within the varicosities. Ask the patient to lie down and empty the varicose vessels. Palpate along the marked area to look for gaps and pits in the deep fascia, which indicates perforator incompetence.

Modified Perthe’s test - A tourniquet is tied around the upper part of the thigh to prevent reflux down the vein and the patient is asked to walk around. In the presence of normal communicating and deep veins, the varicose veins will shrink. If there is any block, the veins will get more distended. An increase in pain and prominence of dilated veins indicate DVT.
questions.learning: 1, 2 Brodie Trendelenburg test and Morrissey's test are performed to test the incompetence of the saphenofemoral valve. Fegan’s method is used to detect perforator incompetence while Modified Perthe’s test is a test for deep vein thrombosis (DVT).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The maximum thermic effect is seen with a meal which has
options: Mixed meal having all 3 in equal amount
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Protein

Among the given options, maximum thermic effect is seen with proteins

Specific dynamic allowance (previously called as thermic effect of food): This refers to the increased heat production or increased metabolic rate following the intake of food (diet-induced thermogenesis).

The values of SDA are:

• 30% for proteins: This means that out of every 100 grams of proteins consumed, the energy available for doing useful work is 30% less than the calculated value.
• 15% for lipids, and
• 5% for carbohydrates.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A middle-aged lady choked while eating fish and has associated symptoms of choking, hoarseness of voice, and foreign body sensation in the throat. On examination, the fishbone was lodged in the pyriform fossa. During its endoscopic removal, which of the following nerves is most susceptible to injury?
options: Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
External branch of Superior laryngeal nerve
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve

The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve is most susceptible to injury.

The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve runs submucosally in the lateral wall of the pyriform sinus. Foreign bodies may lodge in the piriform fossa and cause irritation. The nerve is easily accessible for local anesthesia, and it is through this nerve that pain is referred to the ear in carcinoma of the piriform sinus.

The pyriform fossa lies on either side of the larynx and extends from the pharyngoepiglottic fold to the upper end of the esophagus and forms the lateral channel for food. It is bound medially by the aryepiglottic fold and the posterolateral surfaces of the arytenoid and cricoid cartilages. It is bound laterally by the thyrohyoid membrane and the thyroid cartilage.

The internal laryngeal nerve supplies the larynx above the vocal cords.

The thyrohyoid membrane connects the thyroid cartilage and hyoid bone. It is pierced by the superior laryngeal vessels and internal laryngeal nerve.

Other options:

Option A: Tonsillectomy may damage the glossopharyngeal nerve.

Option B: The trachea of infants and children is soft and compressible, making it difficult to identify, and the surgeon may easily displace it and go deep or lateral to it, injuring the recurrent laryngeal nerve or even the carotid.

Option D: Thyroid surgery, tumours, neuritis, or diphtheria can also affect the external laryngeal nerve, resulting in paralysis of the cricothyroid.
questions.learning: Internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve — The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve is most susceptible to injury. The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve runs submucosally in the lateral wall of the pyriform sinus.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: In the context of pediatric advanced life support (PALS), which component does not correctly correspond to the ABCD approach?
questions.explanation: The "ABCD" mnemonic is a standardized approach used in emergency medicine and Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS) for the primary assessment of a critically ill child. The components are: A : Airway (Option A) – Ensure the airway is clear and maintainable. B : Breathing (Option B) – Assess respiratory rate, effort, and oxygen saturation. C : Circulation (Option C) – Assess heart rate, pulses, and capillary refill. D : Disability – Assess neurological status using GCS or AVPU. "Dehydration" (Option D) is NOT a component of the primary ABCD survey. While assessing hydration status is important in a pediatric history, it is part of the secondary or more detailed systemic assessment, not the initial life-saving survey meant to identify immediate threats to life. Therefore, Disability is the correct fourth component, making "Dehydration" the inaccurate choice in this context
questions.learning: The "ABCD" mnemonic is a standardized approach used in emergency medicine and Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS) for the primary assessment of a critically ill child.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old man has had persistent hypercalcemia for the past 1.5 years, with parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels within the normal range. What is the most likely underlying cause of his hypercalcemia?
questions.explanation: Chronic hypercalcemia with a normal or low Parathyroid Hormone (PTH) level indicates a PTH-independent cause of calcium elevation. In Sarcoidosis, activated macrophages within non-caseating granulomas express the enzyme 1-alpha-hydroxylase. This enzyme converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D into its active form, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol), leading to increased intestinal calcium absorption and persistent hypercalcemia. Malignancy (Option A) often causes acute, symptomatic hypercalcemia through bone metastasis or PTHrP secretion, but the chronic, stable 1.5-year history is more typical of a granulomatous disease. Parathyroid hyperplasia (Option C) would result in primary hyperparathyroidism, characterized by an inappropriately elevated PTH level. Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) (Option D) typically presents with hypocalcemia in the early stages and secondary hyperparathyroidism (high PTH) later on. Thus, the extra-renal production of calcitriol in Sarcoidosis best explains this metabolic profile
questions.learning: Chronic hypercalcemia with a normal or low Parathyroid Hormone (PTH) level indicates a PTH-independent cause of calcium elevation. In Sarcoidosis, activated macrophages within non-caseating granulomas express the enzyme 1-alpha-hydroxylase.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
What contributes to the latent period of muscle twitch?

1. Neuromuscular transmission
2. Excitation contraction coupling
3. Reuptake of calcium back into sarcoplasmic reticulum
4. Transmission of impulse from nerve
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1,2,4

Neuromuscular transmission, Excitation contraction coupling and transmission impulse from nerve coupling contribute to latent period of muscle twitch.

The latent period of a muscle twitch is the brief delay between the application of a stimulus (such as a nerve impulse) and the onset of muscle contraction. During this period, several physiological processes occur, but neuromuscular transmission and excitation-contraction coupling primarily contribute to this delay.

Neuromuscular transmission: The action potential travels down the motor neuron to the neuromuscular junction. Acetylcholine (ACh) is released into the synaptic cleft and binds to receptors on the muscle fiber's sarcolemma, triggering an action potential in the muscle fiber. (Statement 1)

Excitation-contraction coupling: The action potential propagates along the sarcolemma and into the transverse (T) tubules. This triggers the release of calcium ions from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the cytosol. Calcium binds to troponin, initiating the interaction of actin and myosin filaments. (Statement 2)

Reuptake of calcium back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum: This occurs during the relaxation phase, not the latent period. (Statement 3)

Transmission of impulse from nerve: This is a part of neuromuscular transmission and is involved in the latent period. (Statement 4)
questions.learning: 1,2,4 Neuromuscular transmission, Excitation contraction coupling and transmission impulse from nerve coupling contribute to latent period of muscle twitch.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with complaints of blurred vision. On ophthalmic examination, aqueous flare and keratic precipitates are noted. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical findings of blurred vision, aqueous flares (protein in the anterior chamber), and keratic precipitates (KP - inflammatory cells on the corneal endothelium) are diagnostic for anterior uveitis, specifically iridocyclitis. Flare and cells are the hallmarks of active inflammation in the anterior segment. Intermediate uveitis (Option A) primarily involves the vitreous (vitritis) and pars plana. Posterior uveitis (Option B) involves the retina or choroid. While Toxoplasma (Option D) is a major cause of posterior uveitis (retinochoroiditis), "iridocyclitis" is the most direct anatomical diagnosis for the anterior chamber findings described. Clinically, these patients also present with eye pain, redness (ciliary congestion), and photophobia. If untreated, active iridocyclitis can lead to complications like posterior synechiae, secondary glaucoma, and cataracts. Management typically involves topical corticosteroids to reduce inflammation and cycloplegic agents to relieve pain and prevent synechiae. A thorough systemic workup is often necessary to identify underlying autoimmune or infectious causes
questions.learning: The clinical findings of blurred vision, aqueous flares (protein in the anterior chamber), and keratic precipitates (KP - inflammatory cells on the corneal endothelium) are diagnostic for anterior uveitis, specifically iridocyclitis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with crusting of the eyelids along with a sensation of fine threads or strands between the cornea and the eyelids. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chronic blepharitis is a common inflammation of the eyelid margins characterized by eyelid crusting, redness, and a "thready" or gritty sensation. This is often due to bacterial colonization (most commonly Staphylococci) or dysfunction of the oil glands at the lid margin. Yellow crusts typically form at the root of the eyelashes, and removing them may reveal small ulcers that bleed easily. Dry Eye Syndrome (Option B) causes discomfort and a foreign body sensation but does not typically feature the prominent lid margin crusting seen here. Meibomian Gland Dysfunction (Option C) contributes to dry eye and lid discomfort but refers specifically to the blockage of the oil glands. Conjunctivitis (Option D) primarily involves the conjunctival surface, presenting with significant redness and discharge rather than localized lid margin disease. Treatment focuses on lid hygiene with warm compresses and mild cleansers to remove accumulated secretions
questions.learning: Chronic blepharitis is a common inflammation of the eyelid margins characterized by eyelid crusting, redness, and a "thready" or gritty sensation. This is often due to bacterial colonization (most commonly Staphylococci) or dysfunction of the oil glands at…

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A female presented with a history of profuse vaginal discharge. Microscopy revealed the cell shown in the image. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Bacterial vaginosis

The given image shows a clue cell - an epithelial cell with a fuzzy border due to adherence of bacteria. This along with the given clinical features suggests bacterial vaginosis.

Bacterial vaginosis is a polymicrobial infection caused by Mobiluncus curtisii, Gardnerella vaginalis, Mycoplasma hominis, and Haemophilus vaginalis. It has a malodorous (fishy smell) vaginal discharge with minimal vulval irritation.

Amsel's Criteria is helpful in diagnosing bacterial vaginosis when 3 of the following 4 are present

* Thin, white homogenous vaginal discharge

* A pH of vaginal fluid >4.5

* Fishy odor of discharge accentuated by adding 10% KOH-Whiff test

* Presence of Clue cells on microscopy.

Treatment is oral metronidazole 500 mg BD for 7 days. Alternatively, Ampicillin 500 mg or cephalosporin 500 mg

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: 3 months following cataract surgery, a patient comes with complaints of decreased visual acuity. On examination, posterior capsular opacification is seen. What type of laser can be used to treat this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nd-Yag laser

The given history mentions decreased visual acuity 3 months post-cataract surgery and the presence of posterior capsular opacification is suggestive of after-cataract. A posterior capsulotomy (creating a hole in the posterior capsule) using an Nd: YAG laser is the mainstay of treatment.

Posterior capsular opacification, otherwise known as after cataract/secondary cataract, is the most common late complication of uncomplicated cataract surgery. It occurs due to the proliferation of lens epithelial cells that have been left out inside the capsular bag after cataract surgery. The rate of posterior capsule opacification following extracapsular cataract extraction (ECCE) and phacoemulsification varies with the age of the patient, the surgeon, the surgical technique, the type of intraocular lens used, and the duration after surgery.

Symptoms of after cataract include:

* Reduction of visual acuity

* Slowly worsening blurring

* Glare and occasionally monocular diplopia

They can present in different patterns such as:

* Elschnig's pearls: present as vacuolated (pearl-type) grape-like clusters of swollen cells

* Soemmering's ring: present as a white annular proliferation that is formed at the periphery of the capsular bag.

* Fibrosis type: present as fibroblastic metaplasia of the epithelial cells

Treatment:

* Nd-YAG laser capsulotomy: The laser used in posterior capsulotomy is Nd: YAG laser (1064 nm) whose principle is photodisruption. The plasma produced at the laser target expands and disrupts the tissues creating an opening.

* Surgical treatment: Posterior capsular opacification is managed by creating an opening on the posterior capsule along the visual axis, a procedure called a posterior capsulotomy.

Occurs within months to years.

* Posterior capsule opacification (most common)

* Cystoid macular edema

* Secondary glaucoma

* Retinal detachment

* Intraocular lens malpositions:

* Windshield wiper syndrome— intraocular lens haptic rubs on the endothelium

* Sunset syndrome—inferior subluxation

* Sunrise syndrome—superior subluxation
