questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with persistent bone pain, abdominal cramps, and episodes of abnormal behavior noted by her family. To confirm the suspected diagnosis and guide appropriate management, which diagnostic test should be performed first?
questions.explanation: The patient's triad of "bone pain" (skeletal involvement), "abdominal cramps" (renal stones or peptic ulcers), and "unusual behavior" (psychiatric moans) is the classic description of Hyperparathyroidism ("Bones, Stones, Abdominal Groans, and Psychic Moans"). This condition is caused by an overactive parathyroid gland, usually a solitary parathyroid adenoma. Once biochemical hyperparathyroidism is confirmed (high PTH and high Calcium), the most effective diagnostic imaging test prioritized for localizing the overactive gland is the Tc-99m Sestamibi scan. This nuclear medicine study is highly sensitive for identifying ectopic or orthotopic parathyroid adenomas, as they characteristically retain the tracer longer than thyroid tissue. While USG (Option B) is a useful adjunct, Sestamibi provides better functional localization. MRI (Option A) and CT (Option D) are generally reserved for complex, recurrent, or poorly localized cases. Thus, the Sestamibi scan is the standard priority imaging for pre-operative planning
questions.learning: The patient's triad of "bone pain" (skeletal involvement), "abdominal cramps" (renal stones or peptic ulcers), and "unusual behavior" (psychiatric moans) is the classic description of Hyperparathyroidism ("Bones, Stones, Abdominal Groans, and Psychic Moans").

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What phase of the demographic cycle is the low stationary phase of demographic cycle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Phase 4

Phase 4 is called the low stationary phase in which birth rate and death rate are low and they cancel each other.

* It is the 4 th phase of the demographic cycle.

* Population fails to grow.

* Demographic gap is 0.

* Eg. Australia, UK, Denmark, Belgium and Sweden.

Pearl PF0983: Demographic Process and Cycle

* Demographic process

* Fertility

* Mortality

* Marriage

* Migration

* Social Mobility

* Demographic cycle

* Stage 1 : High stationary

* High birth rate and high death rate render the population stationary.

* Narrow demographic gap.

* Stage 2 : Early expanding

* Death rate declines and birth rate remains unchanged

* Demographic gap starts increasing and then becomes maximum

* Stage 3 : Late expanding

* Death rate decline further and birth rate falls

* India is in this stage, currently

* Demographic gap starts declining

* Stage 4 : Low stationary

* Low birth rate and low death rate renders the population stationary

* Narrow demographic gap

* Stage 5 : Declining

* Population begins to decline as birth rate is lower than death rate

* Demographic gap is negative
questions.learning: Phase 4 Phase 4 is called the low stationary phase in which birth rate and death rate are low and they cancel each other. * It is the 4 th phase of the demographic cycle. * Population fails to grow. * Demographic gap is 0. * Eg.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: All of the following are features of central nystagmus except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Fatigability

Central nystagmus results from lesions involving the brainstem or cerebellum. Unlike peripheral vestibular nystagmus, it is non-fatigable, has no latency, may persist for more than 2 minutes, and its direction may change with gaze or head position.

• Fatigability is a feature of peripheral vestibular nystagmus, not central nystagmus.
• Therefore, absence of fatigability (non-fatigable nystagmus) suggests a central lesion.

| Feature | Central Nystagmus | Peripheral Nystagmus

| ------- | ----------------- | --------------------

| Latency | Absent | Present (few seconds)

| Fatigability | Absent (non-fatigable) | Present

| Duration | Persistent (>2 min) | Brief (<1 min)

| Direction | May change with gaze/position | Fixed direction

| Visual fixation | Not suppressed | Suppressed

| Associated symptoms | Neurological deficits common | Prominent vertigo ± tinnitus/hearing loss

Why not the other options?

• A. No latency ✓: Central nystagmus begins immediately after the provoking maneuver.
• C. Lasts for more than 2 minutes ✓: Central nystagmus is persistent and does not fatigue.
• D. Direction changes in different positions ✓: Direction-changing (gaze-evoked) nystagmus is characteristic of central pathology.
questions.learning: Fatigability Central nystagmus results from lesions involving the brainstem or cerebellum. Unlike peripheral vestibular nystagmus, it is non-fatigable, has no latency, may persist for more than 2 minutes, and its direction may change with gaze or head…

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Multidrug-resistant (MDR) tuberculosis shows resistance to which of the following drugs?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Isoniazid and rifampicin

Muti-drug resistant (MDR) tuberculosis (TB) shows resistance to isoniazid and rifampicin.

MDR-TB poses a serious problem in the treatment of TB as isoniazid and rifampicin are the most potent first-line drugs.

The treatment of MDR-TB is curated with drugs grouped into different classes by the world health organization (WHO).

• Group A: Levofloxacin, bedaquiline, linezolid
• Group B: Clofazimine, cycloserine
• Group C: Ethambutol, pyrazinamide, delamanid, ethionamide

In patients treated previously or with additional drug resistance, a longer MDR-TB regimen of 18-20 months is recommended. Drugs belonging to group A are preferred along with one drug from group B whenever possible. A shorter regimen of 6 months including bedaquiline with other drugs can be used in patients not treated before and without extensive disease. In pregnant women with MRD-TB, drugs such as bedaquiline and delamanid should be avoided.

The nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT)/ gene Xpert is used to detect rpoB gene polymorphisms, which are responsible for rifampicin resistance.

The four drugs considered first-line agents in the treatment of TB are isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol.

Isoniazid is an antibiotic that works by inhibiting the synthesis of mycolic acid, an essential component of the mycobacterial cell wall. It is a bactericidal drug. It acts as a vitamin B6 antagonist, so oral pyridoxine supplementation is recommended during treatment. Side effects include peripheral neuritis, seizures, and ataxia.

Rifampicin is a macrocyclic antibiotic that inhibits RNA synthesis and is bactericidal. It is also used in the prophylaxis of meningococcal infections. Side effects include rash, vomiting, and hepatitis. It is a microsomal enzyme inducer that can result in contraceptive failure.

Ethambutol inhibits the mycobacterial cell wall assembly. Side effects include optic neuritis, pruritus, and joint pain.

Pyrazinamide is a nicotinamide analogue activated in acidic conditions. Side effects include liver injury and hyperuricemia.

Other options: Fluoroquinolones are considered second-line agents used in the treatment for drug-resistant TB. Kanamycin, an injectable aminoglycoside is excluded from the new WHO classification of second-line drugs.
questions.learning: Isoniazid and rifampicin Muti-drug resistant (MDR) tuberculosis (TB) shows resistance to isoniazid and rifampicin. MDR-TB poses a serious problem in the treatment of TB as isoniazid and rifampicin are the most potent first-line drugs.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A researcher discovered a new drug which is effective in chronic hypertensives with a p value of <0.10. which of the following is true regarding the same
options: Not more than 10% of the people benefitted by the drug could be due to chance
90% of patients will be benefitted by giving the drug
90% of test results could have occurred by chance
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Not more than 10% of the people benefitted by the drug could be due to chance

P value <0.10 indicates that not more than 10% of people benefitted by the drug could be due to chance.

It can also be interpreted as

• If the test is repeated 100 times, the difference will be statistically non significant only 10 times and difference will be statistically significant 90 times.
• Probability of false positive conclusion that drug is beneficial which in reality is not, is 10%.

It arises in case of statistical studies to accept or reject a null hypothesis.

P value is compared with a predetermined value α; P value < α means the test is statistically significant and null hypothesis is rejected.
questions.learning: Not more than 10% of the people benefitted by the drug could be due to chance P value <0.10 indicates that not more than 10% of people benefitted by the drug could be due to chance.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A doctor is teaching an Intern on how to do the knee reflex properly and a demonstration is done. The intern is asked to do learn the skill as it is very important in clinics.What type of learning is this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Psychomotor learning

This type of learning a skill is called psychomotor learning.

The types of learning are cognitive, affective, and psychomotor learning.

Learning:

* Learning is any relative or permanent change in behavior as a result of practice or experience.

* It includes acquiring knowledge and skills, formation of habits, and development of perception.

* The conditions that affect learning are as follows:

* Intelligence

* Age

* Learning situation

* Motivation

* Physical and mental health

* Types of learning:

* Cognitive learning – knowledge

* Affective learning – attitudes

* Psychomotor learning – skills

* Theories of learning:

* Learning by conditioned reflex

* Trial and error

* Learning by observation and imitation

* Learning by doing

* Learning by remembering

* Learning by insight

* Demonstration

* Field experience

* Problem-solving
questions.learning: Psychomotor learning — This type of learning a skill is called psychomotor learning. The types of learning are cognitive, affective, and psychomotor learning.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text:
A 6-year old boy complains of cough and throat pain. On examination of the oral cavity, a white pseudomembrane was visualized. A swab was taken from it and stained as given in the image below. What is the procedure for the following staining?

1. Albert's stain- I
2. Acid alcohol
3. Gram's iodine
4. Safranin
5. Methylene blue
6. Crystal violet
7. Carbol fuschin
8. Acetone
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 6, 3, 8, 4

The image shows Gram's stain of Corynebacterium diphtheria and the staining procedure is crystal violet, Gram's iodine, acetone, and safranin.

Corynebacterium diphtheria (also called Klebs-Loeffler bacillus) is a gram-positive bacillus with clubbing at both ends. They possess characteristic polymetaphosphate granules also called metachromatic granules.

Gram's stain procedure:

• Fix the smear using heat or methanol.
• Cover with crystal violet stain for 10–30 seconds.
• Gram’s iodine stain used as mordant for 10–30 seconds.
• Decolorize with 30% acetone–alcohol for 10–30 seconds, until the stain cannot flow off the slide.
• Cover with safranin stain for 10–30 seconds.

Image shows gram staining of Corynebacterium diphtheria

Other stains used for corynebacterium diphtheria:

• Albert's stain shows green bacilli with purple-blue metachromatic granules arranged in typical Chinese letter or cuneiform arrangement. The stain requires two reagents:

• Albert’s I solution contains toluidine blue, malachite green.
• Albert's II contains iodine and potassium iodide.

• Loeffler's methylene blue: The granules take up the bluish-purple color.
• Immunofluorescence: This is more specific as the smear is stained with a specific antibody.

Image shows Albert's stain of C. diphtheria

The incubation period of diphtheria is usually 2–5 days (range: 1–10 days).

Respiratory diphtheria is characterized by mild fever, sore throat, difficulty swallowing, malaise, loss of appetite, hoarseness (if the larynx is involved). The hallmark is a gray-white pseudomembrane over the mucous lining of the tonsils (most commonly), pharynx, larynx, or nares. It is tightly adherent to the underlying tissue, and any attempt to dislodge the membrane may cause bleeding.

A few patients develop massive swelling of the tonsils and present with bull-neck diphtheria, due to edema of the submandibular and paratracheal region. Cutaneous diphtheria may present as a scaling rash or as ulcers with clearly demarcated edges and membrane.

The images below shows pseudomembrane, bull-neck, and cutaneous diphtheria respectively.

Treatment of diphtheria includes administration of diphtheria anti-toxin. Recommended antibiotics include penicillin G and erythromycin. Prevention is with the diphtheria toxoid vaccine. It is coadministered with tetanus and acellular pertussis (DPT) and should be given according to the National Immunization Schedule.
questions.learning: 6, 3, 8, 4 The image shows Gram's stain of Corynebacterium diphtheria and the staining procedure is crystal violet, Gram's iodine, acetone, and safranin.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A gentleman presents to the OPD with a saddle nose deformity. He gives a past history of cough, on/off fever, and hemoptysis. On examination, septal perforation is present with pale granuloma. His chest x-ray showed multiple cavitary lesions, and the biopsy showed granuloma, multinucleate giant cells, and caseous necrosis. What would be the probable cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tuberculosis

In a patient with saddle nose deformity, septal perforation with pale granuloma and caseous necrosis on biopsy is consistent with tuberculosis (TB). The history of fever, cough, and hemoptysis along with cavitary lesions on chest x-ray support the diagnosis of TB.

While other conditions like Wegener's granulomatosis (Option A), syphilis (Option C), and sarcoidosis (Option D) can also cause saddle nose deformity, caseous necrosis on biopsy makes TB a more likely diagnosis.

Saddle-nose deformity refers to a depressed nasal dorsum that can involve either the bony, cartilaginous, or both components.

The most common cause is nasal trauma resulting in depressed fractures. Other causes include excessive submucosal resection, destruction of septal cartilage due to hematoma or abscess, and infections such as leprosy, tuberculosis, or syphilis, as well as inflammatory conditions like granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener granulomatosis) and sarcoidosis.

Chronic granulomatous conditions such as lupus, tuberculosis, and leprosy can affect the cartilaginous part, syphilis primarily affects the bony part, and Wegener's granulomatosis and T-cell lymphoma can lead to total (bony and cartilaginous) septal destruction involving both the bony and cartilaginous portions.

TB is an infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and primarily affects the lungs but can also involve the nose and sinuses.

Common symptoms of TB include fever, productive cough, weight loss, night sweats, and hemoptysis. Chest x-ray often shows multiple cavitation lesions affecting the upper lobe and hilar lymphadenopathy. Biopsy findings in tuberculosis typically reveal granulomas, caseous necrosis, and multinucleate giant cells (Langhan's giant cells).

The following images show the histopathological image of tuberculosis:

Other options:

Option A: Wegener's granulomatosis is characterized by vasculitis affecting small to medium-sized vessels. It affects the upper respiratory tract (ear, nose, sinuses, and throat), lower respiratory tract (lung), and kidney and is characterized by necrotizing granuloma which is non-caseating.

Option C: Although nose deformity is seen in syphilis, gummatous lesions (caseating granulomas) are present in tertiary syphilis which is not seen in this patient. Fever, cough, and hemoptysis are not features of syphilis.

Option D: Sarcoidosis most commonly affects the lungs forming non-caseating granuloma with no central necrosis. Laminated calcium and protein-containing bodies called Schaumann bodies and star-shaped inclusions called asteroid bodies are also found in the giant cells of most of these granulomas. Chest x-ray would show interstitial fibrosis and hilar lymphadenopathy.

The image below shows the characteristic non-caseating sarcoid granuloma:
questions.learning: Tuberculosis — In a patient with saddle nose deformity, septal perforation with pale granuloma and caseous necrosis on biopsy is consistent with tuberculosis (TB).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: BCG vaccine provides protection against which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. CNS and disseminated TB

BCG vaccine provides protection against CNS and disseminated TB.

It does not prevent primary infection. More importantly, it does not prevent reactivation of latent pulmonary infection, the principal source of bacillary spread in the community. The impact of BCG vaccination on transmission of mycobacterium tuberculosis is therefore limited.
questions.learning: CNS and disseminated TB BCG vaccine provides protection against CNS and disseminated TB. It does not prevent primary infection.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young patient develops shortness of breath specifically during physical exertion in cold weather, which is relieved after using salbutamol. What is the most likely explanation for this condition?
options: Vagal stimulation due to cold air exposure
Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction triggered by cold air
Airway hyperreactivity due to cold-induced asthma exacerbation
questions.explanation: Transient airway narrowing during or after physical activity is known as exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB). In winter, cold and dry air causes heat and moisture loss from the airways, triggering hyperreactivity and subsequent bronchospasm. This condition is classically relieved by short-acting beta-agonists like salbutamol. Vagal stimulation (Option A) usually causes bradycardia or nasal symptoms rather than exercise-specific breathlessness. Decreased cardiac output (Option B) is not the mechanism for respiratory symptoms that respond to bronchodilators. Cold-induced asthma exacerbation (Option D) is a general term, but EIB is the more precise diagnosis when exercise is the specific trigger described. Spirometry or an exercise challenge test is used for diagnosis, while pre-exercise salbutamol inhalation is the standard management to prevent attacks during intense activity in cold environments
questions.learning: Transient airway narrowing during or after physical activity is known as exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB). In winter, cold and dry air causes heat and moisture loss from the airways, triggering hyperreactivity and subsequent bronchospasm.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: What post-mortem finding is most likely to be observed in a patient who sustained a stab wound to the left side of the chest?
questions.explanation: A stab wound to the left side of the chest (the precordial area) often penetrates the pericardium and the heart itself. In a forensic autopsy, a common and lethal finding is cardiac tamponade (Option A). As the heart bleeds into the relatively inelastic pericardial sac, the pressure rises rapidly, preventing the heart chambers from filling and leading to sudden death. While a hemothorax (Option C) (blood in the pleural cavity) is also a very frequent finding in chest trauma, the mention of the "left side" near the heart specifically emphasizes tamponade as the more immediate and classically tested lethal finding. Fat necrosis (Option B) is a tissue change seen in pancreatitis or breast trauma, not acute stab wounds. Pulmonary embolism (Option D) is a vascular event usually originating from leg veins. Therefore, because the pericardial sac acts as a trap for blood from a cardiac wound, tamponade is the definitive finding
questions.learning: A stab wound to the left side of the chest (the precordial area) often penetrates the pericardium and the heart itself. In a forensic autopsy, a common and lethal finding is cardiac tamponade (Option A).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 70-year-old man with a BP of 170/100mmHg. What is the reason for the increased pulse pressure in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Decreased arterial compliance

Pulse pressure increases with age due to decreased arterial wall compliance.

Diastolic blood pressure falls after 60 years of age due to increased arterial stiffness and decreased compliance, often associated with arteriosclerosis. As the left ventricle contracts against stiffer, less compliant arteries, systolic blood pressure also increases.

As a result of these two changes, pulse pressure increases (↑PP = ↑SBP - ↓DBP)

The factors that affect the pulse pressure:

• the stroke volume output of the heart
• the compliance or total distensibility of the arterial walls
• the character of ejection from the heart during systole (less important)

Pulse pressure = Stroke volume/ arterial compliance

Widened pulse pressure (> 40 mm Hg) occurs with several diseases such as:

• Aortic regurgitation
• Aortic sclerosis
• Severe iron deficiency anaemia
• Arteriosclerosis
• Hyperthyroidism

In the majority of these cases, systolic pressures increase while diastolic pressures remain near normal.
questions.learning: Decreased arterial compliance Pulse pressure increases with age due to decreased arterial wall compliance. Diastolic blood pressure falls after 60 years of age due to increased arterial stiffness and decreased compliance, often associated with…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: While performing a fasciotomy for compartment syndrome, the following layers are incised:
options: Skin, Subcutaneous tissue, Superficial fascia and Deep fascia
Skin, Subcutaneous tissue, Superficial fascia, Deep fascia and a few muscular fibres
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Skin, Subcutaneous tissue, Superficial fascia and Deep fascia

The incision for a fasciotomy involves the skin, subcutaneous tissue, superficial fascia, and deep fascia.

Fasciotomy involves incising the deep muscle fascia and is best carried out via longitudinal incisions of skin, subcutaneous fat, and superficial and deep fascia. The muscle will be seen bulging out through the fasciotomy opening.

The lower limb can be decompressed via two incisions, each being lateral to the subcutaneous border of the tibia. This gives access to the two posterior compartments and the leg's peroneal and anterior compartments.
questions.learning: Skin, Subcutaneous tissue, Superficial fascia and Deep fascia The incision for a fasciotomy involves the skin, subcutaneous tissue, superficial fascia, and deep fascia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Identify the ECG for the diagnosis:
questions.explanation: The provided electrocardiogram (ECG) demonstrates a rapid heart rate (tachycardia) with wide, broad QRS complexes exceeding 0.12 seconds. The rhythm is notably regular, and there is a distinct absence of discernible P-waves, which indicates that the electrical impulse is originating from the ventricles rather than the sinoatrial node. This classic "wide-complex tachycardia" pattern is the hallmark of Ventricular Tachycardia (VT). Normal ECG (Option A) would show narrow QRS complexes and preceding P-waves. Ventricular fibrillation (Option B) is characterized by a chaotic, irregular, and pulseless electrical activity without organized QRS complexes. Misplaced leads (Option D) typically result in abnormal axis deviations or inverted waves in specific leads but do not produce a high-rate broad complex rhythm. Immediate clinical assessment is required, as VT can lead to hemodynamic collapse or degenerate into ventricular fibrillation. Treatment depends on the patient's stability, ranging from anti-arrhythmic drugs like amiodarone to immediate synchronized cardioversion

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Glucosamines are used in which of the following conditions:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Arthritis

The combined use of glucosamine sulfate and chondroitin sulfates in the treatment of degenerative joint disease has become an extremely popular supplementation protocol in arthritic conditions of the joints.

• Glucosamines are amino sugars which form the major component of glycosaminoglycans. (GAG’s are tandem repeats of amino sugar and uronic acid)
• GAG’s combine with proteins to form proteoglycans
• One such proteoglycan is aggrecan containing several GAGs (hyaluronic acid, chondroitin sulphate, and keratan sulphate) and both link and core proteins
• Aggrecan is the major proteoglycan in cartilage
• Hence, from this we can deduce that glucosamines being a major part of GAG’s and proteoglycans such as aggrecan are protective against arthritis.
questions.learning: Arthritis — The combined use of glucosamine sulfate and chondroitin sulfates in the treatment of degenerative joint disease has become an extremely popular supplementation protocol in arthritic conditions of the joints. • Glucosamines are amino sugars…

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 4-month-old female infant, born in breech presentation, is brought with decreased movement of the left lower limb. On examination, there is limitation of abduction of the left hip. Galeazzi sign is positive. Ultrasonography confirms a dislocated hip joint. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Closed reduction and hip spica casting
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pavlik harness application

This infant is 4 months old with confirmed developmental dysplasia of the hip.

Management depends on age:

• 0–6 months:

• First-line treatment is Pavlik harness
• Maintains hip in flexion and abduction
• Allows spontaneous reduction of femoral head

• 6–18 months:

• Closed reduction + hip spica
• Open reduction ± osteotomy

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Open reduction is reserved for late or failed cases

B. Closed reduction is preferred after 6 months of age

D. Osteotomy is used in older children

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: An 80-year-old woman presented with complaints of fatigue. On imaging, she was found to have a scleroatrophic gall bladder with impacted stones in it. A large stone was also present in the common bile duct and the biliary tree is dilated. What is the next step in management?
options: Immediately take up patient for cholecystectomy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography

An 80-year-old woman with imaging showing a scleroatrophic gall bladder with impacted stones and a stone in the bile duct is suggestive of chronic cholelithiasis with choledocholithiasis. ERCP is the next line of management for this patient.

Choledocholithiasis is the presence of stone in the common bile duct (CBD) or biliary tree. It can be primary or secondary:

• Primary stones are formed in the CBD or biliary tree itself and are rare.
• Secondary stones are passed from the gallbladder to the CBD. They are easier to manage than primary stones.

It can be an asymptomatic and incidental finding or present with features such as jaundice (most common), abdominal pain, and fatigue. When there is inflammation of the biliary tree (cholangitis), the patient will have intermittent pain, fever, and jaundice (Charcot's triad).

Investigations:

• Liver function tests will show elevated direct bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase levels.
• Abdominal ultrasound is the first imaging modality done and may show gallstones and dilated bile duct (>8 mm).
• CT is sensitive for CBD stones. It shows stones, location, ductal stricture or block, ductal dilatation, and intrahepatic biliary changes.
• MRCP is highly sensitive and specific for CBD stones, but it is only diagnostic and intervention cannot be performed.

Management:

• ERCP with sphincterotomy is the procedure of choice, followed by the removal of stones using a dormia basket or placement of a stent.
• Despite ERCP being an invasive procedure, it has the advantage of being both a diagnostic and therapeutic procedure and is more suited for elderly patients who cannot tolerate anesthesia and surgery.

Other options:

Option A: Cholecystectomy is not recommended for elderly patients, owing to the risk of old age and associated anesthetic and surgical complications.

Option C: Wait and watch approach can be done for asymptomatic patients, and patients with smaller stones.

Option D: CT is sensitive for CBD stones, but it is only diagnostic and intervention cannot be performed.
questions.learning: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography — An 80-year-old woman with imaging showing a scleroatrophic gall bladder with impacted stones and a stone in the bile duct is suggestive of chronic cholelithiasis with choledocholithiasis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following amino acids is likely to aggregate on the surface of a globular protein circulating in the plasma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lysine

Lysine would likely aggregate on the surface of a globular protein circulating in plasma because it is a hydrophilic amino acid with a positively charged side chain. In proteins that exist in aqueous environments like blood plasma, hydrophilic amino acids tend to orient toward the outside surface where they can interact favorably with water. This arrangement forms part of the tertiary structure of globular proteins, where hydrophilic residues face outward while hydrophobic residues cluster in the interior.
questions.learning: Lysine Lysine would likely aggregate on the surface of a globular protein circulating in plasma because it is a hydrophilic amino acid with a positively charged side chain.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: What is the probable diagnosis of this condition affecting hair?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Trichothiodystrophy

The given clinical image of hair seen under polarising microscopy reveals tiger tail banding (alternating light and dark bands) characteristic of trichothiodystrophy.

Trichothiodystrophy is an autosomal recessive condition causing defective DNA repair. It causes brittle sulfur-deficient hair, photosensitivity, ichthyosis and systemic involvement. Unlike xeroderma pigmentosum (a similar condition with defective DNA repair), there is no risk of skin cancer.

Option A: Trichorrhexis nodosa is associated with node formation and fractures. The classic appearance, shown in the image below, is known as thrust paintbrush appearance as if two paintbrushes are rubbing against each other. It is associated with trauma to the hair shaft and arginosuccinic aciduria.

B- Trichorrhexis invaginata or bamboo hair is characterized by invagination of the distal hair shaft into the proximal portion. It is seen in Netherton's syndrome. It is also called golf-tee or ball and socket appearance as seen below.

Option D: Monilethrix, seen in the image below, is characterized by beaded hair and is fragile at the constricted sites. It occurs as an isolated condition or can occur in Menkes disease.
questions.learning: Trichothiodystrophy — The given clinical image of hair seen under polarising microscopy reveals tiger tail banding (alternating light and dark bands) characteristic of trichothiodystrophy.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A patient presented with unilateral nasal obstruction associated with watery nasal discharge and bleeding. A diagnosis of inverted papilloma is made. Which of the following is true about this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Benign and invasive

Inverted papilloma is a benign and invasive tumor.

Inverted papilloma (Ringertz tumor or transitional cell papilloma or Schneiderian papilloma) is a benign neoplasm of the non-olfactory mucosa of the nose (also called the Schneiderian membrane) and paranasal sinuses. The lateral wall of the nose in the middle meatus is the most common site of origin.

The hyperplastic papillomatous tissue grows into the stroma. It is common in the 4th to 7th decades of life with a male preponderance. Clinical features are unilateral nasal obstruction, nasal discharge, and epistaxis. It is almost always unilateral. It can invade sinuses or the orbit, resulting in proptosis, diplopia, and lacrimation.

An examination of the nose or endoscopy shows a polypoidal mass resembling simple nasal polyps. A computed tomography(CT) scan and/or magnetic resonance imaging(MRI) show the location and extent of the lesion.

MRI is used to differentiate associated secretions in the sinus from the actual tumor mass. A biopsy is essential for diagnosis.

Medial maxillectomy is the treatment of choice, done preferably via endoscopy. Malignancy has been observed in up to 15% of the cases.

Pearl PF1087: Inverted Papilloma

* Inverted papilloma is also known as transitional cell papilloma or Ringertz tumor or Schneiderian papilloma

* It is the most common benign tumor of the nasal cavity

* It is a premalignant condition with 10-15% chances of turning malignant

* Etiology: Human papilloma virus has been implicated in its etiology

* Origin: Arises from the lateral wall of the nose from the non-olfactory epithelium of nose

* Clinical features:

* More common in males

* The age group most commonly affected is 40-70 years

* Unilateral nasal obstruction, nasal discharge, and epistaxis are the main presenting symptoms

* It is a locally invasive tumor and can invade orbit and paranasal sinuses.

* Proptosis, diplopia, and lacrimation can result from orbital invasion

* Findings:

* It is seen as a pale polypoidal mass resembling a simple nasal polyp

* Investigations: A biopsy is needed for diagnosis

* Treatment: Medial maxillectomy via lateral rhinotomy or midfacial degloving approach

* Radiotherapy can lead to malignancy

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What ECG change is associated with the use of the anti-tubercular drug Bedaquiline?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. QT interval prolongation

Bedaquiline is associated with a prolonged QT interval.

Bedaquiline is a newer anti-TB drug used in MDR-TB. Bedaquiline is a bactericidal drug that belongs to diarylquinolines. It acts by inhibiting the enzyme ATP synthase in the Mycobacterium.

Bedaquiline is a diarylquinoline that targets the subunit c of the ATP synthase of M. tuberculosis. This leads to inhibition of the proton pump activity of the ATP synthase and causes a failure in the bacillary energy metabolism. It is largely deposited in tissues owing to its amphiphilicity. Resistance caused by mutations in efflux pumps and their regulators is also observed and is linked to the development of cross-resistance to clofazimine.

CYP3A4 is a major enzyme involved in the metabolism of bedaquiline.

Due to the high risk of QT prolongation, the FDA has issued a black box warning against the use of bedaquiline therefore having restricted use in patients with cardiac conduction abnormalities.

questions.text: A pregnant couple presented to the OPD with concerns about thalassemia in their baby due to a positive family history. Genetic studies revealed that both she and her husband are carriers. What is the probability that the child will have thalassemia major?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 25%

There is 25% probability that their child will have thalassemia major.

β-thalassemia occurs due to mutations causing an impaired synthesis of β-globin chains of hemoglobin (Hb), leading to anemia, hypoxia, and hemolysis. The mutations can be of two types:

* Absent β chain synthesis (β0)

* Reduced β chain synthesis (β+)

Being an autosomal recessive disease, disease occurs only when both alleles are defective. When only one is defective, they are called carriers or trait. Here as both the parents are carriers, their alleles will be β/β0 or β/β+ (1 β-thalassemia allele and 1 normal allele). As the clinical disease doesn't alter much based on it being β+ or β0, its safe to use use β+ to represent a thalassemia allele.

Thalassemia major means both alleles are mutated. And from the table, that can occur in one of the four ways possible. Hence the answer is 25%

Clinical syndromes of β-thalassemia depending on the genetic defect:

Major:

* Severe microcytic hypochromic anemia with target cells, basophilic stippling, and fragmented red cells (typical Hb: 3 to 6 g/dL), requiring regular blood transfusions

* Crewcut appearance of facial bones and skull (due to cortical bone erosion by expanding marrow and new bone formation)

* Speen, liver, and lymph node enlargement (due to extramedullary hematopoiesis)

Minor:

* More common

* Usually asymptomatic

* Mild microcytic hypochromic anemia with target cells and basophilic stippling (important to rule out iron deficiency anemia by serum iron studies)

* Mild erythroid hyperplasia in bone marrow

A third clinical syndrome of moderate severity is called β-thalassemia intermedia. The genotype in this type includes milder variants of β+/β+ or β0/β+ and does not require regular transfusions.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following statements is true?
options: In a population with low prevalence of the disease, positive result with a highly sensitive test means true positive
Sensitivity depends on prevalence of the disease
Positive predictive value depends on prevalence of disease
Specificity depends on prevalence of the disease
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Positive predictive value depends on prevalence of disease

The positive predictive value (PPV) of a screening test depends on the prevalence of the disease. The positive predictive value (PPV) of a test indicates the probability that a patient with a positive test result has actually contracted the disease i.e., the likelihood that a person with a positive test result truly has the disease.

If the prevalence of a disease in a population is high, the more accurate will be the positive predictive value. Therefore, in a population with a high prevalence of the disease, a positive result with a highly sensitive test means true positive. Example: Hypothyroidism is more prevalent in hilly areas than in coastal areas. If someone from a hilly area tests positive he is more likely to have the disease than someone who tests positive in a coastal area.

Likewise, if the prevalence decreases, the PPV will also become low. So in a population with a low prevalence of the disease, positive result with a highly sensitive test need not always mean true positive as it can produce an unacceptably high proportion of false positive results.

Predictive value is affected the most by prevalence. However, both sensitivity and specificity can change the predictive value.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: All are seen in Cystic fibrosis except:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Biliary atresia

Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by CFTR gene mutation leading to thick, viscous secretions affecting multiple organs.

• Gastrointestinal: meconium ileus in neonates, pancreatic insufficiency causing malabsorption
• Respiratory: recurrent infections, bronchiectasis, nasal polyps
• Hepatobiliary: can cause biliary cirrhosis but not biliary atresia
• Hematological: fat-soluble vitamin (vitamin K) deficiency → bleeding tendency

Why biliary atresia is not seen:

• Biliary atresia is a separate obstructive condition of the extrahepatic bile ducts, not related to CFTR dysfunction (bile duct obstruction is seen in CF, not atresia)

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 34-year-old female presented to the psychiatric OPD with low mood, loss of energy, loss of interest in pleasurable activities, decreased sleep, and appetite for the past 2 months. What is the most appropriate treatment to be started?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Fluoxetine

The clinical vignette point towards major depressive disorder. SSRIs like fluoxetine are the most appropriate treatment for major depressive disorder. SSRIs should be continued for 6-9 months after complete remission of symptoms in case of a single episode of depression.

The diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder are as follows:

A. Five or more of the following symptoms have been present during the same 2-week period. At least one of the symptoms is either depressed mood or loss of interest or pleasure.

* Depressed mood most of the day

* Markedly diminished interest or pleasure in activities (anhedonia)

* Significant weight loss when not dieting or weight gain, decrease or increase in appetite

* Insomnia or hypersomnia

* Psychomotor agitation or retardation

* Fatigue or loss of energy

* Feelings of worthlessness or excessive or inappropriate guilt

* Diminished ability to think or concentrate, or indecisiveness

* Recurrent thoughts of death, recurrent suicidal ideation

B. The symptoms cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning.

C. The episode is not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance or to another medical condition.

D. The occurrence of the major depressive episode is not better explained by schizoaffective disorder, schizophrenia, schizophreniform disorder, delusional disorder, or other specified and unspecified schizophrenia spectrum and other psychotic disorders.

E. There has never been a manic episode or a hypomanic episode.

Treatment of depression according to NICE guidelines:

* In recent‐onset, mild depression, cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is preferred and antidepressants are not recommended.

* Antidepressants (SSRIs) are recommended for the treatment of moderate to severe depression and for dysthymia along with CBT.

* For treatment‐resistant depression, recommended strategies include augmentation with lithium or an antipsychotic or the addition of a second antidepressant.

* The use of electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is supported in severe and treatment-resistant depression.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient with chronic renal failure develops progressive cognitive impairment and behavioral changes during the course of treatment, raising suspicion of dialysis dementia. In this condition, which type of amyloid deposition is most commonly found in the cerebral cortex?
questions.explanation: Dialysis dementia, also referred to as dialysis-related amyloidosis, occurs in patients undergoing long-term dialysis due to end-stage renal disease. In this condition, beta-2 microglobulin—a protein that is normally filtered and eliminated by healthy kidneys—accumulates in the bloodstream because of impaired renal function. With prolonged elevation, beta-2 microglobulin deposits as amyloid in various tissues, including the cerebral cortex, contributing to cognitive impairment and neurological symptoms seen in dialysis dementia. Reasons to Rule Out Other Options (B) Amyloid beta microglobulin: Incorrect terminology. The correct term is beta-2 microglobulin, not “amyloid beta microglobulin.” (C) Amyloid transthyretin: Seen in transthyretin amyloidosis, a separate systemic condition affecting nerves and heart, not dialysis dementia. (D) Amyloid beta: Associated with Alzheimer’s disease, where it forms plaques in the brain, and is not related to dialysis-associated amyloid deposition

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: eFAST is least helpful in diagnosing which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Retroperitoneal hematoma

Among the given options, eFAST (focussed assessment with sonography in trauma) is the least useful in diagnosing retroperitoneal hematoma as the sensitivity of ultrasound for the detection of retroperitoneal hematomas is extremely poor.

Computed Tomography (CT Scan) is the investigation of choice for retroperitoneal injury, but it can only be done in a hemodynamically stable patient.

FAST stands for Focussed Assessment with Sonography for Trauma. It is a rapid, non-invasive bedside test for detecting free fluid using sonography used to assess patients for potential thoracoabdominal injuries.

Technique:

• The patient is placed in a supine position and the following regions are scanned:

• Subxiphoid transverse view: assess for pericardial effusion and left lobe liver injuries
• Longitudinal view of the right upper quadrant: assess for right liver injuries, right kidney injury, and Morison pouch
• Longitudinal view of the left upper quadrant: assess for splenic injury and left kidney injury
• Transverse and longitudinal views of the suprapubic region: assess the bladder and pouch of Douglas

eFAST stands for extended FAST and incorporates left and right thoracic views to assess for pneumothorax and haemothorax.

Limitations of eFAST are:

1. Operator-dependent
2. Bowel gas and subcutaneous air distort images.
3. Can miss diaphragm, bowel, and pancreatic injuries
4. Unreliable for assessment of the retroperitoneum
5. Cannot reliably exclude injury in penetrating trauma
6. May need repeating or supplementing with other investigations

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Consider the following statements regarding Wernicke’s encephalopathy: I. It is caused by niacin deficiency. II. It is often seen in alcoholics. III. Ophthalmoplegia, polyneuritis and ataxia are some of its characteristic features. IV. It occurs occasionally in people who fast. Which of the statements given above are correct?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. II, III and IV

Wernicke’s encephalopathy is an acute neurological emergency caused by thiamine (Vitamin B₁) deficiency. It is most commonly seen in chronic alcoholics, but can also occur in prolonged fasting, starvation, hyperemesis gravidarum, and malnutrition. Early recognition and prompt intravenous thiamine administration are essential to prevent irreversible neurological damage.

• Cause: Thiamine (Vitamin B₁) deficiency, not niacin deficiency.
• Commonly associated with: Chronic alcoholism, prolonged fasting, starvation, hyperemesis gravidarum, bariatric surgery, prolonged TPN without thiamine.
• Classic triad:

• Confusion
• Ophthalmoplegia/Nystagmus
• Ataxia

• Peripheral neuropathy (polyneuritis) may also be present.
• Treatment: IV thiamine before glucose administration.
• Untreated cases may progress to Korsakoff syndrome, characterized by memory impairment, confabulation, and anterograde amnesia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The ECG of a patient who presented to the ER is as given below. The patient was already given a carotid massage and IV Adenosine but the BP is currently 60/30 mm Hg. What is the next best step of management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Synchronised cardioversion

The given ECG showing narrow QRS complex (<0.12 s) tachycardia with absent P wave is suggestive of paroxysmal ventricular tachycardia (PSVT). The next best step in the management of a patient with unstable vitals (systolic blood pressure < 90 mm Hg) is synchronized cardioversion.

Synchronized cardioversion is the treatment of choice in unstable PSVT patients, in which shocks are delivered with the defibrillator/monitor in synchronized mode with an initial energy level of 100J. Synchronization times the delivery so that it is given at the peak of the QRS complex.

If the shock occurs in the ST segment or the T wave (unsynchronized), it can precipitate a more serious arrhythmia such as ventricular fibrillation.

Synchronized cardioversion
Defibrillation

Used in unstable PSVT, atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation, and ventricular tachycardia with a pulse

Used in ventricular tachycardia without pulse and ventricular fibrillation.

Shock is delivered in sync with the R wave (in absolute refractory period)
Shock is delivered at any time during the cardiac cycle.

Monophasic: 100-200 J

Biphasic: 50-100 J

Monophasic: 360 J

Biphasic:120-200 J

Other options:

Option A: In the absence of hemodynamic instability, a repeat dose of injection adenosine (maximum of 12mg) could be attempted.
Option B: IV Amiodarone is rarely used in the acute management of PSVT. Instead, it is used as an alternative to calcium channel blockers in chronic suppressive therapy.
Option D: Defibrillation is only done for ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child is brought to the clinic with a two-week history of poor feeding and increased irritability. The family history is significant for tuberculosis, as the patient’s sister is currently receiving treatment for TB. In view of the clinical suspicion, a lumbar puncture is performed for further evaluation. Which cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) finding would be most characteristic of the suspected condition?
options: Neutrophils, low sugar and low protein
Neutrophils, low sugar and high protein
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms (irritability, poor feeding) combined with a strong positive contact history of tuberculosis suggest tuberculous meningitis (TBM). The pathognomonic CSF profile for TBM is lymphocytosis (predominance of lymphocytes), markedly low sugar (hypoglycorrhachia), and very high protein. Acute bacterial meningitis would show a predominance of neutrophils (Options C and D) and low sugar. Viral meningitis typically shows lymphocytosis but with normal sugar levels. High sugar (Option B) is not characteristic of any infectious meningitis. TBM results from the rupture of a subependymal tubercle into the subarachnoid space, leading to a chronic inflammatory response that thickens the basal meninges. This often results in cranial nerve palsies and hydrocephalus. Early diagnosis via LP is life-saving, as the mortality and long-term neurological morbidity associated with untreated TBM are extremely high

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient sustains a road traffic accident and has a normal non-contrast CT scan of the head at admission. After several days in the ICU, the patient deteriorates into coma and subsequently dies. Brain biopsy reveals multiple punctate hemorrhages. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Diffuse axonal injury (DAI) is a severe primary brain injury caused by shearing forces during high-velocity trauma, such as a road traffic accident. These forces disrupt axons throughout the white matter, brainstem, and corpus callosum. A classic feature of DAI is that initial Non-Contrast CT (NCCT) scans are often normal or show only minute, subtle abnormalities. Diagnosis is frequently clinical, based on a prolonged coma without a lucid interval, or confirmed via MRI. Histopathology reveals multiple punctate, petechial hemorrhages within deep white matter tracts. Ischemic injury (Option A) typically presents with localized territorial infarcts. Intraventricular bleeding (Option C) and subdural hemorrhage (Option D) would be clearly visible on the initial CT as hyperdense blood collections within the ventricles or as a crescent-shaped mass, respectively. Thus, the normal CT followed by punctate hemorrhages on biopsy is pathognomonic for DAI
questions.learning: Diffuse axonal injury (DAI) is a severe primary brain injury caused by shearing forces during high-velocity trauma, such as a road traffic accident. These forces disrupt axons throughout the white matter, brainstem, and corpus callosum.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In which type of cataract surgery is suturing with 10-0 nylon commonly performed?
questions.explanation: In Extracapsular Cataract Extraction (ECCE), a relatively large limbal incision (approximately 8–10 mm) is made to remove the lens nucleus in one piece. Because of the size of this incision, multiple interrupted or continuous sutures—typically using fine 10-0 nylon—are mandatory to ensure a watertight closure and prevent complications like iris prolapse or endophthalmitis. Phacoemulsification (Option A) utilizes a very small incision (2.2–3.0 mm) that is typically "self-sealing" and requires no sutures. Manual Small Incision Cataract Surgery (MSICS) (Option D) also uses a self-sealing tunnel incision (usually 6 mm) that generally does not require suturing. ICCE (Option C) is an older technique where the entire lens and capsule are removed through a large incision, also requiring sutures, but it is rarely performed today compared to ECCE. While Phaco is the global gold standard, ECCE remains an important technique for extremely hard (black or brown) cataracts where ultrasound energy may be insufficient or unsafe
questions.learning: In Extracapsular Cataract Extraction (ECCE), a relatively large limbal incision (approximately 8–10 mm) is made to remove the lens nucleus in one piece.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 25-year-old woman presents in early pregnancy with occasional spotting. The diagnosis of missed abortion is made when?
options: No cardiac activity at a CRL > 7mm
No cardiac activity at a CRL < 7mm
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. No cardiac activity at a CRL > 7mm

Missed abortion is diagnosed when no cardiac activity is seen at a CRL greater than 7 mm.

In a normal intrauterine pregnancy, a gestational sac is visible on TVS by 4.5-5 weeks of LMP, the yolk sac appears at around 5.5 weeks, and by 6 weeks an embryo can be seen adjacent to the yolk sac. Cardiac activity of the embryo is usually detected on TVS at about 6–6.5 weeks.

A mean gestational sac diameter of ≥25 mm and a CRL of ≥7 mm are considered critical cut-off values, beyond which the absence of the expected structures is regarded as abnormal. Hence, missed abortion should be suspected if, on USG

* CRL ≥7 mm, and no cardiac activity is recorded (CRL-crown rump length)

* MSD ≥25 mm, and no embryo is seen (MSD-mean sac diameter)

Medical management can be performed with prostaglandin E1(misoprostol) or oxytocin. Surgical management in the form of dilatation and curettage can be performed.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 22-year-old student presented with high-grade fever, and purpuric rash as shown in the image below. CSF sample showed gram-negative diplococci. Which of the following is the most likely aetiology?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Neisseria meningitidis

This patient has a high-grade fever and is a student, so he presumably spends a lot of time in crowded areas. The above image shows a purpuric rash. This patient's features are seen in meningococcemia caused by Neisseria meningitidis, which are gram-negative diplococci.

The organism enters the body through the nasopharynx by attaching to the epithelial cells with the help of pili. From the nasopharynx, they enter the bloodstream producing bacteremia, and the symptoms may resemble upper respiratory tract infection.

Fulminant meningococcemia is the severe form, where the patient presents with high-grade fever and hemorrhagic rash. There is thrombosis of several small blood vessels in various organs with perivascular infiltration and petechial hemorrhages. Some patients with fulminant meningococcemia may also develop disseminated intravascular coagulation, and circulatory collapse, a condition known as Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Thrombosis is initiated by:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Endothelial injury

Thrombosis is initiated by endothelial injury.

Thrombosis is is the formation of a blood clot inside a blood vessel, obstructing the flow of blood through the circulatory system.

Three primary abnormalities, often referred to as Virchow triad, are known to induce thrombosis. They include:

• Endothelial injury - most important factor
• Stasis or turbulent blood flow
• Hypercoagulability of the blood

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following diseases are covered under the scheme represented by the logo shown below?
questions.explanation: The logo displayed belongs to the National Programme for Prevention and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases and Stroke (NPCDCS). This program was launched by the Indian government to address the rising burden of non-communicable diseases (NCDs). The scheme specifically focuses on four major diseases: Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases (CVD), and Stroke. Options A, B, and D are incorrect because they include Bronchial Asthma or Hypertension as primary acronym components, although those conditions may be managed under related health initiatives. The NPCDCS aims to provide health promotion, early diagnosis, and management of these four major NCDs through infrastructure development and manpower training at various levels of the healthcare system. The slogan "Health In Your Hands" emphasizes personal and community-level prevention efforts. This program is a critical component of India’s public health strategy to reduce premature mortality from chronic, lifestyle-related conditions through structured population-based screening and care
